summary_comment:
Originally part of the greater Darwen North Prospect, there remains to the east a small independent structural closure. This is now referred to as the 'Darwen NE Lead'. 
It is very small, has no amplitude support, and has a GIIP range of just 0. - 1.1 - 1.1 - 1.6bcf (P90 - P50 - mean - P10). 
Geological chance of success is estimated at 21%.

Stratigraphic trap in Lower Cretaceous Coracle Sandstone Member, sealed by Hauterivean mudstones. Reservoir facies are deep-sea turbidites sourced from the north-west. Top and lateral/base seal provided by combination of Hauterivean mudstones and some pinchout against the BCU. Basin modelling suggests prospect is underlain by hydrocarbon generating Mid-Jurassic, Late Jurassic and Devonian intervals. Migration via faulting likely to have taken place during the Early Cretacoues/Tertiary. Amplitude response similar to that seen on Norfolk prospect (cp12_16_7). No parameters provided - entered cf. 'Norfolk' prospect.

The Valanginian prospect is defined by an isopach thick between Top Valanginian and Top Berriasian. Reservoir is envisaged to pinch out onto the BCU to the northwest and west, with dip closure to the east and south. Reservoir expected to consist of interbedded sands, silts and shales  of Valanginianage (Punt Sandstone Member). Local wells show relatively low NTG, however prospect is updip and may be closer to sediment source. Lateral/base seal provided by KCF, top seal provided by transgressive muds at top of Valanginian interval. No parameters provided - entered cf. Norfolk prospect (cp12_16_7).

Prospect in Alness sands in fault block closure adjacent to the Sigma discovery. Beatrice upside in Sigma South Beatrice prospect. Alness sands have high porosity but low permeability because of clay matrix and quartz cement.

Prospect in Beatrice sands in fault block closure adjacent to the Sigma discovery. Main reservoir interval (Alness) entered as Sigma South Alness prospect. Beatrice sands possibly in communication with Alness sands, or structure may not be filled to spill.

Complicated series of tilted fault blocks set up against a major easterly-dipping normal fault. Sherwood and Carboniferous reservoir levels. Structurally on trend with Ballinlea-1 oil discovery. Lead extends beneath the island of Rathlin - no polygon provided. No risking provided.
Tertiary leads (Cranberry, Lemonade and Ginger) are 3-way stratigraphic traps adjacent to the basin bounding fault.

Whilst comparable to the other Lower Cretaceous leads in terms of play type, the Cardamom and Vesper leads are deeper and located in the more distal hyper-extended part of the basin, prone to intrusives (Figure 5.20). The intrusions (seen on seismic as very strong, bright reflectors that may cross cut stratigraphy) add additional trap seal risk for both leads. Trap closure is poorly resolved on the current 2-D dataset.

The srt97_98_u98b 3-D dataset was screened using frequency decomposition and colour blending in GeoTeric. Regionally, this Tertiary interval appears to be predominately slope/bypass and likely mud/shale prone, with feeder systems of varying width and sinuosity seen. Mint is clearly imaged on the GeoTeric volume as a distributive fan with a well resolved feeder system (Figure 5.21) and on the NNE-SSW seismic section in Figure 5.22.

Seismic images across the Sloe lead can be seen in Figure 5.6 (NW-SE orientated seismic section across Juniper, Orris and Sloe), Figure 5.11 (south-north) and in Figure 5.17 below. The Lower Cretaceous clastic reservoir and potential source rock appear relatively thin in the precursor rift section, and trap closure is poorly resolved on the current 2-D dataset. The crest of the Sloe structure is at 4,070 m TVDSS, with a water depth of 870 m.

The Damson lead can be seen in Figure 5.16 (SW-NE) and in Figure 5.18 (NW-S seismic line through Damson and Angelica leads) below. As with the more inboard leads, the Lower Cretaceous clastic reservoir is interpreted to be charged by Jurassic Type II marine source rocks and preserved within a Jurassic 'back-basin', in a low-side fault dependent trap with a sub-unconformity top seal. The crest of the Damson structure is at 4,540 m TVDSS, with a water depth of 840 m.

Elderflower is the sole Upper Cretaceous lead, mapped on the PGS Rockall 98 3-D, and interpreted as a possible deepwater distributive lobe. On seismic, truncations can be seen beneath, with onlap onto the top of the greater package; the internal geometry of the package has relatively parallel stratigraphy (Figure 5.22). The absence of bidirectional dip and compensational stacking reduces confidence in the interpretation but, given the depth and data quality issues, does not rule it out.

The Juniper lead is part of the most proximal terrace of the south eastern UK Rockall Trough, immediately adjacent to the main basin-bounding fault. This greater terrace area is approximately 220 km2, with the Juniper lead in the north, being about 70 km2. This is one of the shallowest leads in the inventory, located in approximately 140 m of water, with the crest around 2,400 m below mudline.
Juniper is interpreted as a Lower Cretaceous clastic reservoir, charged by Jurassic marine (Type II) source rocks and preserved within a Jurassic ‘back-basin’ (Figure 5.1). As the actual top reservoir pick in this back-basin is unresolved, trap configuration may be described as either a low-side fault dependent trap (likely when reservoir is deeper, with the ultimate updip seal against the basin bounding fault) or as a sub-unconformity trap (if top reservoir is shallower and therefore truncated by the Albo-Aptian unconformity before reaching the basin margin).

The Orris lead can be seen in Figure 5.6 (NW-SE orientated seismic section across Juniper and Orris), below in Figure 5.16 (on the edge of the Orris) and also in Figure 5.17. Postulated Lower Cretaceous stratigraphy can be seen in the pre-cursor back-basin below the Albo-Aptian unconformity. The crest of the Orris structure is at 3,640 m TVDSS, with a water depth of 735 m.

Trap closure is poorly resolved on the current 2-D dataset.
Tertiary leads (Cranberry, Lemonade and Ginger) are 3-way stratigraphic traps adjacent to the basin bounding fault.

Lemongrass is a relatively small (25 km2) lead, inboard of the basement high (Figure 5.18), in a water depth of ~800 m and shown in Figure 5.19 (NW-SE seismic line) below. The Lower Cretaceous clastic reservoir is expected to be preserved within a Jurassic 'back-basin' (poorly defined on current data), charged by a Jurassic Type II marine source rock, with a sub-unconformity top seal. The crest of the Lemongrass structure is at 3,200 m TVDSS.

However, Tonic has a hard top (positive reflection coefficient) and dims with offset on OGA line L03. This is counter to the modelled response of a hydrocarbon bearing sandstone which significantly increases the prospect risk. Lemon is one of the large (100-400 km2) north-south trending, basement highs along this margin. The faults defining the Lemon lead are relatively well imaged and closure is currently interpreted to be in granitic basement. With a depth to crest of 2,970 m and in 1,650 m of water, this lead has a wide range of success case volumes that reflect the uncertainties.

Quince is interpreted as a sub-unconformity rotated fault block, with Lower Cretaceous clastic reservoir and Jurassic type II marine source rocks preserved within the Jurassic ‘back-basin’.
Like Juniper, the Quince lead is also located within the most proximal terrace, immediately adjacent to the main basin bounding fault (Figure 5.2). The western extent of Quince is defined by the basement high (Lemon - fractured basement lead). To the north, the basement high and basin bounding fault converge, restricting the northernmost limit of the lead. To the south the greater fault trend/terrace extends along the basin margin. At ~2,200 m submud, Quince is at similar depths below mudline to Juniper but in greater water depths of ~1,600 m.

The Rufio prospect (Appendix 2:2) is comprised within an overall 4-way closure at the Upper Jurassic Piper Formation level with the reservoir pinching out towards the crest. 
The Rufio prospect is situated relatively far from the South Viking Graben kitchen area and with two near-by wells (15/10-1 and 16/06b- 6) being dry, migration is the key risk to the prospect. 
Reservoir presence is considered moderately risky, with seismic mapping and nearby-by wells indicating a thin reservoir.

The Octopus prospect is a structurally defined trap with dip closure towards the east. 
The key risk to the prospect is trap-seal along the down-faulted northern prospect boundary. The fault throw is limited and the down-faulted reservoir is juxtaposed against Devonian strata. The reservoir is assigned a moderate risk as it likely to be thin and may pinch out against the dip slope of the fault defining the southern prospect boundary. The migration distance from the kitchen is more 
than 10km and migration into the prospect would require the Estella South trap to fail.

The Crocodile prospect is a combined stratigraphic pinch-out and structural down-faulted trap. The key risk to the prospect is trap-seal due to poorly defined updip stratigraphic pinch-out. 
Migration poses another significant risk to the prospect due to the long migration distance from the South Viking Graben to the east. The prospect outline has been significantly reduced compared to the time of access following the updated mapping and removal of the AVO dependency.

They carry a significant risk on reservoir as they are in an area that might have been exposed during time of deposition or eroded by the BCU. Fairy Dust is a Upper Jurassic 4-way closure in between Hook and the GB 15/14a-3 well. The main risk is reservoir.

At the time of application the Skylights prospect was only partly covered by 3D seismic data with the western prospect edge being defined on a sparse 2D seismic grid. Following the purchase of the PGS14003 the prospect is now fully covered by 3D seismic data. The Skylights prospect is a down-faulted 3-way trap bounded by faults towards the west and south. Lateral trap-seal poses the key risk to the prospect. The downdip closure towards the east has been revised to take out the AVO dependency, resulting in a decrease in prospect area. The proximity to Pip and the 15/14a- 3 well, in which the Piper Formation sands are present, means reservoir risk is low. 
Shows in 15/14a -3 were most likely sourced from the Wytch Ground Graben from the west. The migration risk is high regardless of which kitchen is invoked. Migration to Skylights from the west and southwest (Wytch Ground Graben) seems unlikely as it would require downdip migration from the crest of the Fladen Ground Spur structure and any migration through the 15/14a- 3 well location would require migration across the fault invoked as the updip sealing element. Migration from the South Viking Graben to the east seems highly unlikely due to the migration distance.

Magwitch (aka Smee) was one of the key prospects in the licence at the time of application. Like the neighbouring Pip prospect, the Magwitch prospect outline relied heavily on AVO, with the observed anomaly allowing for a number of smaller closures to be combined into one accumulation. 
Considering the Pip well result and removal of the AVO dependency in the prospect definition, the prospect has been reduced to a small 4-way closure in the southwestern corner of the original outline. It is located just to the west of the Smee prospect on the down-faulted side of the pronounced Hook-Smee E-W striking fault. The AVO attributes support presence of hydrocarbons. The main prospect risk for the Hook prospect is trap seal and migration.

Originally defined as a prospect, Curly has been redefined as a cluster of leads following the drilling of the Tiger Lily well and update of the licence velocity model.
The prospect was defined as a subtle 4-way closure at the Base Cretaceous Unconformity with limited volume potential and high risk. The prospect was proposed to have an Upper Jurassic Piper Fm reservoir, charged from mature Kimmeridge Clay Formation in the South Viking Graben to the east and sealed by Cretaceous calcareous claystones and chalk. Updated mapping and post-drill depth conversion of the Curly prospect, and a review of risk, in light of semi-regional studies, indicate that the prospect is likely to be broken into several smaller closures and at best offers a low volume, high risk opportunity with low resource density. Given the Tiger Lily well outcome, the Curly cluster is of no further interest to the partnership.

summary_comment:
The Neverland prospect is located to the south of the Hook Smee SW trending fault. It is a down-faulted structural trap with a Tertiary reservoir, and is characterized by a strong amplitude anomaly.
Stacked reservoir target in the Late Palaeocene-Early Eocene.

The Magwitch South lead (aka Smee South) is a small 4-way closure situated immediately east of the original Magwitch polygon outline. 
In light of the Pip well migration is the key risk to the lead, with reservoir risk being moderate and seal risk being low.

Comet prospect is an amplitude driven stratigraphic trap. The trap is purely stratigraphic and facies controlled. The top, bottom and lateral seals are all marine shales which encase a glacial outwash siltstone. Analagous to the Aviat Field. Expecting biogenic gas (99.5% C1).

The Abbotsford prospect is a three way structural closure of the Hugin Sandstones. The trap is formed by the combination of a top seal provided by the Upper Jurassic shales and a fault related lateral seal formed by the juxtaposition of the Hugin Sandstones against clays of the Upper Jurassic sequence. Company recoverable reserves given only as oil/gas reserves (mmboe).

During drilling of the Tiger Lily well the Paleozoic succession was found to be extremely tight with ROP <3m/hr and the Paleozoic succession is interpreted as granitic basement. Unlike the Cairngorm discovery wells, no losses were observed in the Tiger Lily well and the Paleozoic succession penetrated in the well is believed to be tight with no flow potential. Shows were observed to a depth of 2420m TVDss, 25m shallow to the likely OWC observed in the Cairngorm structure. Whilst the Tiger Lily Paleozoic penetrated at the well location does not constitute a reservoir rock it seems likely that it is part of the Cairngorm granitic complex and that the encountered shows could relate to a mega-closure at OWC level. This would assume a working lateral seal, as well as competent top seal, which is unproven by the well. The extent of the Cairngorm complex is uncertain, albeit somewhat constrained by the presence of Devonian sub-crop in the near-by 16/02a- 2 well and the seismic character at Top Paleozoic level. An attempt to quantify the in-place volume in a potential Tiger Lily granite segment (Figure 8 and Appendix C) has been made, yielding a potential, but highly uncertain, mean in-place volume of approximately 128 mmbbls. The apparent lack of fractures in the Tiger Lily basement suggests a significant risk on producibility and hence low recovery factor. The Tiger Lily well went straight from Kimmeridge Clay Formation into very hard granitic basement with low ROP (~3m/hr). Sampling in the granite is limited to cuttings, based on which there is no evidence to suggest the presence of a conglomerate or significant weather zone at Top Paleozoic level.

Enroll is a four-way dip closure mapped at BCU level on the SW flank of the Fladen Ground Spur, immediately up-dip of well 16/26- 1A. Anticipated reservoir is U. Jurassic Glamis-type sands. Well 16/26- 1A encountered 108ft net sand of U. Jurassic (Volgian) age with oil shows. Main risk is reservoir presence. P50 recoverable of 6.6 mmboe stated. No other parameters provided.

Edzell prospect is a 3-way dip closure mapped at BCU level on the SE flank of the Fladen Ground Spur. Anticipated reservoir is U. Jurassic Glamis sandstones. Prospect is located at the tip of the South Viking Graben, where the graben bounding fault terminates. The preferred interpretation is that shallow marine sandstones were deposited via a relay ramp in the bounding fault, rather than Brae-type conglomerates deposited against a steep fault scarp. Main risks are reservoir presence (as distribution of U. Jurassic is irregular) and trap effectiveness. P50 recoverable of 4.7mmboe stated, but no other parameters provided.

The TR1 prospect is a Triassic Skagerrak sandstone onlapping the Maureen salt dome in the northwest area of the structure underlying the JR1 prospect. Well 16/29-3 also encountered good porosity Skagerrak sands (below 10630ft), with shows, although they were water bearing, testing 2000 bwpd from DST #2. The updip seal for the TR1 prospect is the same significant fault that is mapped to trap the stratigraphically younger Jurassic Hugin sands of the JR1 prospect.

summary_comment:
The Estella South (aka Tinker Bell South) prospect is a structural-stratigraphic trap situated along the eastern edge of the Fladen Ground Spur. At the time of application, the definition of the prospect outline relied heavily on the AVO attribute and an apparent depth conformancetowards the east. 
Trap-seal was, and is, the key risk to the Estella South prospect as the updip stratigraphic pinch-out of the reservoir sand can no longer be mapped with confidence and is further 
compromised by the presence of Piper Formation sandstone in the updip 15/10- 1 well. The updip sealing potential may benefit from the presence of small-scale faulting, however, these faults cannot be mapped in detail and appear unlikely to form a continuous barrier. 
A revised prospect outline has been defined assuming the presence of an updip structural-stratigraphic seal, albeit considered extremely risky, and dip closure towards the east. The presence of Piper Formation sandstone within the redefined prospect outline is considered relatively low risk. However, the presence of Piper Formation sandstone deposits forming a continuous carrier bed downdip of the prospect is not supported by the sand-flag attribute, nor the downdip 16/6a- 1 well and hence effective migration into the prospect is very risky.
North Star is a Tertiary lead and is an amplitude bright south of the Dalmore discovery. There is a high risk on reservoir presence for this lead as the amplitude bright could be cemented sandstone.

Duffield T38 is a subtle 4-way dip closure identified below Base of Balder, in the T38 prograding clinoforms. The trap formation is related to Neogene inversion. Top seal relies on a basal T45 flooding event (seen in Balder in 204/17-1). Despite the absence of HC shows in 204/17-1 or 204/22-2 wells at this level, presence of gas chimneys above indicates migration either along the faults or vertically. Reservoir is expected to represent clinoform topset to foreset environment, represented by shoreface and outer shelf storm deposits, which are preserved in a sand-rich interval in 201/22-2, getting more heterolithic towards 204/17-1. Stratigraphic interval within closure is dim, which may be  a reflection of shallow gas above masking true amplitudes. Locally, however, the dim spot is conformable to structure. Top seal is the main risk for the prospect.

Duffield T36 is a subtle 4-way dip closure with a fault bounded upside with a reservoir in the  'Kintail' and 'Cuillin? turbidite aprons  of T36 ? T35 age.  The turbidite deposits are amalgamated at this location and therefore presence of an intra-formational seal is unlikely. An analogous 204/19-3A 'Cuillin' well penetrated 42m net T36 reservoir beneath the Kettla Tuff with an 8m oil column. Nearby 204/18-1 and 204/22-2 had shows at T35 level. Charge is assumed via underlying and/or bounding faults, and possibly also laterally within the sequence. The top seal is provided by Kettla Tuff or late T36/T38 mudstones. Stratigraphically equivalent turbidite sandstones found in 204/17-1 and 204/22-2 were silty and often thin-bedded, however, seismic attributes indicate more axial environment for the prospect. The closure is mainly seismically dim, but lithological variation within Kettla tuff masks potential fluid expression. Seal is the main risk.

Chatsworth and Cruachan are four-way dip closures, both carry significant seal risk due to
faulting and possible pressure breach due to sill emplacement.

Cruachan T40 is a subtle structural four-way dip closure. Top seal relies on a basal T45 flooding event (204/18-1 drilled shales and coals at the base Balder). A fluvial to paralic reservoir sequence is expected, based on a regional mapping of an incised valley and wells which typically found 70-160m sand-rich T40 sequences. The underlying muddy foresets of the T38 clinoforms might have hindered charge migration into the structure, as indicated by absence of shows in T50-T38 levels of 204/18-1. However, the deep seated faults underneath likely acted as a charge conduit, judging by gas clouds above the crest of the structure.  These may, on the other hand, indicate top seal breach, or partial leakage of gas across the T40/Balder boundary. No amplitude conformance with structure or other DHIs were observed. Amplitude dimming occurs below the gas clouds. Top seal is the main risk for the prospect, and because of its shallow crest, there is a risk of biodegradation if oil is encountered.

name_others: cp204_18_4 Fleet A  REL02167 Fleet West REL01670 Fleet A
summary_comment: A combination trap defined by a T35 canyon fill and an updip fault offset, separating it from a dry well 204/23-1. Several faults offset the reservoir interval, but reservoir self-juxtaposition is likely. The trap is defined by a fault with the largest throw. The top seal is provided by a thin shale developed above T35 sandy sequence. Unlike the good-quality T36 reservoir in the updip 204/23-1 well, T35 is a cemented conglomerate there, likely causing the very strong amplitude with a hard leading edge. This amplitude response remains unchanged along the extent of prospect. Brightening is also present at the soft loops below the hard top, suggesting development of reservoir quality sand below a hard abandonment surface. Downdip part of the closure is relatively dim. Charge is expected via deep faults intersecting the channel. Gas chimneys are present both downdip and updip in the overburden. Main risk is the top seal erosion by overlying T36 channels and updip fault seal integrity.

name_others: cp204_18_5 Fleet B and C  REL02168 Fleet East REL01671 Fleet B and C
summary_comment:
Fleet East is a combination structural-stratigraphic trap in the  'Kintail' and 'Cuillin' turbidite aprons  of T36  T35 age, onlapping truncated older stratigraphy on the Westray ridge. An analogous 204/19-3A 'Cuillin' well penetrated 42m net T36 reservoir beneath the Kettla Tuff with an 8m oil column. 
There are no T36 successes in the Kintail wedge, the most recent wells include 204/18-2b, 13-1, 14-2 and 18-1. 
The trap is defined by an incision/lateral pinchout of the late T36 channel beneath the T36 Tuff, and an E-W fault offset, which separates the prospect from the dry 204/23-1 well updip. The top seal is provided by Kettla Tuff or late T36 mudstones. 
Good quality reservoir sandstones were found in 204/23-1(S) and 204/14-2 (N). Charge is assumed via underlying and/or bounding faults. 
There is a brightspot across the trap, but lithological variation masks the potential fluid expression. Locally there are hints of a flatspot. An AVO anomaly of variable character has been observed.

A structural/stratigraphic trap defined by the thinning and pinchout of the T10 basin floor turbidite fans onto the Westray ridge , assisted by the offset along two intersecting fault trends (NE-SW and E-W). 
Dip closure is implied by the presence of a structural nose plunging to the NW at T10 sequence boundary. Lateral and up-dip seal for the T10 relies on fault seal juxtaposition against presumably mud-prone Upper Cretaceous. Top seal is provided by a significant shale drape interpreted below the T20 sequence in  the 204/18-1 well. 
Based on the analogy with other T10 penetrations in the area (204/22-2, 204/16-1 and 6004/16-1z), porosity in the range of 10%-15% with permeability from 5-200mD can be expected. 
The main risk is seal and trap definition. Reservoir effectiveness and migration are also issues, but boundary faults are deep seated and igneous dykes may also act as conduits.  
No DHI support, but dimming approximately fitting to contours exists over the crest of the structure.

name_others: cp204_18_6 Macdui  REL02165 Macdui Basement REL01672 Macdui
summary_comment: MacDui is a rotated fault block forming a 4 way closure filled with an opaque seismic pack of pre-rift stratigraphy.  The current assumption informed by nearby wells is that it contains Triassic sediments that have been draped by a KCF and Cretaceous sequence. Column height is likely top-seal constrained with concerns around presence of seal and effectiveness of seal at the crest.  Assuming the top seal is effective, the column would exist within an unknown arrangement of Foula and Otter Bank sediment.  Regional work shows a correlatio between lithostratigraphy and rock quality with the productive rock existing within the Otter Bank. Based on basin modelling the prospect is expected to be gas filled and it is lily that the degradation in rock quality due to depth of burial will result in a dependency between phase discovered and chance of developability. Alternatively the prospect could be Clair Group however the current well interpretation and seismic data do not support this.

name_others: cp204_18_11 Moussa  cp204_18_3 Cruachan  REL01669 Cruachan
summary_comment: Cruachan T32 is an subtle-relief four-way dip closure identified at the top of the T32 sequence. Its crest is approximately coincidental with that of the shallower T38 & T40 closures, indicating trap formation related to Neogene inversion. T32 represents the uppermost sequence of a very sand-rich, 100s m thick amalgamated succession without significant muddy drapes that could provide seal (as seen in 204/18-1, 18-2b, 13-1, 17-1).  Elsewhere, T32 is overlain by a channelized T34 fan, which appears to bypass the area, allowing for the development of a potentially working seal below base of T35.  Presence of gas chimneys above the structure may indicate migration either along a fault or vertically. Reservoir is expected to be a very sand-rich basin-floor turbidite fan system (lack of heterogeneity indicated by low amplitude seismic facies).  Stratigraphic interval is very dim in the closure and no DHIs were observed. Top seal and charge migration are the main risks for the lead.

Sgurr nan Gillean is a fault dip stratigraphic combination trap in an embayment to the West of the Westray Ridge.  It is filled with a Lower Cretaceous stripy seismic package. 
The trap is reliant on faults that seal and, in the larger cases, a stratigraphic edge.  Seals are regarded as the critical risk as shows are seen in the overburden. When mapped the stripy response has a fan like shape, which can be seen clearly on SNA extractions, this appears to be sourcing from the south and entering the embayment at a saddle point between the Westray Ridge and the Macdui structure. 
The prospect is down dip and across a fault from the 204/19-1 well which penetrates the same stripy seismic package and encounters a high NtG Lower Cretaceous section.  This section was cored and has good properties for the depth (15% poro & circa 200 mD), sedimentology suggests a sub-marine flow and is very well sorted. Charge appears to have reached the well and leaked into the overburden; the key risk is seal.

A combination trap consisting of a stratigraphic pinchout of slope channels and a lateral/updip fault offset. The closure is identified at the top of the lower part of T38 sequence, in a succession interpreted as toeset turbidite aprons  at the base of prograding clinoforms. Nearby 204/13-1 (Tornado) discovery encountered gas in good quality sands in the same setting, in a slightly younger T38 clinoform. Lower T38 sands were also present in 204/18-1, 18-2 and 14-2 wells. T38 sands are relatively thin and typically low amplitude when brine filled, brightening significantly when gas filled. Charge is possible via deep-seated faults downdip of the closure, and laterally. Top seal is assumed to be provided by muddy clinoform foreset deposits of upper T38 (204/18-1 drilled significant amount of silty shales at that level). Top seal and charge migration are the main risks , and because of its shallow depth below mudline, there is a risk of biodegradation if oil is encountered.

Am Basteir is a strat, fault dip feature in a thickened section of Upper Jurassic sediment.  The adjacent 204/15-2 well penetrates a similar section a finds a thick J70 KCF equivalent with thin sands suggestive of the Solan system in Quad 205.  The lead would be encased within the KCF and will require pinch out as the sand onlaps the Westray ridge. Assessment of the volumes is currently immature due to a challenge mapping the reservoir extent however scoping volumes based on area multiplied by thickness suggests that the option is small.  Petroleum systems modelling in the AOI suggest that the source is mature for gas. A significant cementation risk exists which is in part mitigated by the expectation of a gas discovery.

The Bedlington prospect primary target was the Palaeocene T31 Lower Sand unit, with secondary targets of sand units within the Palaeocene T10 to T35 intervals. The main Hearach prospectivity is located in block 209/14a. The Hearach prospects were identified on the TGS Non-Exclusive 3D survey (Northern Lights 2014) reprocessed seismic data and became the primary prospect for the P2044 licence during 2017. Prospectivity was identified at the Flett and Lamba levels. The Tertiary prospects have been delimited by Class IV AVO responses and represent structural/stratigraphic traps with interpreted Flett aged (T45) channel fill sands pinching out onto basement and Lamba aged (T38) shelfal sands. Rock physics well studies have identified that both high porosity and gas filled sands can produce Class IV AVO responses and it is interpreted that the lack of sealing capacity indicates a strong possibility that the sands are brine saturated. Seismic reconditioning work was undertaken in an attempt to improve the conformance to structure, following a work programme of gathers
conditioning the amplitude response showed the same poor conformance to structure and as such could not be incorporated into Nexen's DHI risking matrix. The uncertainty in the amplitude response and lack of containment resulted in the overall size of the prospect being significantly reduced.

The Megan prospect is a stratigraphic trap defined by the onlap of Upper Jurassic sands onto the southeast flank of the Margarita spur/Manet ridge. The trap is defined by stratigraphic pinch out and truncation of Upper Jurassic sands beneath the BCU to the North and West and by lateral facies changes and dip closure to the South and East. Top seal is provided by Cromer Knoll shales and base and side seal requires the presence of a shaly Brent/Dunlin section below. 
Base and side seal are the highest risk elements of the prospect. 
The reservoir at Megan is interpreted to be Upper Jurassic sand, deposited as part of the channelized feeder system to the Magnus fan to the South. 
Hydrocarbons are sourced from organic rich Kimmeridge Clay Fm and Heather Fm shales.

NE Lewis is a downthrown fault block with dip closure, located to the north of the Harris Field. Anticipated reservoir is Upper Brent sands. summary_comment: Haggis is a Brent Gp fault block, downthrown against the main bounding fault of the East Shetland Platform. Structural closure lies at around 5800ft, with a spill point at 7800ft (just up-dip from the dry well 210/29- 2). Mapping of the Brent is a key risk due to the structural complexity of the area. Erosion of the high is evident on seismic, but the extent of erosion of the Jurassic is unclear. Charge is an additional risk, as the distance to the source kitchen is considerable. However, 210/29a- 3 encountered oil at Brent level and may help to de-risk the prospect.

Glendullan is located in the Faroe-Shetland Basin, extending across the Flett High and SE margin of the Flett Sub-Basin. Contained within a stratigraphic trap, Glendullan demonstrates a distinctive sedimentary morphology, apparent on a number of seismic amplitude extractions, and interpreted as a slope channel and channelised lobe system.  The reservoir objective is interpreted as an intra-T35 Vaila sandstone, mapped as a low-impedance 'soft' event on 3D seismic data. Top, base and lateral seal is provided by T35-aged Vaila mudstone and the source rock is proposed as Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation. The prospect is identified by a DHI signal, derived from intercept and gradient seismic volumes, and is comparable to the nearby Laxford discovery anomaly. The prospect sits in a water depth of approx. 530m. Based upon the results of basin modelling is expected to be gas-bearing.

The Talisker prospect is a four way dip closure at top volcanic level and is attributed to have formed due to the formation of seaward dipping reflectors following continental breakup around 55 Ma. The two plays are 1) base volcanic Early Paleocene marine sandstones which are equivalent to the Egga Formation offshore Norway and 2) Mid-Late Cretaceous marine sandstones equivalent to the Springar, Nise and Lysing Formations offshore Norway. The recoverable resource prognosed in the Talisker prospect was 73 MMboe (P10), 200 MMboe (P50) and 556 MMboe (P90) and the hydrocarbon type was modelled to be predominantly oil.
For each play, the primary source rock is considered as Late Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation which is present elsewhere along the UKCS. The nearest hydrocarbon accumulations in the area are in the Tobermory/Erlend discovery well 214/4-1 and in the Tulipan discovery offshore Norway (6302/6-1).
Following the drilling of the Lagavulin exploration well, a reappraisal of the license was completed. This resulted in a downgrading of the recoverable resource in the license, housed in two separate prospects, Talisker East and West (Figure 5). The recoverable resource in Talisker East is 10.26 MMboe (P10), 31.88 MMboe (P50) and 99.15 MMboe (P90). The recoverable resource in Talisker West is 2.99 MMboe (P10), 9.71 MMboe (P50) and 30.88 MMboe (P90).

summary_comment: Faun remains the only other prospect defined on the licence. It is interpreted to be a Frigg Member stratigraphic trap that is observed to show possible gas bright spots. Python is located in blocks 36/28 and 36/29. It is located roughly 40km NW of the nearest producing field (Breagh) and around 30km north of the nearest hydrocarbon shows (42/09-1) and 42km NNW of the nearest Zechstein shows (42/10b-2). This build-up is encased within Stassfurt halites and therefore, in effect, forms a four-way-dip closed structure.   Python is a Zechstein Hauptdolomit lead. The blocks applied for host the Balvenie lead which has been mapped as a large low-relief 4-way dip structural closure on near top basement level. Overlying Lower Carboniferous sandstones and Devonian Old Red Sandstone constitute the main reservoirs with Kyle Carbonates as a possible secondary reservoir. The Balvenie lead is expected to contain relatively dry gas generated from Carboniferous age gas-mature shales and coals in basins located south, east and possibly also north of this lead. The Balvenie lead has a large volume potential with a most likely recoverable volume of 2.7 tcf gas with 17 MMboe associated condensate. The geological risk is currently estimated at 10%, and needs to be de-risked through the use of additional data and conducting geophysical and geological studies.

Lead Q41-A lies within Block 41/3 and consists of a large, undrilled structural closure within the Carboniferous. The lead has been mapped as a four-way dip closure, although the structure might be partially defined by faults, and is likely to be compartmentalised. As mapped, the structure is defined by a closing contour at 5,000 ft, with an area of 107 km2 and a maximum relief of 900 ft (a second closure lies immediately to the NE and is included in the lead to give the high case area of 145 km2). The reservoir is expected to be sandstones in the Namurian and Dinantian sequences. Lead Q41-A would rely on intra-formational and possibly fault seals and is expected to be sourced by gas from locally mature Carboniferous shales and coals.

Lead Q41-B lies within Blocks 41/4 and 41/9. It consists of a large, undrilled structural closure within the Carboniferous. The lead has been mapped as a three-way structural nose, with up-dip fault closure to the West. Again, the lead is likely to be compartmentalised. As mapped, the structure is defined by a closing contour at 7,000 ft, with an area of 115 km2 and a maximum relief of 1,600 ft. The reservoir is expected to be sandstones in the Namurian and Dinantian sequences. Lead Q41-B would rely on intra-formational and possibly fault seals and is expected to be sourced by gas from locally mature Carboniferous shales and coals.

Bunsen East is a four-way dip closed structure located midway between the Bentley and Bressay fields in Block 9/3c.  Closure is at the Upper Dornoch formation (now regarded as Lower Eocene age), with top seal being provided by the Eocene Balder tuffs and overlying Eocene shales.  The closing contour is slightly deeper than Bentley Field at 3,750 ft TVDSS.  It is considered likely that Bunsen East will be charged with oil as the structure lies on the migration route for oil spilling from Bentley into Bressay, however the slightly deeper spill point increases migration risk somewhat.  Oil is likely to be of very similar quality to that found in Bentley and Bressay with an anticipated API of between 10 and 11 degrees.  
Bunsen East measures approximately 1.0 km by 0.5 km, with the structural crest estimated at 3,715  ft TVDSS.

The Grampian prospect (subsequently renamed Manuel) was targeting stacked Upper and Middle Jurassic sands in block 11/29, approximately 10km west-southwest of the Beatrice Alpha platform.
The Manuel well 11/29-1 was drilled to the west on the prospect in February 2008 targeting stacked reservoirs in the Upper and Middle Jurassic. The well failed to find any significant sand in the Volgian, and Kimmeridgian sand was absent. In the upper Oxfordian, 40 ft of oil-bearing Lower Brora sand was found to be separated from an overlying 90 ft water bearing Upper Brora sand by a 15 ft shale. The MDT pressure tool demonstrated the water sand had good permeability of about 950 mD, whereas the oil-bearing Lower Brora sands was found to be tight.

The Echo Prospect was primarily targeting the Beatrice Formation A and B Sands on an upthrownfault block, 5 km southeast of the Beatrice Field that straddles blocks 11/26c and 11/30a. The western two thirds of the structure lay outside the P1392 licence in block 11/30a, operated at that time by Talisman Energy. The A and B sands have been observed in the adjacent 11/30a-A29 and 12/26-3 wells, with oil shows in the A sand. The structure, mapped on limited 2D seismic data, was a footwall 3-way dip closure against a SW-NE trending fault (Figure 10). The 3-way dip closure of -6,378 ft TVDSS yielded an estimated STOIIP of 4.7 MMstb and corresponding reserves in the range 0.7 to 1.0 MMbbls.

The 11/30-6 discovery was drilled by Mesa in December 1977 on a poorly defined upthrown fault block, 12 km southwest of the Beatrice Alpha platform. The gross depth structure is illustrated in Figure 12, which shows a triangular shaped fault block at Top Beatrice Formation that is fault sealed to the west and east and dip closed to the north. The structure straddles blocks 11/30b, 11/29, 17/4a and 17/5a.
The Beatrice Formation A and B sands interval was found to be about half the thickness off that seen in the Beatrice Field with very poor reservoir quality. It was speculated that the thinner and poorer quality interval in 11/30-6 could be the result of a fault intercepted by the well which had faulted out a better reservoir quality section.

summary_comment:
The Kappa-Asland Permian Lead has upthrown fault closure to the east, downthrown closure to the north and mainly dip closure to the south and west. The Kappa - Asland Permian Lead requires fault seal along its eastern boundary (the East Deemster Fault). This is because the throw on this fault exceeds the Cumbrian Coast Group top seal thickness (500ft to 600ft thick) - so leaving Collyhurst sandstone juxtaposed against the Triassic Sherwood Sandstone Group. Imaging is poor and interpretation difficult along the eastern-most section of the South Deemster Fault which forms the northern closure for the lead. This makes the throw of the fault and the juxtaposed stratigraphy in the footwall uncertain. 
The main risk is around the efficacy of fault seal along the on the eastern boundary East Deemster Fault. Trap mapping is also a significant risk particularly with respect to characterising the fault and downthrown closure along the South Deemster Fault to the north.

The Ormskirk Sandstone Formation is an excellent reservoir in the Kappa well 110/13-17.

The reservoir target is the Carboniferous sandstone (Westphalian or Namurian sandstones, which are developed in nearby wells 110/9a-2 and 110/13-1).  Top seal is provided by intra-formational shales.

Located just to the south of the Lennox field.the trap for the Beta Lead is an east-west trending horst block, which is bound by faults to the north, south and west, and has dip closure to the east. The reservoir target is the Sherwood Sandstone section (well developed in the Lennox field 5 km to the north).  
The reservoir is sealed by a thick Mercia Mudstone section.

The Impala Lead is located just southeast of the Douglas field and southwest of the Hamilton field.  The trap comprises a faulted north-south trending horst block, with fault closure to the west and east and dip closure to the north and south. To the northeast of the Darwen North Prospect (110/8a-7 Ventnor Discovery), the Lytham Lead is a potentially much larger structure, with a GIIP range of 54 - 119 - 144 - 265bcf (P90 - P50 - mean - P10). However, the structure is a hanging-wall anticline without independent four-way dip closure, and relies entirely on cross-fault seal of the Sherwood Sandstone reservoir against older Permian St. Bees Sandstone. It is therefore very high-risk (effective hanging-wall seals are in general high-risk, and have not been proven in the East Irish Sea to date). In addition to fault seal risk, the structure is poorly constrained to the east (on the Bains 3D seismic data) where additional poorly-imaged faults are needed to effectively close the structure. Furthermore, there is no amplitude anomaly that is indicative of gas having been retained in the Sherwood sandstone. The geological chance of success is probably in the order of 5%.

It was drilled on a N-S trending tilted fault block and found a 7m oil column at the top of the Sherwood Sandstone. On account of encountering >2000ppm H2S whilst drilling, the well was not tested. The structure, which is not full to spill and appears to have been tilted and/or breached, was re-mapped by Serica, and is estimated to contain STOIIP of just 1.6 - 2.0 - 2.0 - 2.4mmbo (P90 - P50 - mean - P10). The Norfolk Amplitude prospect trapping mechanism is entirely stratigraphic (Figures 5 and 6). The crest of the structure is at 750m. Amplitude extractions and seismic to well ties suggest the reservoir is within the Coracle Sandstone Member. Hauterivian mudstones form the top and lateral/base seals.
The prospect is situated within the Caithness Basin and directly overlies Mid Jurassic and Upper Jurassic shales mature for oil. In addition, Devonian lacustrine shales of the Orcadia Formation beneath the prospect are mature for gas.

The Punt Channel is a relatively small four way dip closure with stratigraphic upside in the Punt Sandstone member, and a structural crest at 1000m. The PCOS is 25% with a relatively small the recoverable volume range (P90/ P50/ P10) of 1/ 4/ 10 mmbbls. Biodegradation is the critical risk for this lead.

Girraween lead - large dip-closed elongate dome - transpressional fold on the corner of the Smith Bank High; the boundary fault of the High is a major strike-slip fault. Volgian sands proved locally are highly likely in closure, with intraformational seals. Potential for additional closure in the Upper Jurassic sequence, reliant on the fault for side seal - high risk as the footwall comprises Devonian & Triassic fractured sequences. Main risk is late Tertiary structure deformation cracking the trap, without replacement of oil from Devonian and/or early Jurassic source rocks. CoS = 34% (reservoir effectiveness reduced 100>50%; seal reduced 100>50%).

Eugenie is a tilted fault block lead at Beatrice Formation level mapped on the 1986 Western Geco data, owing to poor signal to noise ratio on the First Oil data set at this depth. Updip seal is formed by two faults which in most places do not appear to go to surface. The lead is dip closed to the south. Top seal is provided by Heather Formation mudstones. The critical uncertainties with this lead are associated with the mapping of faults and top seal integrity, related to faults. The chance of success was set at 27%, but recoverable volumes are relatively low (P90/ P50/ P10: 4/ 9/ 20mmbbls).

Libra South lead - 4-way dip closure along E-W Punt channel; closure developed over N-S L Cretaceous structural nose, with stratigraphic component in pinchout at channel margins. Strong evidence of compactional drape over sand body. Area increased 1000>1177 acres to match Arc polygon. Trap presence reduced 60>25% due to poor seismic coverage over lead.

The prospect is predicted to have Beatrice Formation sands as the reservoir. These sands are predicted to laterally pinch out by facies change into deeper water shales. The prospect has been identified as an acoustic impedance anomaly on several lines. Company CoS = 11%.

The reservoir is predicted to consists of fluvial sands capped by 300ft+ of shales in the upper portion of the Bosies Bank Formation. The prospect has been identified using reprocessed 3D seismic data in the frequency domain. Trapping is provided by antithetic faults which are rooted in a listric fault developing on the Smith Bank High.

The Badger Prospect is a west-east oriented stratigraphic /structural trap at Coracle and Punt Sandstone level. 
Structural dip closure is recognised to the east and downthrown fault closure to the north. 
The principle Coracle reservoir relies on up-thrown fault closure against the Buckie Ridge to the south and stratigraphic closure to the west where the Coracle (Upper Punt) channel sands thin and appear to pinchout.

Upper Jurassic pinch-out - the closure is bound by a stratigraphic pinchout of the Burns sand to the west and fault sealed to the north and south. The exact location of the pinch out of the Ferrick prospect has a degree of uncertainty because it is beyond the limit of current 3D seismic coverage. The trapping style is similar to the oil bearing Upper Jurassic turbidite sands found in the Dee discovery further south along the West Bank High.

A frontier exploration play has been identified in the offshore Rathlin Basin, Northern Ireland, analogous to the EISB.  No wells have been drilled offshore to date, however source rock is proven onshore.  Adequate seal may be a risk, as borehole information indicates that the Mercia Mudstone can be sand prone in some horizons.  It is hoped that this facies is more mud rich in the offshore basin depocentre. Reservoir and adequate quality sand in either the Permo-Triassic is not deemed a significant risk, as these are already proven within the onshore basin. summary_comment: Fault-bounded hangingwall 3-way closure on the northern flank of the Halibut Horst and is defined as a fault bound, hanging-wall, three way dip closure at Lower Cretaceous and Upper Jurassic Levels. Both upper Jurassic and lower Cretaceous sandstones may form a joint payzone complex. Reservoir presence in the primary target of the Burns Sandstones was confirmed along strike to the west by 14/21a-1; however only traces of hydrocarbons were found in this well. 14/21a-1 also confirmed the presence of the Lower Cretaceous Scapa sandstone interval, however the sands present were thinly bedded and poorly sorted in nature, interbedded with chalky limestones.

RF amended to match reserves data.

Trap integrity, seal and migration are all significant risks. P10 only parameters provided; other parameters entered cf. cp14_23_1. 
CoS = 4% (downgraded by high play risk).

The Scapa Lead is a structural-stratigraphic trap located between wells 14/25a-3 and 14/25a-6A. 
The objective reservoir is of Lower Cretaceous age comprising intercalated sandstones. The lower Scapa sand interval shows significantly better reservoir properties than the overlying interval. Cementation is the main control over reservoir quality. Good quality Lower Cretaceous sands in the lower Scapa sequence were encountered in the 14/25a-3 well although they were water-bearing.
The sands are interpreted to pinch out up-dip to the west and are not present in the 14/25a-6A well, where the Scapa interval represented a secondary target to the primary Jurassic Piper objective.

Finn lead - step terrace between Rob Roy/Ivanhoe area and East Halibut Spur with Carboniferous (Namurian) target cf. 15/21b-41 and oil sands in 15/21a-7 (700 bopd). Juxtaposed against tight Devonian strata of Halibut Horst. Possible Piper/Sgiath sands may occur as target instead cf 15/21-5. 
CoS 11%; downgraded by play risk.

Finn Shallow lead pinchout trap of Beauly Sands against delta front to W & dip closure to E. Beauly oil leg (21 ft) in 15/21b-45; mapped spill point updip from well (depth conversion problem/local stratigraphic variation). CoS 25%; downgraded by play risk, likely seal risk.

The Perth West prospect is a potential extension of the Perth Field into Block 14/25. This extension of the field contains 13% of the field GRV as currently mapped, but it may be partially isolated from the field by a SW to NE fault mapped at Rattray level.

The Scapa Lead is a stratigraphic trap, formed by a hanging wall fan in the North Halibut Trough. The trap geometry is subtle, and is identified by a thickening of the BCU to SA interval and a structural nose at SA (Valanginian) sandstone level, (just west of 14/25a-6a).

summary_comment: Amity is a drill ready 4-way dip closed prospect stratigraphically above the Ranger prospect. Amity contains a DHI in the form of a clear flat spot that is coincident with the lowest closing contour of the structure, is consistent at all azimuths through the prospect, is the expected hard kick response and is analogous to the flat spot seen at Macculloch. The reservoir is considered to be the Upper Forties Sandstone Member. Sitting above Amity are a number of Eocene amplitude anomalies that are considered to be heavy oil deposits. Amity would be fully evaluated with the firm well commitment to drill the Ranger prospect.

summary_comment: Roberts is an Andrew sandstone amplitude reflectivity and CI (Colour Inverted) anomaly identified within an onlapping sandstone. The trap geometry for the prospect is dip closure to the east, west and south; therefore providing a 3-way dip closure. To the north the sandstone either pinches out or is sealed by a small fault that has formed in response to the topography produced by the underlying regional graben bounding fault. Reservoir presence can be correlated to the 15/16b-18 and 15/16b-21 wells where the Andrew Formation is evident. The overlying seal is the Balmoral Tuff Member and its associated shales. Hydrocarbon source is the underlying Kimmeridge Clay Formation, and charge into Roberts is likely up the bounding graben fault or vertically through fracture networks. Roberts COS is determined to be 24%.

Kidd is an Andrew sandstone amplitude reflectivity and CI anomaly identified within a play fairway orientated approximately N-S on the western edge of the block. The strength of the CI anomaly is greater than that encountered at Roberts, perhaps indicating increased likelihood of hydrocarbons or increased porosity. The prospect?s trap is a combination of dip and stratigraphic closure. To the east there is clear dip closure, while to the west a trap is provided by pinch-out or possibly fault seal. To the north and south the trap is more ambiguous and while some structure exists to provide dip closure, a stratigraphic component is also thought to be evident. The overlying seal is the Balmoral Tuff Member and associated shales. Hydrocarbon source is the underlying Kimmeridge Clay Formation, and charge into Kidd is likely laterally along the regional Andrew fairway. Kidd?s COS is determined to be 24%.

Ward is an Andrew sandstone amplitude reflectivity and CI anomaly identified within the same play fairway as Kidd. The prospect?s trap is a combination of dip and stratigraphic closure in the same configuration as Kidd. However, the stratigraphic trapping element of this prospect makes it slightly more risky than Kidd. The overlying seal is the Balmoral Tuff Member and its associated shales. Hydrocarbon source is the underlying Kimmeridge Clay Formation, and charge into Ward is likely laterally along the regional Andrew fairway. Ward?s COS is determined to be 22%.

Morgan is a Lower Cretaceous, prospect that is up-dip of good hydrocarbon shows in 14/20b-29 at an equivalent stratigraphic level. The prospect is partly defined by a CI amplitude anomaly, possibly caused by small volumes of hydrocarbons seeping into the sediments immediately beneath the base chalk creating a Class 3 AVO response. The CI amplitude anomaly approximately conforms to structure. The prospect is a down faulted terrace from the Colonsay prospect (P1292) in the block to the north. Trap is a combination of dip closure and either pinch-out or fault seal to the north. Hydrocarbons are likely sourced vertically up the regional graben bounding faults.

summary_comment: Birnam is a down-thrown fault terrace situated immediately up-dip of wells 15/16b-18y and 15/16b-21 which encountered water bearing Piper sandstones with oil shows. Both wells show pressure depletion in the Piper sands, either through the regional aquifer or by cross fault leakage. The Claymore sandstones in well 15/16b-18y were, however, encountered at virgin pressure.

The structure is three way dip closed sitting on a downthrown terrace to the Saltire field. 
The Piper sands are interpreted to be wet in 15/17-8A, based on the lack of oil shows in the Piper core, in contrast to the Galley sand cores, which were partly oil stained. 
The most likely interpretation is that the well was drilled outside the structural closure at top Piper.

The Westray structure comprises a downthrown terrace overlying a deep seated tilted fault block. It is downthrown relative to the Egilsay structure, which lies 2.4 Km to the north. The trap relies on fault /dip closure defined by east-west trending faults and dip closure to the west and east.  This structure is complicated by its location on a zone of fault transfer that runs from NE to SW through the 15/17-24z well location

 * Gas recovery factor is 50-60-70.   Gas to Liquid ratio is 216 bbl/MMscf.   Galley sandstone is not currently part of the base case development plan.

Taransay lies 2km N of Saltire. It is a dip and fault bounded structure at Galley level. There is dip closure to the E and upthrown fault closure to the N,S & W. The primary reservoir targets are the Galley and Piper sands which are present in down-dip 15/17-20, drilled in 1988and encountered a gross interval of 78ft Galley sands at 9,677ft and 131ft gross Piper sands. N:G was 0.87 and 0.84 respectively. The sands were water bearing. The 15/7-19 well drilled to the west in an adjacent fault block also encountered water bearing Galley and Piper sands. With two nearby dry holes, hydrocarbon charge is considered a major risk in Taransay as the prospect may lie in a migration shadow. Parameters cf cp15_17_5.

At Galley level Tiree has dip closure to the S and upthrown fault closure to the N, W and E. Like cp15_17_12 the main reservoir targets are the Galley and Piper sands. The 15/17-19 well, drilled on an adjacent fault block to the W encountered 155ft gross Galley sands at 9,022ft TVDSS and 233ft gross Piper sands. N:G was 0.81 and 0.91 respectively. Both sands were water bearing. Hydrocarbon migration is considered the key risk due to the nearby dry wells. Furthermore the Galley is eroded towards the crest of the structure where it is directly overlain by the Valhall, thus vertical seal may be an issue. Parameters cf cp15_17_5.

summary_comment:
Blackhorse Extension and Galley West prospects are expected to be sealed by the Kimmeridge Clay Formation including top and lateral seal. 
Also, hydrocarbons are believed to have been sourced from the Kimmeridge Clay Formation and migrated into Galley reservoir sandstones. 
Little risk is thus seen in relation with top seal and charge aspects. 
Sealing capacity of the fault separating Blackhorse Discovery and Blackhorse Extension does not impact the prospect volumes and risks
but, in the case of Galley West Prospect, the eastern fault must be sealing for the trap to be viable.

The primary Dirk Sandstone target has a gross thickness of 113ft. Net to gross was significantly lower than anticipated at 26%, the potential reservoirs within the sequence being encountered as 4 thin sandstone units (Dirk Sandstone A-D) with average porosity 14%. 
Petrophysical analysis, RCI pressure gradient and sampling data indicate that only the uppermost Dirk Sandstone unit (Dirk A sandstone) is hydrocarbon-bearing, the lower units showing residual hydrocarbon saturations and water on test. The individual Dirk Sandstone units are not in pressure communication internally or with the Bugle discovery to the south. The deeper Galley Sandstone was also water-wet, and RCI pressure data indicates that it is some 1100 psi depleted relative to the regional Galley aquifer gradient. On the basis of these results, the well was P&A'd without testing. 
Post-well remapping  and re-assessment of prospect resources based upon a downgraded reservoir quality model indicate that the North Bugle prospect contains 9.2 Mmbo recoverable in total. - not considered to be a commercial hydrocarbon volume.

summary_comment: ProspectThe Cornet prospect is a 3-way fault-dependent trap at Piper Formation reservoir level, in a steeply-dipping fault block at the base of the Telford Ridge bounding fault. The main reservoir concern is quality, with the Piper being tight in the deeper 15/23-3 well just to the east. The Telford reservoir is normally pressured whereas the 15/23-3 well is over pressured, as are the Bugle and Blackhorse discoveries. This would support the theory that the Telford ridge bounding fault is sealing. Concerns remain, however, over whether it may have leaked with the crest of the Cornet fault block being a high point for the Piper (along with the Galley field) in the area.

summary_comment: The Griffith structure comprises a stacked prospect with Galley and Dirk reservoirs present within a down thrown fault block. It is associated with the Telford fault and is bounded to the north by the W-E fault which defines the Bugle structure. The Galley fault block is well-defined and forms an isolated trap of limited extent. The Dirk structure dips to the southeast where it forms the down dip extension of the Bugle discovery. Penetration of a deeper OWC in Bugle would therefore suggest that hydrocarbons are also present in Griffith as part of a single, larger oil accumulation. The Dirk level trap, as described above, is the main objective. The small fault block identified is highly reliant on the seismic interpretation of the faults present. The prospect is dependent on multiple fault seals.

summary_comment: Bowmore is an elongate fault and dip-closed gas-condensate discovery mapped at Base Cretaceous level with a crest at approximately 13,800ftTVDSS, bounded to the N by a fault and to the S and SW by dip-closure. Bowmore is proven by the 15/24a-4 and 15/24a-9 wells. An easterly thinning of the Upper Jurassic across the structure results in pinch-out of Upper Jurassic Claymore and Galley turbidite sandstones onto the underlying tilted fault block, thereby providing a combination stratigraphic-structural trap, overlying deeper shoreface Piper Sandstone. Wireline log analysis confirmed all three sandstones as hydrocarbon-bearing.  The Galley Sandstone was thinly-developed in 15/24a-4 but thickens markedly down-dip in 15/24a-9. Core data indicates modest but effective reservoir quality. Logs and RFT data in 15/24a-9 confirmed a hydrocarbon contact at 14,342ftTVDSS. Mean recoverable reserves for the Galley Sandstone are calculated at 11.7mmbbls condensate and 41.4bcf gas.

Combination structural stratigraphic trap (3 way dip with updip strat pinchout), Balmoral Sandstone reservoir with AVO anomaly.  Sealed by Sele shales, source - Kimmeridge Clay Formation. Dunscaith lies over a positive AVO anomaly. The bright amplitudes from the extracted maximum positive attribute on the far minus near envelope volume define the prospect. The N & S edges are marked by a change in seismic character and the lateral limits are defined by the extent of the AVO anomaly and a change in reflection character associated with a change in depositional facies. Downthrown fault closed BCU structure with Jurrasic Piper Sandstone Reservoir.  Source and seal provided by Kimmeridge Clay Formation. Bright seismic amplitudes in the tilted fault block sitting below the BCU are believed to be indicative of Jurassic sandstones. Reservoir presence and fault seal would be the main risks. Seismic mapping of the Piper and Claymore sandstones in the Jurassic levels and the Kimmeridge Clay Fm would have to be undertaken in order to fully address the key risks and uncertainties.

Stratigraphic trap with reservoir of Grid Sandstone sealed by Horda Formation shales and sourced from Kimmeridge Clay Formation. Bright seismic amplitudes are observed on RMS amplitude map (in a 200ms window beneath the Top Grid) in both full stack and far minus near offset data. It is postulated that whilst hydrocarbons migrate up-dip through the Balmoral Fm sourcing Palaeocene plays, an alternative migration pathway facilitates migration into shallower stratigraphic intervals. This is supported by the presence of hydrocarbons in the Grid Fm in some offset wells. Eocene conical sand injectites have been interpreted down-dip of the Rowallan Lead during an in-house geological study in the area. During this study, several large sand injectites have been mapped. Some of these injectites are truncated by shales and could have the capability to form reservoirs, whilst others are observed to reach the base of the Grid Fm thus potentially acting as migration pathways into the Grid sandstones.

The reservoir objective is the Upper Jurassic Galley Sandstone Member which is dip closed to the north, west and east. The Durness lead is a stratigraphic pinchout of the Upper Jurassic Brae Formation onto an intrabasinal high to the east. This high has been tested by wells e.g. 16/18-1, 16/23-4 which confirm the Brae Formation reservoir is absent and the Upper Jurassic consists of a condensed section of Kimmeridge Clay Formation overlying the Hugin Formation.

The reservoir objective for the Aston prospect is the Hugin Formation sandstone, which comprises shallow-marine and marginal-marine sediments deposited during the overall transgression and southward retreat of the ‘Brent Delta’ systems. Interpretation of the new seismic data has increased the principle risk of lateral seal as only a flexure is seen rather than a significant fault on the easterly updip edge of the prospect. The prospect trends from south-west to north-east across 16/23b and extends into the southern end of 16/18c, similar to the 28th Round application mapping.
This flexure may be the result of a lineation of small faults. It is probable that these faults will be discontinuous along the length of Aston and because of their minor offset and discontinuous nature, they are unlikely to be an effective seal for trapping. 
The optimal place to test the prospect is in 16/23b where the overlying Alcedo (Heather Formation) prospect can also be tested. However, the overall geological chance of success is considered low due to trap risk and reservoir presence.

name_others: Sadie, Topanga, Sienna cp16_23_17 Cambria cp16_23_47 Wrasse   REL01314 Sadie
summary_comment: The Middle Jurassic Wrasse Discovery was made by well 16/23-4. The accumulation comprises a small gas condensate faulted 4-way dip closure located on the northern edge of the Andrew Ridge. The discovery has been mapped on 3D MegaSurvey seismic data where a top Middle Jurassic coal marker can be mapped as a proxy to the top Hugin Formation reservoir. The Hugin Formation reservoir encountered at the 16/23-4 Wrasse Discovery well is thin and fairly poorly developed (gross Hugin Formation thickness of 23.3m). The reservoir is characterised by coaly sandstones and heterolithics that have been deposited in coastal plain to shoreface marine depositional environments. Azinor Catalyst have undertaken petrophysics on the discovery well and has the following petrophysical calculations; 12.2m Net Pay, 18.2% average porosity and 52% average NTG. The well tested gas and 47 API condensate at rates of up to 4 mmscfpd and 2,190 bcpd.

The Basil Prospect is a Heimdal Member, compactional four way dip closure analogous to the nearby Kinnoull and Arundel discoveries. 16/18-3 within closure TDd in Alba. It is located down dip of the 16/23-2 exploration well (10m thick sand with a moderate hydrocarbon saturation -46%). The trap forms a very minor closure in time which after depth conversion becomes more pronounced. The seismic expression of the top reservoir is a weak seismic event and presents a challenge when mapping. Trap is considered a key risk for this lead.

The Palaeocene Kidd Discovery was made by well 16/23-3. The accumulation has been mapped as a small low relief 4-way dip closure at top Heimdal Member level and is on trend to the Kinnoull Field which shares the same reservoir age sands. Top seal is provided by the shales of the Palaeocene Lista Formation. The discovery has been mapped up on 3D Mega Survey seismic data.  The Heimdal Member reservoir encountered by the discovery well comprise stacked turbidite channels. Petrophysical analysis of the Heimdal Member sands estimates porosity to 24% and oil saturation to 70%. Permeabilities are typically measured in the hundreds of mD but may range up to several Darcies. An oil-down-to has been established at 2,484 m TVDSS and a water-up-to at 2,492 m TVDSS, coincident with the mapped spill point of the structure to the southwest. An oil sample recovered to surface confirmed a 33 deg API oil.

The Bermuda Prospect is defined as a sub-unconformity trap in the Hugin Formation. The trap is delineated by structural dip to the south and east, by the erosion of the reservoir to the west-northwest and partially by faulting to the north.The reservoir target is the Hugin Formation shallow marine sandstones, with top seal provided by the overlying mudstones of the Heather and Kimmeridge Clay formations. It is crucial for the Bermuda Prospect that the upper part of the Pentland/Sleipner Formation is an effective base seal since the Skagerrak and thin Pentland/Sleipner Formation sandstones present in Well 16/23-3 are water bearing. The lack of base seal is considered to be the primary risk for the prospect. Another key risk associated with the Bermuda Prospect is charge.

FLETT FORMATION LEADS - The Cumberland are defined at T40 seismically, partially on 3D data but the critical up-dip fault closure is not fully covered by fully migrated 3D. The seismic pick used is the Top T40, which corresponds to the top of the Colsay Mbr., lava sequence, within which is siliciclastic sandstone in 164/25-1z

Top and base seal is interbedded volcaniclastic claystone and is considered robust. The fault seal is juxtaposition of the Colsay Mbr., sequence and the sealing fault up-dip which is a significant risk, although
sealing faults in such sequences are proven (see Walker et al., 2013). The trap is formed by normal faulting in the Eocene, for which the downthrown block to the west is the Cumberland leads. Tilting from the Eocene to present formed the dip component, which dips westwards. 
Both leads are substantially the same, separated by a ~E-W trending normal fault. Migration is prognosed to be from the NERB to the west, where oil shows were encountered in 164/28-1A.

ProspectThe Nash prospect is located 10 km to the west of Nexen's Buzzard Field within block 19/10b on licence P.2101 as shown in Fig. 5.1 and targets the Oxfordian Sgiath sandstone member at the base of the Upper Jurassic sequence. A regional stratigraphic column can been seen in Fig. 5.2. Well 20/06a-B31, also shown in Fig. 5.1, was drilled as a producer targeting Buzzard sands in the Buzzard Central Panel and encountered 26 ft of net Sgiath pay and an Oil Down To (ODT) at ~8208 ft TVDSS. The Nash prospect, located updip of the 20/06a-B31 well was evaluated for the 27th Licence Round and deemed worthy of licence application. After the award of licence P.2101, technical work was completed to de-risk the Sgiath sandstone around the Buzzard area and regionally within the Moray Firth. However, the following 2016 evaluation determined that the Nash prospect is higher risk than previously deemed in the licence application with reservoir presence and charge as the greatest risk elements.

The Buzzard-aged reservoir is regionally present within the Moray Firth. A Top Buzzard equivalent reflector has been mapped from the Buzzard licence area across the P.2101 licence area where 2 Buzzard-age equivalent leads are highlighted. The reflectors pinch out in a north westerly direction onto the tilted fault block with the Nash structure at its crest. However, westwards from the Buzzard Field, Buzzard-aged sands pinch out down dip of well 19/10a-1 creating an effective and proven seal for the field. Therefore the up-dip locations for Leads A and B probably represent an area of sediment bypass or non sandstone deposition. The seismic thickness of the Buzzard-aged unit also halves from 19/08-1 well to the Lead A location and is even thinner at the Lead B location.

Cretaceous - Numerous Lower Cretaceous leads over P.2101 were defined by the western most stratigraphic pinch out of the Punt age-equivalent sandstones. The up-dip offset well, 19/08-1 contains Punt age-equivalent sandstones that are interpreted to be shoreface sandstones that have been reworked by wave action. The key horizons used in these Lower Cretaceous lead evaluations are the BCU and the Top Valhall Marl. The Top Valhall Marl has been identified in the 19/10-1 from a synthetic well tie and was mapped across the P.2101 licence area where it represents an approximate Punt-equivalent age reflector. A thickness map between the Top Valhall Marl and the BCU shows the main westerly pinch-out can be separated into a number of scalloped shaped features, as shown in Fig. 5.7. The event at the BCU appears highly erosive in this area and is followed by sediment infill. However, down-dip offset well data does not indicate that Punt age equivalent sandstones are present and as a result has placed a high risk on reservoir presence.

Cello is a Carboniferous lead located in blocks 20/11 and 20/12 in the south of the P2283 licence. The lead was identified on the basis of minor residual oil shows in well 20/12-3 immediately down-dip of the lead.
The well penetrated multiple reservoir intervals including the Zechstein Halibut Dolomite, Lower Carboniferous sands of the Buchan Formation and the underlying Devonian sands. No shows were indicated within the Carboniferous or the Devonian, however minor residual oil shows where recorded within the Zechstein, possibly related to thinner algal rich shale beds of the Kupfershiefer Formation. 
The lead is trapped by stratigraphic pinchout to the northeast and southwest of the Lower Carboniferous sand drilled in the well onto the Peterhead ridge and is defined on 2D. 
Re-interpretation of the top Zechstein interval using new 2D data does not reveal any clear trap at this stratigraphic level.

Jurassic accommodation space against Triassic Smith Bank pods.

The Glansdale Lead is located within an entry point into the graben. To both the north and south of this area the well control (20/10-2, 20/15-1) indicates thinned Jurassic and lower Cretaceous sections. Both of these wells drilled salt cored structures. summary_comment: Linnet is a three-way dip-closure prospect at the Tay Mbr level, supported by an AVO amplitude which shows a strong class 3 signature and good conformance to structure. The brightness of the amplitude and associated QI work suggests the trap is gas-filled, although it is possible that a thin rim of heavy oil might also be present. Heavy oil accumulations are common in this area, hence, any gas response may be a result of released methane from continued biodegradation of contained heavy oil. Linnet's reservoir depth at 3,300'ss extrapolates to an oil gravity of 16 API

Sendero Limited has undertaken a study of the general Allington area based on an extensive regional merged 3D dataset supplemented by selected modern 2D lines and offsetting well control. This work has highlighted exploration potential in Block 20/16 which is located on the south flank of the Peterhead Ridge in the West Central Graben, south of the Ettrick field in the Moray Firth. This area is informally named Allington West..  The 20/12-3 well is a key Zechstein well at Sendero's Promote Block 20/12. It was drilled to the Devonian at 5615 feet in 1986 by Mobil and found 42 meters of impermeable Zechstein Halibut Formation dolomite in a structurally high position.  Sendero's conclusion is that this well drilled impermeable backreef dolomites and anhydrites. Amplitude analysis suggests possibly hydrocarbon filled porous reservoir slightly down dip of this well on the south flank of the Peterhead Ridge.  Estimated Technical Chance of Success.   Source    50%.   Reservoir   50%.   Trap    50%.   Seal    95%.   Total Chance of Success = 11%

Upper Jurassic pinchout trap in Ettrick Sst. interval in the South Halibut Basin, highlighted by an ampolitude anomaly dying out towards the NW. The bulk of the prospect may be located in the held block to the south. Two seismic events tied to wells 20/2-5 and 20/2-6 and representing the top and base of the Ettrick Sst. are seen to converge and pinch out to the north and west, illustrating the potential of a stratigraphic pinch-out trap updip of these wells.

Turbiditic Punt sst stratigraphically-trapped against the Grampian Arch. Topseal is provided by Valhall shales and base seal by KCF. The Marten Discovery is in Block 20/3c and was discovered in 1984 by the 20/3-4 well drilled by Amoco and encountered an oil column in Buzzard aged sandstones. 
Marten is a three-way dip closed structure to the north, south and west, with a stratigraphic pinch-out component to the east.
The reservoir for Marten comprises four stacked sandstones: three relatively thin oil-bearing sands of J66 - J64 Buzzard age above a thicker, J64, water bearing Buzzard main sand.
Mapping suggests there is a spill point at around 10,750ft which is where the 20/3-4 well penetrated the J66 section, however the CPI (Fig. 13) suggests that the ODT is 10,951ft TVDSS and the WUT is 11,007ft TVDSS.
Blob only. Lies east of Blackbird and south of Ettrick.

The Golden Goose Lead is also purely a stratigraphic trap, within the Upper Jurassic Burns turbidite sands. It was identified from interpretation of the seismic package immediately beneath the Goshawk Prospect. The depositional concept for the Burns turbidite sands is similar to the Goshawk Prospect, invoking deposition from the Halibut Horst to the north and stratigraphic pinch-out in all directions.

The Badger Prospect is a downthrown hanging wall block located to the north of the 20/4-1 ridge. 
The reservoir interval lies within the J66 - J62 Buzzard Sandstones. 
The lowside Badger case is a three-way dip closure to the north, east and west and fault closed to the south against an east-west trending down to the north normal fault. This fault forms the northern margin to the central horst structure in Block 20/4a. 
The upside Badger structure is fault closed to the south along the same east-west trending fault and to the east along a north-south, down to the east fault.

summary_comment:
The Verbier prospect comprises of a Upper Jurassic submarine fan complex that has accumulated in the hanging wall of the Buchan trough. The deep-water sands are interpreted to be the Burns Sandstone (J64 in age) based on observations from the 20/05a-10 & 10Y wells. The sands are charged directly from the surrounding Kimmeridge Clay Formation which is mature at the prospect location. The Verbier prospect has a Pg of 1 due to the 20/05a-10 & 10Y wells location within the 'base case' polygon outline. 
PostDrill Update: The well encountered a ODT within 16m of Burns sandstone which flowed at 4804 bopd. Main well reservoir was dry. Oil discovery in unplanned sidetrack (20/05b- 13Z) updip of the main well location.

The reservoir is expected to be a high-quality deep-water turbidite sand.  The prospect is split by a fault into North and South segments.  The prospect is stratigraphic, with most of the edges defined by sand pinch-out within a channel.  The up-dip pinchout within the channel is the riskiest element of the trap.  Calibration of amplitudes with SW Foinaven suggest that Glas Maol North has oil and gas, whereas Glas Maol South has oil.  The prospect on its own is likely to be uneconomic, but could be considered for development as part of the larger inventory of opportunities in this application.

The Tarsuinn Prospect is a four-way dip closure defined at Base T40 (Palaeocene).  
The structure has a well-defined flat spot and seismic rock property modelling suggests that the structure is likely to be oil-bearing.  The reservoir is anticipated to be shallow-marine T38 sands and the seal is assumed to be T45-T60 mudstones and coals.  
The Kimmeridge Clay source rock is mature in this area, but the low temperature of the reservoir (40-50degC) means that oil biodegradation is likely (hence low assumed recovery factor).  
The prospect on its own is likely to be uneconomic, but could be considered for development as part of the larger inventory of opportunities in this application.
