Sanda prospects have a very similar morphology to the Schiehallion and Foinaven Fields, but with lower amplitudes. This could be due to thinner reservoir, or the slightly
greater burial depth at Sanda, or indeed a product of the seismic processing. Sanda is interpreted as an up-dip pinch out of Sullom/ Lower Vaila Formation turbidites. This play
has been successfully tested in Quadrants 204 and 206, but between these two areas there have only been a few wells that have tested this play, most unsuccessfully. Oil and gas shows were recorded in wells, 205/8-1 and 205/10-2b, but the reservoir was poorly developed in these wells, which are situated outwith the 205/13 anomaly. Identification of Vaila/ Sullom pinch out traps is generally only possible from seismic attribute analysis. All the neighbouring discoveries show a clear amplitude response due to fluid fill (oil and/or gas) and down-dip amplitude shut off at the oil or gas water contact. This amplitude response is complicated by the reservoirs being channelized, resulting in significant changes in reservoir thickness and therefore amplitude response in the hydrocarbon column. The presence of gas caps above oil can further complicate this amplitude picture. However, in all the neighbouring discoveries the Vaila reservoir sands are seismically invisible unless hydrocarbon bearing. Amplitude driven: Amplitude to be checked by a geophysicist. Trapping towards Sanda N & S? Oil scenario 50/50%. New modern broadband 3D seismic is required.

The Dunrobin lead is as a combined structural and stratigraphic trap within Lower Cretaceous strata. It is defined by an area of strong amplitudes and located within a regional three-way closed structure. These amplitudes are interpreted to represent a package of sand within a shale dominated section of Albian age.  Probabilistic input parameters used.  Those shown are P90, P50 and P10..   Gas condensate assumed to be the most likely hydrocarbon phase. It is recognised that reservoir presence is a key risk for Dunrobin, particularly as downdip well 205/16-1 failed to find any
significant sand. This well drilled on the fringes of the bright amplitudes and may lie on the distal edges of a turbidite fan system. In addition the immediate zone around 205/16-1 is characterised by lower amplitudes and indications of faulting. This may be the reason why no significant sand was encountered, and updip potential remains.

Therefore P90, P50 and P10 inputs/outputs are shown above rather than absolute minimum, most likely and absolute maximum. The P90 and P10 values are the primary tie points for input distributions. Longjohn was identified during the 28th Round as a Palaeocene prospect within the T36 reservoir, one
stratigraphic level above the T35 reservoir of Laggan and Tormore. It involved a mixed trap with a fault

Lower Clachaig prospect is a stratigraphic trap mapped at T35.4A sandstone level The trap is developed along the SE pinch-out of the T35.4 depositional fan system onto the Tormore (Flett) high. The prospect is defined on the basis of a high amplitude/low impedance event at T35.4A Sandstone level, taken to represent the channel axis of a high density turbidity current, which shows lateral pinchout to the east. AMS data suggests the T35.4 depositional system runs from a NE-SW direction through the 205/9-1 well where no closure is mapped. The overall structure dips to the north-west with updip pinchout to the east. A critical element of the trapping mechanism is provided by an E-W trending fault that provides part of the updip seal. The fault appears to be sealing, with significant changes in the amplitude response between the footwall and hangingwall. Fault displacement across the E-W fault is estimated to be 30m.

The Mardyke prospect is located in the south of block 209/05 and covers an area of approximately 26km2. It lies outside the area influenced by overlying basalt flows, and can therefore be mapped with relative confidence. The prospect sits within a downthrown fault terrace, and is interpreted to consist of a series of stratigraphically trapped Early Cretaceous deep water sands, ponded within the terrace. The sands pinch out to the south against the underlying BCU, and the prospect is dip closed to the north, east and west. Additional upside is recognised in an alternate scenario, by invoking a structural trapping element. In this case, a fault seal is required between Early Cretaceous sands juxtaposed against the basement footwall to the south. The crest of the prospect is at 3,850m below sea level.

summary_comment: The Topper Lead is a potential structural and stratigraphic trap related to a channel-like, or slump, feature within the Tertiary sequence. Some structural conformance is supported by potential 4-way dip (P90 closure within block 21/1a) while larger closure relies on stratigraphic trapping. The P1 closure extends across blocks 21/1a and 21/1b with ca. 40% mapped within 21/1b. The objective reservoir likely relates to the Forties depositional system but has also been interpreted as possible Lower Eocene, Cromarty Sandstone. Sele Formation shales are interpreted to provide top and lateral seal. Hydrocarbon migration into the Tertiary could be vertically, via faults, or by longer distance migration. There is a risk of biodegradation based on the relatively shallow depth of the target reservoir interval.

Stratigraphic prospect, being a submarine fan of late Jurassic (J64) age located on the terrace northeast of Buchan field that debouched onto the basin foor towards the north and east.

These sands pinch out basinward and were not penetrated by the Tweedsmuir North and Tweedsmuir South wells in the northeastern part of the block. To the south, these sandstones truncate against normal faults that bound the northern flank of the Buchan Horst.

summary_comment: Ingui has an Upper Tay Sandstone Member reservoir. The trap is formed by stratigraphic pinchout into Horda Fm mudstones to the SW with 3-way dip closure. Wells 21/24-5 and 21/25-10 both contain sand at the Ingui reservoir level. The stratigraphic element to the trap is supported by amplitude extractions and change in seismic character which ties to mud intervals in offset wells. There is an updip seal risk, as evidenced by updip well 21/24-1 which encountered shows and a thin sand at the Ingui lead level. Well 21/24-7 also encountered a thin sand (10ft) at this level. Ingui is not overlain by any seismic amplitudes which would suggest the presence of gas. However there is some brightening on the seismic which may hint that hydrocarbons are present at reservoir level. These amplitudes are not as bright as those observed at 21/24-3 and only have moderate conformance to structure. Along strike well 21/23a-10 (Constance) found oil shows possibly within the same Tay channel system.

Owel is a low-relief structural closure with potential for stratigraphic upside within the Eocene Tay Member. It does not appear to be on trend with any channel like feature on regional seismic attribute maps. In seismic cross section it looks to be a broad feature with some bright seismic amplitudes with complex geomorphology.  A possible interpretation is for Owel to be a channel feature with sand in the central areas.  Another is that it is a sand injectite feature with the steep shapes being the ?wings? injected upwards from a sandy central base. Injectites are interpreted to provide significant connectivity between the Tay Sandstone units in the producing fields to the south.  Reservoir where encountered is generally good quality reservoir with up to 30 pu porosity and 1 Darcy permeability.  Seal for the Tay Member is provided by the overlying thick, regionally extensive, Upper Eocene and younger Tertiary marine shales.

summary_comment: Grasshopper is a 4-way dip closure mapped in the Paleocene near top Forties Member. It is possible that that there is a stratigraphic component to this trap with the Forties sandstone pinching out up dip.  The whole Forties sequence pinches out onto the West Central Shelf up dip of the Grasshopper structure and is overlain by Late Paleocene/Early Eocene deep marine shales, which act as a seal in the neighbouring producing fields.

The Cyclone prospect is a Upper Palaeocene Cromarty Formation prospect, with a gas cap and oil rim lying in 21/6b and the majority of the down dip oil lying in 21/7b. It has a convincing AVO anomaly which is comparable with similar AVO anomalies recently drilled in the adjacent block to the East (21/8). Sands transported down the slope have ponded against mappable paleo relief, setting up a fill-spill-fill mechanism for material moving down slope. The trapping mechanism is primarily stratigraphic, relying on up and down dip pinch outs across mappable by pass zones, with a differential compaction expression evident over the sand lobes. 
The applicant group plan to test the down dip oil leg in 21/7b, with an expected spud date in Q3 2012.

Mastiff is a Palaeogene stratigraphic onlap trap that pinches out onto the northern flank of the Margarita Spur. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits sourced from the west or southwest. Charge is interpreted to be from the Kimmeridge Clay with an invoked vertical migration pathway to the Palaeogene. The top seal is formed by Palaeogene mudstones. The nearest wells are wells 210/5-1 and 210/4-1 which targeted Jurassic and Triassic reservoirs. These wells penetrated a low net to gross section at the same stratigraphic interval as the Mastiff Lead. However, the wells were drilled on stratigraphic highs updip of the interpreted pinch-out of reservoir sands at the lead. No positive AVO anomalies were observed (Figure 25) and the seismic facies did not show any evidence for coarse clastics. As a result, the lead was downgraded and not matured.
Troilus South Triassic lead. Stacked below cp210_30_1.

The Upper Jurassic Deep Play was identified as a seismic package within the Upper Jurassic section in the mature basin to the east of the area. The lead follows the same concept as the Thunder prospects in the basin to the north with Upper Jurassic turbiditic sands, similar to those that fed the Cladhan system, extending into the basin and occupying the available accommodation space.

The Balder Lead was identified as a bright amplitude directly below the Top Balder reflector. The lead is located at the extremities of the Palaeocene Dornoch deep water turbidite fan system. Although the bright amplitudes do not correspond to the structure at the Top Balder, they appear to form a linear-type shape which could be indicative of a channel and could allow stratigraphic trapping of hydrocarbons at this level.

The Heimdal Lead was identified to the south of the license area as a seismically mappable package, with downlapping internal geometries, which can be tied to the 002/5-12a well up-dip. The lead is located at the northern edge of the northern Heimdal fan which is interpreted to comprise fault-scarp slumps and channelised slope sands, and the pinch-out of this system can be seen on the seismic line. The Lead would rely on stratigraphic pinch-out.

The Saluki Lead identified at the time of the 28th Round application was Paleocene in age and was a stratigraphic onlap trap comprising sands that pinched out onto the northern flank of the Margarita Spur. Subsequent mapping on the 3D survey resulted in the identification of two stacked leads at Saluki which were Paleocene and Eocene in age. However, the absence of seismic facies and positive AVO anomalies suggesting sand presence and hydrocarbons resulted in the downgrading of this opportunity.

The Alsatian Prospect is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap that pinches out onto the northern flank of the Margarita Spur. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastics. Charge is interpreted to be from the Kimmeridge Clay and the top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. Within the prospect there are multiple zones/targets with varied amplitude responses. The nearest wells are 220/26-1 and 220/26-2 which are ~5km to the east. Cretaceous sands were observed in well 220/26-1. Shows in the Cretaceous were observed in both wells. However, no positive AVO anomalies were observed on the 3D survey and the seismic facies did not show any evidence for coarse clastics. As a result, the prospect was downgraded and not matured.

Landseer was identified in the application work on 2D seismic as an undrilled Mesozoic structural high. The reservoir sands were interpreted to be Jurassic shallow water or Triassic fluvial sands in a combination trap, with a top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. On 2D data during the licence application work, there was thought to be evidence of faulting in the Triassic which separated the Landseer Lead from both down-dip and up-dip wells, which both have shows in the Triassic (220/26-2 and 210/5-1 respectively). The Jurassic was absent in both wells and the Triassic was sand-rich but tight. 
However, further mapping on the 3D data has shown there is limited to no compartmentalisation between Landseer and the down-dip and up-dip wells and therefore the lead was down-graded and not matured due to high trap and reservoir risk.

Deerhound is an Upper Jurassic lead on a Mesozoic structural high with a combined structural stratigraphic trap. The high is likely to expose Permo-Triassic/Devonian deposits with potential for Jurassic reservoir sands to have been preserved on the high in isolated lows. The analogue to this lead is Johan Sverdrup. Charge is interpreted to be from the Kimmeridge Clay with the top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. The nearest well is Well 210/4-1 which penetrated the high 10km to the east, but did not encounter any Jurassic deposits. On 2D data the lead had a low geological possibility of success and more detailed mapping on the 3D seismic led to a further downgrading of the lead due to the absence of seismic facies indicative of Upper Jurassic sands as well as the absence of a well-defined trap.

Alano is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits charged from the Kimmeridge Clay in the Magnus Basin with Cretaceous mudstones forming the top seal. Alano is updip of the Cretaceous sands penetrated by the 210/10-1 well in a stratigraphically younger sequence. This well penetrated a thick, high net to gross interval of sands which were dry. However, no positive AVO anomalies were observed on the 3D survey and the seismic facies did not show any evidence for coarse clastics. As a result, the prospect was downgraded and not matured.

Greyhound is an Upper Jurassic lead on a Mesozoic structural high with a combined structural stratigraphic trap. The high is likely to expose Permo-Triassic/Devonian deposits with potential for Jurassic shoreface sands to develop on the high. The analogue to this lead is Johan Sverdrup. Charge is interpreted to be from the Kimmeridge Clay with the top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. The nearest well is Well 210/13-1 to the south of the Greyhound Lead. This well did not encounter any Jurassic sequences and was plugged and abandoned dry after no hydrocarbon indications were observed.

Broholmer is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits charged from the Kimmeridge Clay in the Magnus Basin with Cretaceous mudstones forming the top seal. The key risk is seal; seat seal is deemed high risk due to the potential of onlap onto Triassic sands and fault seal is deemed high risk based on potential late fault movement after charge. No positive AVO anomalies were observed and the seismic facies did not show any evidence for coarse clastics. As a result, the prospect was downgraded and not matured.

summary_comment: Shepherd is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap to the south of the Manet Ridge. The reservoir is interpreted to be shallow water coarse clastics charged from the Magnus Basin by the Kimmeridge Clay, with the top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. Updip of the Shepherd Prospect, 211/2-1 penetrated younger Cretaceous deposits which did not encounter shows. The well was plugged and abandoned as dry. On 2D lines, the Shepherd Prospect is generally observed as single cycle and more rarely, multi-cycle bright seismic events. On a number of 2D lines, downdip amplitude dimming and/or cutoffs can be observed.

infrastructure: BELLMOUTH AT ABANDONED WELL D9 :1288 - WELLHEAD
summary_comment: Camus is interpreted as the syn-rift fill of an Upper Jurassic half-graben. The reservoir is interpreted to be both shallow-water and genetically related deep-water coarse clastics. Charge is from the Kimmeridge Clay with the top seal formed by Upper Jurassic/Cretaceous mudstones. The trap is defined by both stratigraphic pinch-outs and fault seal. Updip of the Camus Prospect are two wells; Well 211/1A-1 to the west did not penetrate any Upper Jurassic, but penetrated sands in the Lower to Mid Jurassic and Triassic with shows in the Lower Jurassic. To the east, Well 211/2-1 also did not penetrate an Upper Jurassic sequence, but shows were observed in sands in the Lower Jurassic and Triassic. In both wells, the Lower Jurassic and Triassic are interpreted to be tight whilst the Upper Jurassic is interpreted to have pinched out downdip.

summary_comment: Broholmer is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap to the west of the Alano Prospect in a stratigraphically younger sequence. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits charged from the Kimmeridge Clay in the Magnus Basin with Cretaceous mudstones forming the top seal. Similar to the Alano Prospect, the Broholmer Prospect is updip of the Cretaceous sands penetrated by the 210/10-1 well in a stratigraphically younger sequence. This well penetrated a thick, high net to gross interval of sands which were dry. On 2D seismic lines, the Broholmer Prospect is identified as a number of bright, single cycle reflectors which onlap onto the slope margin of the East Shetland Platform.

summary_comment: The Lead comprises potential Middle to Late Jurassic sands preserved in a small basin on the Manet High, northwest of the Magnus Basin. The sediments are stratigraphically trapped beneath the BCU with Cretaceous mudstones forming a top seal. The depth of the reservoir is 38004300 m TVDSS. infrastructure: BELLMOUTH AT ABANDONED WELL D9 :1288 - WELLHEAD
summary_comment: Structural dip provides closure to the S, up dip seal to the N is provided by stratigraphic pinchout beneath the BCU. Lateral seal to the W and E is provided by pinchout of the sands. As the lead is located where the shale prone Brent/Dunlin has been totally removed by erosion, base seal is dependent on sealing capacity of Triassic sands and shales, and thus carries additional risk. The age of the interval constituting the lead is outside the area where the U. Jurassic can be mapped with confidence. It is oriented N - S and is clearly controlled by N - S trending faults. It is thus likely that the anomaly forms a channelized slope feeder for the greater Magnus depositional system, thus the sands were sourced from the NNW and fed into the basin towards the basin floor in the Magnus area to the S.

summary_comment: Mossat is an upthrown trap in which the primary reservoir is Brent Group and secondary reservoir is Banks Group. The prospect is located within an actively generating hydrocarbon kitchen. "Mossat is a faulted 4 way dip closed structure which, although clearly elevated above its flanks is difficult to properly evaluate due to poor quality seismic data over the prospect." Due to the depth of the Brent Group over the Mossat prospect, around 11,800ftTVDss, special circumstances are required to have preserved or enhanced reservoir quality, such as early oil emplacement. Due to the proximity of the Mossat prospect to the kitchen "southern portion of 211/13" it is conceivable that Mossat received an early oil charge.

Caliban North is a small lead in block 211/18c. This small lead comprises a Brent reservoir in a downthrown trap sealed by the Humber Group with lateral seal against the Dunlin Group. The depth of burial of the Brent reservoir in this lead would suggest that the Brent Group is likely to be of good quality. Updip of the Caliban North prospect is the aforementioned dry Halibut High. Due to the proximity of this lead to the Halibut High there is a significant lateral seal risk and/or the prospect being off the migration pathway.

Additional potential could exist in the Staftjord Formation (Nansen sandstones, productive in the Don N05z well), but the fault juxtapositions may not be optimal for trapping hydrocarbons at this level. summary_comment:
The Hammerhead prospect is located 3km north of the 214/30-1 Laxford gas discovery well which was drilled near the crest of a mud mound high, onto which the Hammerhead prospect on-laps. The Laxford well (214/30-1) contains a condensed (or non-complete) Vaila Formation sequence (55ft) which is much thinner than surrounding wells (which can extend to >500ft). However due to the nature of the high, the sands penetrated on the mud mound are younger and thinner than those interpreted at Hammerhead and therefore are not a direct analogue.
Hammerhead sits in a stratigraphic low created through differential loading of turbidite flows onto mobile shales which created mud-mounds. This deposition was also disturbed by igneous intrusions and possible reactivation of deeply seated faults. The prospect dips to the north-west where it is interpreted to shale-out onto a localised mud high and potentially spills and fills deeper lying ponds. Up-dip, the prospect on-laps onto a prominent mud high that appears to have grown during turbidite deposition. This mud high separates the Hammerhead fan from feeder channels on the south-east of the high.

summary_comment: Cnut prospect. Mostly in Norwegian waters (total area = 67,731 acres). Palaeocene turbidite fan sands in closure at Top Balder Tuff. CoS = 18%. Relinquishment: the results of chemostratigraphy and heavy mineral analyses did not validate GDF SUEZ hypothesis that sands sourced from East Greeland could reach the Cnut structure. The Shetland platform and Western Norway are today seen as the most likely sand supplies for the area. Clear geometries supporting sand presence have been observed on some 2D lines. This does not however apply to the large Cnut Prospect where sub-parallel reflectors are mapped at the location of the 4-way closure. Hence res effectiveness downgraded.

name_others: REL02142 Cock of the North V
summary_comment:
The COTN prospect was initially interpreted as an extensive Lower Eocene fan complex with an amplitude supported up-dip stratigraphic closure (see Figures 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3) with estimated in place gas volumes of 5.1Tcf. 
The results of the seismic reprocessing and inversion, and rock physics analysis have clearly indicated the absence of gas saturated reservoir sands within the Eocene. 
Detailed seismic to well ties and event mapping attribute the identified amplitude anomaly to the presence of Balder formation volcanics. A subsequent ‘exotic reservoir study’ has determined that the Balder Formation volcanics are likely to be of non-reservoir quality.

The facies prediction of the Arwen lead went from sands, to incision of a muddy and shaly slope. However, it was also recognized that it could also be a feature caused by hydrothermal activity, being the surface imprints due to magma activity below. Analog features to Arwen and Eowyn caused by magma tectonism are observable in the Norwegian Vøring Basin at the Top Balder Formation level. No matter which of the two models the conclusion was the same that Palaeocene reservoir presence is considered unlikely.

The mapped seismic package lies directly above the Base Cretaceous Unconformity (BCU) and is defined by pinchout of the top Lower Cretaceous pick (Valhall Formation) onto the BCU. Deep water submarine fan sequences are likely to form the reservoir sequence in this prospect. A sediment entry point for a 'channel complex' is interpreted to be present at or near the prospect crest and is possibly controlled by active Jurassic - Early Cretaceous faults that intersect the main east - west channel boundary fault. Petrophysical evaluations of the 22/21-4 and 22/21-7 wells have interpreted the intervals in the Sola Formation to be marly sands containing hydrocarbons with levels of 60-65% hydrocarbon saturation. The main risk for this play is reservoir presence and quality and there is a high risk of trap failure along the combined pinch out and fault edge towards the northwest and north.

The Tenterden Lead is a four way dip closed anticline at Top Lower Cretaceous level. It has, however, not been possible to identify the presence of any sand development within the Lower Cretaceous here so it is not considered a viable target. There is likely to be an upside element of stratigraphic closure against the main bounding fault to the east. Stacked Jurassic sands pay is possible although the most likely reservoir target within the Jurassic here is thought to be the Volgian Ribble and/or Freshney sands as seen in nearby well 22/22b-2y. summary_comment: The Culzean N/NW prospect consists of two stacked prospective reservoir intervals. The deeper of the two prospective intervals is the regionally extensive Pentland Formation (mid Callovian-mid Oxfordian in the Culzean area) coastal plain which underlies an Upper Jurassic interval with potential for shoreface and deepwater sand reservoir development. The trap for both intervals is a 2-way fault, 1 way stratigraphic pinch out, which in part relies on a salt ridge to the west, and dip closure to the east. The Pentland trap is more extensive than the Upper Jurassic trap. The Pentland interval relies on a base seal of the Triassic Jonathan mudstone interval, a proven pressure seal at the Culzean discovery. The base seal for the Upper Jurassic would be intra Heather Formation shales. The top seal for both segments is a combination of intra Heather Formation shales and the Cromer Knoll Group marls. The charge route into the prospect is from the Lomond deep to the east where the Kimmeridge, Heather and Pentland Formations are all mature.

The Bass Prospect is a stratigraphic updip pinch-out trap within the Maureen Sandstone, with potential upside in the Mey Sandstone. The hydrocarbon distribution in Everest suggests an initial oil charge, displaced by gas as the source matured to leave a small oil rim. The Bass prospect is situated in an intervening saddle region above which the Maureen thinned through attenuation or non-deposition of the 'M1 Lower' unit. However, high net to gross reservoir sections are developed in 22/5a-11 and 22/10a-8z; the wells immediately north and south of Bass respectively. Hence, there is a high probability of encountering Maureen reservoir at Bass. There is a risk of reservoir degradation, principally through incorporation of non-reservoir, often chalky material which slumped off the Jaeren High. Such intervals are common in East Everest.
The Bass prospect is located close to the pinch-out edge of the Mey Sandstone. This is a significant, secondary reservoir in East Everest but not developed in Fleming and therefore represents potential upside in Bass.

The Bjorn lead is defined on the CGG Veritas PSTM full stack seismic data and as a downthrown trap against the Triassic pod that underpins the Arran South Forties discovery. Koala is mapped on the PGS MegamergePlus seismic data. The Koala trap, as defined on the Base Chalk reflector map, is a three way dip closure on the downthrown side of a fault defining the edge of the Jaeren High, and lies above Jurassic interpod Bjorn Lead. The identification of Koala is based on the existence of a highly reflective package of Lower Cretaceous sediments on the downthrown side of the main Jaeren fault and the recognition of a marked unconformity at the base of this package, which is thought to be related to a mid Lower Cretaceous tectonic phase initiating uplift and subsequent erosion at the crest of flanking, grounded Triassic pods.  CoS has not yet been assigned to this lead

Ursus is regarded as a play concept at this stage.It is a Lower Cretaceous sedimentary wedge lead that wraps around the west and north-western flanks of the Triassic Cinnamon prospect. The base of the Ursus trap is defined by a slightly westerly dipping seismic event, that onlaps the western flank of the Cinnamon prospect. The top of the lead is defined as a steeper unconformable event that dips westward and into a rim syncline adjacent to the Mungo diapir. 
Lower Cretaceous sands are present in several offset wells. 23/16b-2 had a poorly developed Lower Cretaceous sand of less than 6ft thickness and Lomond wells 23/21-2 and -2z both penetrated thin Lower Cretaceous sands, as did 22/19-3. 
The closest offset well, 23/16d-6, has a Lower Cretaceous Valhall section described as being silty, grading to very fine grained sandstone with 'reasonable' porosity; increased connection gas levels were also noted through this zone.

Bear is a partially grounded Triassic Skaggerak formation 'pod' perched on the edge of the East Central Graben. Fault bounded on 3 sides including elements of stratigraphic seal, All the available 3D seismic data suffer from a degree of multiple contamination within the anticipated reservoir section, which presents some risk and confidence issues with respect to the current fault interpretation, degree of compartmentalisation, the stratigraphy, its architecture and clarity and indeed the selection of a suitable well location. The Bear trap is defined at Base Cretaceous Unconformity (BCU) level by a four way dip closure to the north, west, east and south. This four way dip constrains the minimum modelled hydrocarbon column of 560ft (171m). The trap becomes more complex with depth with a combination of stratigraphic seal against salt walls on the north and eastern edge along with fault seal along the north, east and southern edges of the structure.

Four way dip closed Tay Sandstone lead SE of Elke discovery  EnQuest define the geological probability of success,(Pg), as getting on to the predicted the range defined by the P90 - P10 distribution..   .   Trap: 100%, Seal: 80%, Reservoir: 40%, Migration: 70%, Total: 22%.   .   EnQuest uses a probabilistic method for the calculation of resource estimates in exploration targets. Usually input variables are entered as normal distributions, except GRV which is entered as log-normal, and except where offset data indicates otherwise. These are primarily based on the P90 (downside / Min) and P10 (upside / Max) estimates of each input parameter, whilst ensuring P99 and P01 values as reality checks. If the base case is quoted in this application it corresponds to the Pmean value of the distribution. .   It is to be noted that the volumes calculated in the required DECC 'Part 4' prospect summary sheet will therefore be different from the volumes will be carried internally within EnQuest.

The Slough prospect is a 4-way dip closed structure mapped at BCU and Upper Jurassic Fulmar levels. The structure is situated with a NW-SE trending salt-related paleovalley between two Smith Bank Formation (SBF) pods.  The upside to Slough is a stratigraphic pinchout of the Upper Jurassic Fulmar sands against the SBF pod to the west. 
Top seal is provided by shales of the Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation. Slough is reliant on long distance migration (25-30km) along the palaeovalley system linking to the early mature Kimmeridge Clay on the Western Platform and the mature Central Graben. 
Presence of a continuous permeability pathway within the palaleovalley network is the key risk.  
Volumetric parameters are from probabilistic models. MIN = P90, ML = P50, MAX = P10.   .

summary_comment: The Vulcan South Lead consists of a SW-NE trending nose over a salt ridge with the trap reliant on stratigraphic pinchout against the Smith Bank Formation pods. Limited 4-way dip closure may exist on the block boundary of 29/16. The predicted top seal is the mudstones of the Kimmeridge Clay Formation (KCF), which are expected to overstep the Fulmar sands, generating an effective continuous top seal. Blenheim Prospect is a Paleocene synclinal pinchout trap with fault seal on the northern side which exhibits strong amplitude and AVO anomalies. Thin sands found within the Paleocene at well 29/16-1 are seen as an indicator of a nearby sand fairway. 
The postulated 'Blenheim-Watling' fairway differs from those proven and postulated to the North in that it is believed to overly and infill the topography created by a series of Early-Mid Paleocene Mass Transport Complexes. These MTCs are clearly visible in seismic across the application area and tie with Early-Mid Paleocene slump deposits in 29/16-1. Later input of Paleocene turbidite sands flowing from the South West off the shelf are postulated to have ponded immediately above these MTCs, with turbiditic flow possibly influenced by the slump scar. It is these sands which Statoil propose as the reservoir interval for the Blenheim Prospect

summary_comment: Well 29/9a-1 discovered 120 ft of light hydrocarbons in thick Mey sands (in excess of 300 ft gross thickness) and well 29/4a-1 encountered 90 ft gas shows in 465 ft Mey Sands. Looking closer at the log characters the Mey Sandsare generally much thicker than the Cromarty sands but with overall less porosity. They are interbedded with Paleocene silts and claystones representing periods of non-deposition and tectonic quiescence. Hence, these sands have been interpreted as sand sheets or slope apron fans composed by sand lobes and intraformational sealing units. Regional isopachs, DECC Promote UK 2014, suggest the Lista thickens to the south west away from the 29/9a-1 and 29/9a-5 wells, across and beyond the mapped four-way dip closure. It is thought the thickening of the gross interval is related to presence of a thickened Mey sequence. Reservoir quality is seen here as key risk as the sands are likely to become more silty laterally towards the edge of the sand sheet as verified by well 29/9a-5  where poor quality Paleocene sands where encountered.

The interpretation of the Cordelia bounding fault to the west of the well, placing the well inside the Puffin Field, led to an increased the risk of no Skagerrak reservoir on the fault footwall. The Forties lead comprises the Forties Sandstone Member within a trap involving structural dip in 3 directions, plus a stratigraphic edge located benetath the Capercaillie prospect. The lead is located at the very distal end of the Forties Sandstone fairway and as a result sands, where developed, are thin.   
Locally, wells have encountered oil shows in thin, poorly developed sands and silts, but insufficient modern well data are available to resolve saturations confidently in the Forties lead. Furthermore, offset fields (Fram and Courageous) have wells with poor calculated saturations, and yet they flowed dry oil at reasonable rates in DSTs. Consequently, producibility is a key uncertainty for the Forties lead.  It is likely that the Forties lead is in communication withn the overlying Capercaillie reservoirs.

Dawkins is a small dip and fault closed (in the maximum case) structure mapped at the BCU and likely to be a Triassic Skagerrak Sandstone reservoir. Reservoir presence and quality is yet to be proven. Heimdal target with good CoS but possible heavy, viscous oil. However, the sedimentological model and seismic interpretation imply that the Heimdal reservoir target pinches out immediately updip and therefore may not have access to meteoric waters, reducing the risk of heavy oil. The Heimdal Sand can be split into three lobes, L1, L2 and L3. The L1 basinal sands on-lap from the east and are poorly represented on the block.
The L2 and L3 sands were deposited from a medium scale submarine channel-fan
system seen on seismic as a discrete lobe with a 'bird's foot'? morphology. The feeder
channel crossed the East Shetland Platform and spilled onto the Transitional Shelf near well 3/27-2. This access point is at the intersection of a re-entrant fault at the edge of the platform. On the shelf-slope the sediments form braided mid fan channel lobes that shale out to the east and south east. The lobes can be separated out on well data and mapped on the 2D seismic as distinct intervals. The proximal L2 and L3 Heimdal sands have net to gross ratios in excess of 80%, porosities of 30% or more, and excellent permeabilities in the order of 20D. Parameters entered cf cp3_22_1 to _3.

summary_comment:
Ockley is a discovered resource in the same UK Licence block P2455 in Quadrant 30 (see Figure 2). It overlays the Oakwood discovery at approximate burial depth of 12,500ft TVDSS. The field was discovered by BP in 1983 with the 30/01c-2 exploration well and the well abandoned afterwards due to very low-test rates. Between 2008 and 2012 Maersk Oil drilled three appraisal wells (30/1d-10, 30/1d-12 and 30/1d-12z) to further access the viability of the field. Tests in two of the wells (30/1d-10 and 30/1d-12z) failed to achieve stable economic rates. However, the test performance of the 30/1d-12z well following propped and acid fracture stimulations with approximately 70% of the total 4MMscf/d well test rate coming from the one failed propped hydraulic fracture stage, gave some room for optimism for a possible development route for the discovery. 
Ockley is a high pressure (11,000psi) and high temperature (310 degF) gas condensate Hod chalk discovery with extremely low porosity (10 - 12%) and matrix permeability (10 to 50?D). This re-evaluation work covered subsurface re-assessment of the Ockley accumulation to provide Harbour Energy a view on the In-place and recoverable volumes. The work scope also explored available well drilling, completion and stimulation technologies/techniques that would allow better performance success to the prospective wells. The results and lessons learnt from the Maersk 30/1d-12z well formed the basis for the well performance improvement studies undertaken.

The Baffin discovery is situated in the Jacqui sub-basin, in an inverted Upper Jurassic feature that is dip closed against a principal east-west fault system. The basin has three existing discoveries, all testing hydrocarbons within the Jacqui Sandstone Member of the Heather Formation (primary target).  The structure is a faulted anticline with five main compartments that are defined on the basis of fluid type and PVT data. The discovery has been tested by 3 wells, the 30/13-4 and the 30/13-6 wells, and the 30/13-3 well that was drilled in a separate fault block and encountered a restricted hydrocarbon column. The main risk is reservoir connectivity as each discovery well has shown different PVT and pressure data. Compartmentalisation is considered to be both stratigraphic and structural. The 30/13-4 well tested volatile oil/condensate with a GOR of >5000 scf/bbl.  
The well has an apparent ODT @ 13308ft TVDss, which has been used to define a P90 volume for this compartment.

summary_comment: The fill and spill of a Palaeocene aged palaeo-anticline with the growth of the Orion diapir may have resulted in the trapping of hydrocarbons against the northeastern flank of the Orion structure. The palaeo-anticline is formed by differential compaction around a Jurassic and Early Cretaceous NW-SE trending fault or small late stage movement of the same fault. However, the end Palaeocene anticline may be a seismic artefact resulting from pull-up from a high velocity Palaeocene lineament. Iris also overlies a gas chimney and can also be explained by direct charging from a Jurassic age fault.

The P.2050 licence was awarded with a contingent commitment to drill a well on the Komodo prospect to 2150m or 50m beneath the Base Zechstein, whichever is the shallower.
The original interpretation of Komodo was based on 2D seismic data which identified a large low relief structure with primary prospectivity in the Carboniferous to Devonian Buchan Formation.
The acquisition of new 3D seismic in 2012/2013 allowed more detailed and regional mapping and identified the Zechstein carbonates as an additional reservoir target on the Western flanks of the Komodo structure. Zechstein reservoir presence was also supported by a regional well and literature (e.g. publications on the Auk and Argyll fields) study undertaken in 2013 that suggested the Komodo high (an extension of the Auk Ridge) was the site of shallow water carbonate deposition in the Late Permian.

competent base/lateral seal as any Fulmar reservoir is likely to unconformably overlie permeable Palaeozoic

summary_comment:
Dulcy was originally a lead defined as a structural trap at Top Palaeozoic level with potential reservoir targets in the Zechstein carbonates and Rotliegendes/Carboniferous/Devonian sandstones. 
With the new 3D dataset the whole of the Dulcy structure has been clearly mapped and the primary reservoir target is prognosed to be Devonian sandstones as the Permian and Carboniferous are only present on the flanks of the structure.

The Bison Blocks represent a new play within the Southern North Sea. The unconventional resource potential currently being identified onshore UK can be directly mapped to the Bison Blocks. The Carboniferous sequence drilled in Well 41/01-1 is over 4,700 ft. The shales and coals of the Lower Carboniferous section act as both a source of dry gas and also a reservoir as the gas will adsorb onto the surface of organic matter and pool within the intergranular porosity and porosity created within the organic matter as it breaks down during gas generation. The sandstones and limestones will also act as reservoirs and can be further used as carrier beds. This means that horizontal wells could be drilled within these brittle facies and then fractured. It is more efficient to initiate a fracture within a brittle facies and propagate the fracture into a more ductile shale. Using carrier beds in fracture design leads to higher recovery rates for individual wells.

The prospect is an untested 3-way dip closure structure approximately 5 km east of the Tyne platform and between the Tyne North and Tyne South hydrocarbon accumulations. 
The only well available in the area (44/18a-5) has failed to fully evaluate the potential of the structure. 44/18a-5 was drilled in 1997. 
At the well both main targets, the Caister Sand and Lower Ketch were water wet. A gas accumulation occurs in the Transition Sequence above the Lower Ketch, but this was not tested. Petrophysical interpretation of the logs give a Gas Down To (GDT) of 12311' (TVDSS) and a Water Up To (WUT) of 12417'(TVDSS). The RFT plot shows an intersection between the water and gas gradients close to the WUT (cc 12400' TVDSS).  The gas accumulation in the Lower Ketch is still unproven. There is no base Permian closure, and any trap will require a top seal in the shale-prone Upper Ketch. This is similar to the trapping mechanism in the Tyne Fields, but not identical. In Tyne, the top seal is provided by a combination of both Upper Ketch shales and Silverpit Formation shales, the base of the latter truncating the Carboniferous section. There is no base-Permian truncation over the 44/18a-5 area. The fundamental issue is: can a GWC from the Transition Zone accumulation be extrapolated into the Lower Ketch?.   .   
Within the Transition Sequence, the low net to gross ratio suggests that connectivity is likely to be poor.

summary_comment: The Carboniferous Wheatsheaf Lead is a combined structural and stratigraphic trap. It is a major NW-SE trending horst block closure bounded to the north by erosional truncation of the Westphalian C/D reservoir sandstones and to the south by a sealing cross fault. Lateral seal would be provided by the abundant and continuous intra Carboniferous coals and shales of the Westphalian B.  The reservoir target is the Lower Ketch sandstone. The sandstones are developed on-block in wells 44/27-1 and 44/27-2, where they were found to be thick and well developed. The sandstones had a gross thickness of 750 to 1020 ft and 33-35% Net to Gross. Porosities were approximately 10% on average; even at depths of 13,120 ft. Regional data on porosity-permeability relationships indicate that the Westphalian C and D sandstones would have good permeability at the predicted porosities and reservoir depths for the identified prospect.

All three prospects exhibit a high confidence closure at Top Zechstein, Top Rotliegendes and Top Carboniferous levels. However, each structure has a large throw along the NNW-SSE fault, which potentially results in the juxtaposition of the Rotliegendes section against the Bunter Sandstone. This constitutes a considerable risk to a trap breach and is the main factor behind the decision to relinquish the block.

The Admiral and Tempest prospects are both stratigraphic traps comprising a Maureen Formation (Paleocene) sandstone reservoir, and a topseal and lateral seal of Lista Formation shales. Oil is sourced from the Kimmeridge Clay Formation in the South Viking Graben to the east, and is believed to have migrated along a fill-spill pathway through the Mariner Field. Tempest is located to the northwest (up-dip) of the Boatswain Discovery (8/15a-3) and Admiral is located to the west (up-dip) of the Cadet Discovery (8/15-1). 
Detailed mapping of the top Maureen sandstone reflector on new 3D seismic data reveals the Admiral and Tempest fairways in much greater detail than was available prior to application. 
The fairways appear to comprise amalgamated channels and show evidence of later removal of the sand in places.

The Mermaid up-dip prospect represents the up-dip component of the Maureen fairway drilled in 9/11c- 13. The Maureen Fm. thins to the south of the main Mariner Maureen canyon fairway, and in an up-dip north-westerly direction.
An up-dip stratigraphic pinch-out trap is invoked for the Mermaid up-dip prospect, but the extent of the trap geometry and whether it pinches out is uncertain. The Lista Fm. is considered the top seal, but this could be compromised by top-seal breaching by the sand-injectite processes which led to formation of the overlying Heimdal geobodies. Both trap geometry and top seal risks impact the geological chance of success.

The Lista Fm. within the license is relatively thin and shows no indication of the significant jack-up structures or clear seismic reflectivity that characterises the exploitable hydrocarbon-bearing Heimdal Sandstone Member within the Mariner Field (Figure 9 and Figure 10). There are some indications from the seismic data of isolated Heimdal Sandstone Member accumulations, but these are (in general) deeper than the oil-water contact from the nearest wells. 
Indeed, the Heimdal Sandstone Member is present within the two closest wells, 9/11- 3 and 8/15a- 3, at 2 m and 40 m TVD thickness respectively, but both are 100% water saturated.

Bunsen is a four-way dip closed structure located midway between the Bentley and Bressay fields in Block 9/3c. Closure is at the Upper Dornoch formation (now regarded as Lower Eocene age), with top seal being provided by the Eocene Balder tuffs and overlying Eocene shales.  The closing contour is approximately the same as Bentley Field at 3,730 ft TVDSS, which is also the OWC of Bentley; thus it is assumed that Bunsen would be filled to spill. It is considered likely that Bunsen will be charged with oil as the structure lies on the migration route for oil spilling from Bentley into Bressay.  Oil is likely to be of very similar quality to that found in Bentley and Bressay with an anticipated API of between 10 and 11 degrees.  Bunsen measures approximately 1.5 km by 0.5 km, with the structural crest estimated at 3,649 ft TVDSS

The prospect morphology at Camm is similar to that of Chadwick, Cartwright and Clement, in that it is three-way dip closed with lateral seal provided against the East Shetland platform. There are however some differences. Firstly, it is located on an east-west offset of the Viking Graben bounding fault where there is increased structural complexity and some potential fault terraces.

The Church Knowle prospect is mapped as a low relief 3-way and fault, footwall closure. Reservoir potential and trapping configurations have been identified within the Cornbrash and Bridport reservoirs. Additional potential may exist within the Sherwood reservoir although it was not possible to map this due to the poor seismic data quality. The prospect is located in the same fault block as the Bushey Farm and Creech exploration wells, both of which were P&A with oil shows in the Bridport and Cornbrash. It is the belief of this study that both of these wells failed because they were drilled outside or on the edge of structural closure.

The Cloughton prospect has been drilled up by Well Cloughton-1 by Bow Valley and Partners in 1986. The well was targeting a large fault bound Carboniferous anticline imaged on 2D seismic.  DST 2 successfully tested a Carboniferous sandstone interval 7736-7845 ft RKB. This interval is now recognised by Third Energy to be the Skipton Moor Grits. The DST over this interval flowed gas up to 6 Mscf/d without any stimulation. The pressure date from DST 2 did not allow for a reasonable estimation of reservoir pressure and the zone was not regarded as commercial. The sandstones are tight, averaging 7% porosity and saturation was low, up to 35%. The DST on the Skipton Moor Grits flowed  at rates of up to 6 Mscf/d without fracture stimulation. These low flow rates are uncommercial and would require some form of hydraulic stimulation to enhance the flow rate.

The Skipton Moor Grits Derwent Lead is a fault bound footwall anticline plunging to the North. It forms part of a major carboniferous N-S trending antiform which is intersected by younger NNW-SSE faults, which cross cut the structure. The Skipton Moor Grits is a conventional tight gas play, implying that hydrocarbons conform to structural highs. The Skipton Moor Grits are fine to very coarse-grained feldspathic sandstone interbedded with grey siltstone and mudstone. The formation represents the progradation of a turbiditic fronted delta system that migrated from the north to overlay the Bowland Shale equivalent basinal shales.

The Skipton Moor Grits South Derwent Lead is a domal dip closure with a degree of plunge towards the North East. It forms part of a major carboniferous N-S trending antiform, which is intersected by younger NNW-SSE faults which cross cut the structure. The structural configuration of the South Derwent structure is less well defined than the Derwent structure as it is only covered by 2D seismic. The Skipton Moor Grits is a conventional tight gas play, implying that hydrocarbons conform to structural highs. The Skipton Moor Grits are fine to very coarse-grained feldspathic sandstone interbedded with grey siltstone and mudstone. The formation represents the progradation of a turbiditic fronted delta system that migrated from the north to overlay the Bowland Shale equivalent basinal shales.

The West Hose Prospect is based upon two intersecting 2D lines, and lies 3 km north-west of the Long Clawson Oil Field.  A depth structure map of the prospect, at Top Namurian is attached. This places Westphalian and Namurian sands within closure. The closure is based upon a rollover created by a deeper seated fault.  The proximity to Long Clawson Oil Field and to the Kinoulton-1 well means that reservoir presence and quality are low risk.  Additional 2D seismic is required to confirm closure.    An interesting aspect of this prospect is what has been described as a ?flat spot? beneath the closure.  There is possible column height of approximately 170 m from the top of the structure to the base of the ?flat spot?, if indeed this anomaly represents an oil/water contact. Conventional reserve calculations results in 8.2 STOIIP MMbbl and recoverable reserves of 2.46 MMbbl in a maximum case from the Rough Rock sand. Crawshaw, Ashover Grit and Rempstone sands are also possible pay zones.

Yearsley is one of a series of elongate NE-SW anticlines to the north of the east-west trending Flamborough Head fault zone. The structural configuration was defined by isopaching upwards from the deep mid-Asbian seismic marker based on the thickness of the relevant intervals encountered in wells Kirby Misperton-1, High Hutton-1 and Sessay-1. Using this method Top Lower Bowland, Top Upper Bowland, Top Skipton Moor Grits and Top Sabden Shale maps were defined.  Seismic imaging within the Carboniferous is poor on existing 2D data and closure to the south-west needs to be confirmed in any future work programme.

The primary objective in this block pair is the stacked gas saturated sandstones of Namurian and Visean age.  This interval was drilled and logged in several wells in the region, including the Kirby Misperton #1 (which is located about 6 miles north of this block in SE77), a key well for this region.  This area of the Cleveland Basin is the most productive onshore gas province in the UK. Nearly the entire Lower Carboniferous section appears to be gas saturated, similar to areas of East Texas and western Wyoming which are very productive out of stacked, very tight sandstones.   Recent advances in hydraulic-stimulation techniques have made these types of reservoirs attractive targets.  There are a few shale intervals within the Visean section that could also provide secondary targets in the area.  These are seen on the wireline logs of the Kirby Misperton #1 with resistivities averaging 20 ohms; NuTech analyzed these shales and calculated pay for many of them.

The primary objective in this block pair are the tight sandstones of the Millstone Grit seen in all the offset wells in the area.  These sandstones are approximately 80-100 ft thick and are found in the upper Namurian with some additional potential in the lower Westphalian sections.  NuTech petrographic analysis indicates they are tight but HC bearing.  On wireline logs, the sandstones do indeed appear tight (about 10% F), but the mudlogs from the Anston #1 and Warmsworth #1 (which is located in SE50) note gas shows, fluorescence, and HC cut in several of these sandstones.  These types of tight sandstones are productive in many portions of the US, including North Texas and several Rocky Mountain basins, where recent drilling and stimulation techniques have proven effective.  These sandstone reservoirs appear to part of a basin-center type HC accumulation where much of the movable water originally present in the sandstones is driven off and replaced with migrating HCs.

This Application Area, located to the south of Lancaster on the northern limit of the Carboniferous Bowland Basin, has been identified to contain organic rich deep marine shales within the Dinantian Lower Bowland Shales.  By consideration of their geochemical and physical characteristics, the Lower Bowland Shales, of between 200 m to 500 m thick, across the central and western area of the Application Area are both considered to meet the minimum requirements for potential shale gas development. The BHU is organic rich, thermally mature for gas, and is the most prospective, and therefore the major new play concept, within the application area.    The main issues are lack of top seal (thick Wilpshire Grits) and loss of organic rich material on the top of the Rossendale High as evidenced by Roddlesworth 1 (see cross section).  The applicants believe the thicker and deeper basin on the flanks of the Rossendale High may provide for either sufficient thickening of the BHU and/or loss of the Wilpshire Grit sandy facies such that top seal will not be a confining issue.  Using the Visean isochron map, it is seen that the section that contains the BHU thickens from the region of the Rossendale High towards the southwest. The assumption is that a thicker Visean will also mean a thicker BHU, with the potential of the shale being thick enough that the energy from a hydraulic frac would not have height enough to break into the Wilpshire Grit.      This new play area constitutes ~200 km2.

The Kirk Smeaton-1 well to the east has been used to better constrain this play in the licence application areas.  The Bowland Shale of the BHU is an organic rich source rock expected to lie in the wet gas window across the licence application area.  Calculated TOC ranges from 1.1% to 5.96% in the local Kirk Smeaton-1 well, indicating an organic rich source rock. Results from the Kirk Smeaton-1 well indicate that hydrocarbons lie in the wet gas window with Ro values from 1.3% to 1.4%.  The BHU, 135 m thick at Kirk Smeaton-1, has good bottom and upper top seals.   Within the licence application areas, the Bowland Shale is expected to be most prospective in the central basinal areas in between the structural highs associated with the Askern-Spital High/Morely-Campsall fault belt and the Crigglestone Station Fault Belt.  Based on the TWT map at the top Dinantian interval, this prospective paly area consists of approximately 91 km2.

Namurian, Kinderscout shales, as noted in well Kirk Smeaton-1 from 1260 m to 1458 m, may be an attractive target as they have a good bottom seal in the Upper Bowland Shale, and is sufficiently thick at 188 m to endure the poor top seal of the Kinderscout sands. NuTech calculated an OIP MMbbl/sec of 4.579 with but with unfavourably low permeability and porosity. Whether these poor values are due to deep burial or to a local unfavourable facies is unknown at this time. However, thin sands may behave as reservoirs. At Kirk Smeaton-1, a Kinderscout sand between 1345 m and 1351 m tested gas with no water and a flow rate of 1,500 scf/d. This sand had porosities <2% but would provide storage and possible productivity assuming a hydraulic fracture within the shale itself.

Late Namurian (Kinderscout) fluvial sheet sandstones form the principle reservoir target for these conventional play systems; the Rough Rock and Woodhead Hill formations.  The system is sourced by basinal Dinantian and Lower Namurian shales expected to be oil and gas-prone.  Westphalian shales provide the seal to accumulations; and trapping is reliant on both fault and dip seal. Seven Namurian to Westphalian sand zones were tested at Kirk Smeaton-1.  If the sands are within a ?basin centred? accumulation, no structural trap will be required for an accumulation of hydrocarbons.  Poro-perm values calculated by NuTech were low, but the sands are thick enough that they may be considered to be tight gas sand targets that could produce at economic rates through multistage perforations in long reach laterals.

The Hodder Formation is the only unconventional play to have been hydraulically fractured in the UK.  However, in the Cleveland Basin, the lowermost Carboniferous section has not been penetrated by a well and is therefore unproven.  Within the Craven Basin, the Hodder Formation is of Holkerian age and predominantly grey to dark grey mudstone, with subordinate and variable detrital limestone, siltstone and sandstone.  The formation has not been penetrated by any wells within the centre of the basin, although Well Sessay-1, which is on the basin flank, did penetrate a series of Holkerian mudstones and limestones, that are presumed to be the Hodder Formation.  Seismic data shows that this sequence identified at Well Sessay-1 continues down into the centre of the basin and is located beneath the TD of Wells Kirby Misperton-1 & -8.

summary_comment: The Cheshire shale prospect is made up of the upper and lower Bowland shale sequence (Namurian/Dinantina age shales) with thickness upto 1250m and good quality rock properties. The primary objective in this pair of blocks is the lowermost Namurian shale.  This shale interval was drilled and logged in the Blacon East #1 (which is located in SJ36, about 10 miles west of the subject block pair).  This shale is located between 6126 and 6299 ft in this well.  The character of the wireline logs across this shale is similar to what we see in the core area of the Barnett Shale play in the North Texas. This is the optimum stratigraphic situation for a shale play because the limestones act as fracture barriers, allowing for a more effective fracture stimulation.

The basin centre tight gas accumulation (BCGA) prospect relies upon deeply buried Carboniferous Westphalian tight sands with low porosity (5-10%) and extremely low permeability (single micro-darcy) to greatly restrict the migration of gas generated from the interbedded coals.  With continued gas generation over time overpressure conditions could be generated to overcome high capillary pressures, and yield high gas saturations and exceed the frac gradient of intervening shales.  Based on analogues (eg Piceance Basin, Colorado) this process of gas generation, over-pressuring, vertical migration and fracturing on a massive scale in the deeper parts of the Cheshire Basin could result in a pervasive fracture system that provides enough reservoir permeability to allow the microdarcy matrix sandstones to be commercially attractive.

In the Widmerpool Gulf the Upper Dinantinan section tends to be referred to the Widmerpool Formation. Source potential appears to be richest towards the top of the sequence.  In Long Eaton-1, our petrophysical analysis indicates TOC?s of between 0.5-1%, calibrated against measurements from cuttings samples. In Ratcliffe-on-Soar-1, this unit has interpreted TOC?s of between 1-2%, increasing to 1.5-2.5%, locally up to 4.5%.  Cuttings sample analyses over the same interval range from 1.1-3.6% TOC, with measured S2 values of between 1.3-8.8 kg/tonne, indicting moderate source potential.  Two wells (Strelley-1, Old Dalby-1) have penetrated the platform sequences of this age in the area.

A significant Bowland Shale interval was penetrated at all wells in the block, except in Long Eaton-1 where it is eroded. Gross thicknesses range from c.55m at Strelley-1 to at least 296m at Ilkeston-1, where the well TD?s in the Bowland Shale and greater thicknesses are likely. TOC's are generally > 2%, indicating rich source potential. The Bowland Shales are characterised by interbedded sands and carbonates within the shale formations, which may also present the option of a hybrid play ? the presence of carbonate horizons will also enhance the potential for successful hydraulic fracturing operations due to the inherent cleavage in many carbonate minerals. A conventional oil discovery at Rempstone-1 is likely sourced from the Bowland Shale, as are the oil shows in fractured limestones and volcanics at Strelley-1. Overall, the potential for source quality mudstones is proven to exist in the Widmerpool Gulf: of the two blocks, SK44 has the greater Namurian potential.

This prospect represents the upper part of the Long Eaton Formation and may be separated from the lower part by a significant hiatus. The Arundian-Holkerian represents a period of major sea level rise and transgression, when many of the platform highs were drowned.  In Long Eaton-1, our petrophysical analysis indicates TOC?s mostly of between 0.5-1.5%, locally up to 2.7%, calibrated against numerous measurements from cuttings samples. Restoration to original TOC (TOC0) values to account for maturation indicates original organic carbon contents of between 0.8-1.8%, locally up to 3.8%. Whilst spot samples show some good source potential, a thick hot shale interval remains to be identified: as noted above, we expect better quality Arundian-Holkerian source rocks to be developed in other parts of the Widmerpool Gulf.

The Bowland Shale, is a marine, organic rich deposit and 120m-150m thick locally.  Its lateral extent is locally governed by the bounding faults of the Widmerpool Trough. The shale has a good bottom seal and a thick dolerite top seal.  Petrophysical work contracted by the applicants suggests clay content between 30% and 47%, average porosities between 1.5% and 6.9% and TOCs between 2% to 3%.  None of the petrophysical work has been calibrated to core, which is critical to understanding the mineralogy and productive capability of the shale. The shale also has a good bottom seal and a thick dolerite top seal. The calculated OIP differs greatly in wells along the Hoton Fault and wells in the basin centre or along the Cinderhill Fault system; attributed to syn-sedimentary deposition and therefore a lower percentage of organic rich material and higher bulk volumes of water. Combining the better OIP area and drilling depths of 1200m+ results in a high graded area of over 101km2.

The Hodder Formation is the only unconventional play to have been hydraulically fractured in the UK.  However, in the Cleveland Basin, the lowermost Carboniferous section has not been penetrated by a well and is therefore unproven.  Within the Craven Basin, the Hodder Formation is of Holkerian age and predominantly grey to dark grey mudstone, with subordinate and variable detrital limestone, siltstone and sandstone.  The formation has not been penetrated by any wells within the centre of the basin, although Well Sessay-1, which is on the basin flank, did penetrate a series of Holkerian mudstones and limestones, that are presumed to be the Hodder Formation.  Seismic data shows that this sequence identified at Well Sessay-1 continues down into the centre of the basin and is located beneath the TD of Wells Kirby Misperton-1 & -8.

The Early Jurassic aged Lias Group is an organic rich shale hundreds of feet thick. Where mature it is the source rock for oil and gas fields in the UK and throughout Europe, for example Wytch Farm and Oil fields in the Dutch sector. With the increasing interest in unconventional resources the Lias Group has potential for tight oil extraction. Onshore and in the Southern North Sea the Lias is generally considered immature, however there are pockets of Lias that may have been buried deep enough in the past, before being inverted, to generate oil. This area of deep Liassic burial is covered by blocks TA07a and TA08.

summary_comment:
The primary target of the Bertha Lead was originally seen as Beatrice Formation A and B sands.
However, reservoir quality of the A and B sands was now anticipated to be poor west of the Beatrice Field, following the results from the 11/29-1 Manuel and 11/30-6 Sybil wells. Since the Bertha prospect lies broadly between these two wells the chance of finding reservoir quality A and B sand reservoir was now judged to be very low. Consequently, the focus for finding commercial volumes switched to the deeper Middle Jurassic Brora Coal Formation and the Lower Jurassic Orrin Formation reservoirs.
The Top Brora Coal Formation structure was re-mapped using the PA Resources 2012 2D seismic data, which covers the western two thirds of the prospect (Figure 22). This structure has been used to serve as a proxy for the deeper Orrin Formation H and I sands. The estimated STOIIP for the Orrin Formation H and I sands is in the range 18 – 46 – 107 MMstb (Low – Med – High) with corresponding reserves of 3.5 – 14 – 43 MMbbls. The overall chance of success for the prospect was estimated to be low.

summary_comment:
The Eris West Prospect is currently referred to as Aphrodite. Aphrodite is a NW-SE elongate elongated low-relief structure located to the east of the York/Rough fields and to the northwest of the Mercury field. The prospect measures 10km (NW-SE) by 2km at its widest point. It requires hanging wall fault seal at the crest against the Mercury field to the southeast.
The Prospect is defined by faulting on southern, eastern and western sides and dipping to the north side. The crest of the structure lies at the southern end of the prospect where the faulting has limited throw or may not be continuous and so represents a major trap risk.
The primary target is the Permian Rotliegend Leman Sandstone Formation comprising aeolian, fluvial and clastic sabkha facies. Carboniferous potential has not been identified in this area due to poor reservoir quality.

summary_comment: The Inner Pear Discovery was made by well 20/8-2 which proved oil in the Upper Jurassic Buzzard Sandstone Member. The proven accumulation comprises a small oil-bearing 4-way dip closure with an unproven combination structural/stratigraphic upside. The discovery has been mapped on reprocessed 3D seismic data where a top and base J62-64 interval have been picked and cut-offs applied to the resulting isopach to define the pinch-out of the Buzzard Sandstone Member reservoir down-dip of the shale prone 20/8-1 well.  The Gross Buzzard reservoir interval encountered at the 20/8-2 well is 102.1m and contains 10.1m net reservoir sands mostly present within two main sand intervals. The upper of these intervals has an ODT at -2,797 mtvdss whilst the lower sand is water-bearing. The ODT within the 4-way dip closure defines the discovery P90 area whilst the P10 case assumes the sands are filled down to the WUT of -2,840 mtvdss in the lower sand of the 20/8-2 well.

summary_comment:
The Polly discovery (formerly the Delta Prospect) was drilled by well 12/26c-5 in June 2008 on the western margin of the elongate, tilted fault block structure (Figure 6). The reservoir was 88 ft deep to prognosis with the well finding a 14 ft oil column above a -6,856 ft TVDSS OWC in the A sand (Figure 17). The underlying Middle and Lower Jurassic sands were water bearing. The well TD was in the Triassic at 7,959 ft MD (-7,809 ft TVDSS).
The gross A sand thickness was 59 ft with a N:G of 75%, average porosity of 12% and water saturation of 24%. The average porosity was lower than expected when compared to that of the neighbouring Beatrice Field at 17%. Petrographic analysis of cuttings suggest that porosity has been reduced by diagenetic quartz overgrowths and carbonate cementation. The impact of reduced reservoir quality was seen in the MDT programme which failed to establish pressures in the water leg due to a tight reservoir and seal failures in the oil column

summary_comment:
The Dragon discovery was first drilled by Marathon in 1994 and subsequently appraised in 2005 with well 103/1-2. On Providence's interpretation Dragon extends from Irish block 51/1 into UK block 103/1.
In 2014 the Dragon 3D seismic dataset was re-reprocessed, with the aim of improving data quality to yield higher confidence depth structure maps and to assess the validity of a hydrocarbon related EEI anomaly. Data re-processing and subsequent re-interpretation was completed in 2015. The results of this work yielded improved imaging of the structure of the Dragon field, however quantitative analysis indicated that no direct-hydrocarbon indicator (DHI) was evident. The presence of apparent DHI on the older seismic dataset was attributed to lithological effects. Resultant volumetric calculations show greatly reduced gas-in-place volumetric estimates, and no indication of upside potential as previously indicated by EEI.

summary_comment: The Christian Discovery was drilled by Shell Exploration in 1991 targeting the Jurassic anticline approximately 4km from north to south and 2.5km from east to west situated on the western margin of the Western Central Graben. The Tobermory lean (<1 bbl/MMscf) gas discovery is located in ~1600 metres of water and situated 175 km NNW of the Shetland Gas Plant on the Shetland Isles and 120 km NNE of the Laggan Field. The Tobermory discovery well (214/4-1) was drilled in 1999 by the licence operator at that time Mobil. 
The Tobermory thermogenic gas accumulation at a depth of 2625 m TVDSS, is trapped by a combination of gentle folding (Miocene) and morphology of the depositional lobes. The 4-way dip structure is 8.5km x 3km and the average gas column along the main axis of the fan is about 35m. There is good agreement between the last closed contour, an amplitude anomaly and a seismic flat-spot. The reservoir belongs to the extensive Mid Eocene Strachan turbiditic fan system, located at about 1 km burial depth.

The Bunnehaven minor discovery (well 214/9-1 drilled in 2000 by the licence operator at that time; ExxonMobil) is located 18km south of Tobermory in 1540m water depth. 
The well is considered to have found 6.5m of net gas sand stratigraphically trapped in sands of the Upper Paleocene interbedded with volcanic sills at a depth of 3800m TVDSS. Logged porosities were low ~17%. The discovery well was not cored nor was it tested. Cased hole pressure logging was attempted but was inconclusive probably due to the absence of cement behind casing. The absence of any permeability information means that productivity from any wells is a key risk although gas shows were observed whilst drilling. Note that sands below the volcanic sill were deemed tight at time of drilling.

The 9/15b-3Z discovery is an oil discovery made at two levels. Both the Alpha and Alpha East prospects are injectite wing features within the Eocene Frigg formation host shale.

Recent exploration work in-house to explore the prospectivity of the Cambo Basement and Lancaster discovery trend has shown that there is potential in similar buried hill basement plays, including the Nave basement structure. Bridge Petroleum has successfully modelled and history matched the Galapagos Field (previously known as NW Hutton and Darwin) and has submitted a FDP for a redevelopment.  In doing so Bridge Petroleum has attained a deep level of knowledge on the geology of the region, which is seen to continue updip to the East into the now abandoned Qwest and Hutton Field Brent Fields.  With the event of a redevelopment in the Galapagos region, new infrastructure will be in place that could allow further re-evaluation of Qwest and the Hutton Field with the aim of identifying any remaining targets that could be tied into this development, thus maximising economic recovery of the region.

The Scalesia Prospect is a fault bound terrace, situated between the upthrown Hutton and downthrown NW Hutton Fields.  The throw along the terraces bounding faults is variable, although there is offset, there is Brent ? Brent juxtaposition on both the Eastern and Western faults.  This highlights the key risk on the prospect, containment, due to this apparently unfavourable juxtaposition relationship.  However local data in the NW Hutton field identifies that seismically mapped faults with this juxtaposition relationship are capable of holding 100?s ft of column height and can act as sealing compartment bounding faults.  Fault seal analysis will be a key component of this applications work programme for the Scalesia Prospect. No wells penetrate the terrace, but two key exploration wells in the region, 211/27c-12 and 211/27-7 encountered a full Brent sequences with good reservoir quality and as such provide controls on the stratigraphy and properties likely present within the structure.

summary_comment: The Bennett structure lies beneath the north western limb of the Gordon Field near the southern margin of the block. It forms elongate structure approximately 9Km long by 2Km at the crest of a northerly dipping rotated fault block under a NW-SE trending salt swell. Regional information from Cavendish suggests that the principle reservoir is the Westphalian A shoreface sands which are overlain and sealed by the coals and shales of the Caister formation. A secondary reservoir may exist in the Namurian Kinderscoutian as seen in the offset Kepler and Copernicus discoveries . A simple migration path from beneath is expected, as the Gordon Field above is charged via the adjacent Tertiary dykes. Imaging of the lead is moderately good, although depth migration is required to properly position the rotated fault block and faults. Sand quality is expected to be very good with porosity and permeability above the regional Carboniferous average.

The Suilven Jurassic Prospect comprises a 3-way dip closed structure, truncated against a fault or fault escarpment.

The seismic event is predominantly evident as a basement parallel reflection, indicative of a pre-rift setting, with no observed thickening into faults. 
The prospect has been hypothesised as Jurassic Kimmeridge Fm. through seismic facies, indirectly tied to the J110 sequence in the 204/15-2 Nave well, located on the crest of Nave intra-basinal high. summary_comment: Camomile: The most promising lead given its proximity to the graben; however, the basin model suggests that the Kimmeridge Clay Formation would only be relatively immature here due to the lower throw of the WCG Fault tipping out towards the south. Charge access to the basinal source rocks is likely impeded by a Smith Bank pod and the Zechstein evaporites towards the south and the retreating thrust front of the Centurion complex towards the north. summary_comment: Ferrobustamite is a large, very uncertain 3-way dip closed structure against the major Rona Ridge bounding fault. It sits in a large basement embayment which is likely to have been a favourable position for sediment deposition. Seals are likely to have formed within the Early Cretaceous and Jurassic, creating potential for three separate columns defined at K60, K40 and Top Jurassic. Volcanic sills, significant burial depths and a gap in the 3D seismic in the middle of the lead mean that the lead is poorly imaged and largely model driven. Gas is assumed to be the most likely phase, in which case the traps are thought to be limited by column height, and much smaller in area. Key risk is Reservoir Deliverability or quality.

summary_comment: The Godet Prospect is located in the northern part of Block 14/28. The target reservoir is the Piper Fm sandstone, analogous to the productive reservoirs in the Renee, Ivanhoe, Rob-Roy and Hamish fields. The trap is formed across a broadly N-S trending structural nose that is highly faulted resulting in the potential for significant compartmentalisation. The Piper reservoir appears to be completely eroded off the very crest of the structure resulting in a stratigraphic element to the closure. The trap is dip-closed to the east with a combination of fault and pinch-out closure to the north and west. The top and lateral seals are provided by the overlying Kimmeridge Clay Fm. The prospect area and reservoir thickness is defined by directly mapping the top and base of the Piper reservoir interval on the PGS Megasurvey seismic dataset.

The Paget Prospect at Galley level comprises a stratigraphic trap with Upper Jurassic turbidite sands mapped to pinch-out to the west onto an underlying Upper Jurassic tilted fault block. The structure is dip-closed to the south and east and in the P10 case relies on fault seal against downthrown Kimmeridge Clay / Valhall Formation to the north. The presence of reservoir sands are proven in the down-dip 14/29-1 well.

The Stokes Lead area is defined by an area of negative (soft) seismic amplitude in the PGS Megasurvey, which is believed to correspond to an oil-bearing Andrew Member channel sandstone.
