trap_type_comment: stratigraphic trap with up-dip onlap on to topographic high
summary_comment: Burgess was initially defined by a far offset seismic reflection anomaly (Class 2P) at the Forties level. Ji-Fi inversion indicates an anomalously low Vp/Vs signal (i.e. Vp/Vs <1.7), which after facies classification is attributed to either an oil or a gas/condensate facies response. Burgess is located at the distal end of two converging channel systems, one emanating from the Kilgour anomaly and another larger, differentially compacted, channel that flows down the western edge of Block 23/21b. This larger channel splays into the vicinity of the Burgess anomaly. Burgess?s trapping geometry is less robust when compared to Kilgour and Hardie, with little obvious dip closure to the north, south or west and therefore is primarily a stratigraphic trap. Clear up-dip, on-lap onto the topographic high south of Lomond separates the Burgess anomaly from the Toad discovery and the Toad North lead.

trap_type_comment: combination trap with on-lapping pinchout to topographic high to the east
summary_comment: The Hardie prospect is also defined by a far offset seismic reflection anomaly (Class 2P) at the Forties level and is again verified by the Ji-Fi inversion to have anomalous Vp/Vs (i.e. Vp/Vs <1.7), consistent with a mixed oil or gas/condensate bearing facies response.  The Hardie prospect is also situated within an unconfined distributary channel. Hardie is anticipated to have reservoir properties similar to those of Kilgour and Burgess. Hardie is a combination trap with on-lapping pinch-out to the east, onto the topographic high separating Hardie from Columbus. To the north, south and west, subtle dip closure is evident and appears to be caused by differential compaction of the channel lobe. The nearest well to the Hardie anomaly is 23/16f-11, which is the Columbus discovery well, drilled 1.8 km up-dip.

summary_comment: The Kilgour prospect is an Upper Forties Member prospect situated within a distributary channel that diverted around the Mungo diapir and splayed into the unconfined space in the local basin west of Lomond. Kilgour is expected to have reservoir properties similar to the Columbus and Toad reservoirs but with elevated net to gross ratios due to its location within the graben and the main Forties fairway. A strong ?Class 2P? reflectivity response at Kilgour has the expected phase change between near and far offsets, anomalously decreased Vp/Vs (i.e. Vp/Vs <1.7) and associated hydrocarbon attributes (Hydrocarbon Projection & Ji-Fi Facies) that are similar to those of Columbus. Kilgour is a combination trap that pinches out to the east, onto the topographic high of the Lomond Field?s diapir. To the north, south and west subtle dip closure is evident and appears to be related to differential compaction of the channel system. The nearest well to the Kilgour anomaly is 23/21-7 ~2.4 km up-dip.

summary_comment: Toad North is part of the Toad discovery. The Toad discovery well tested a channel feature that runs along the western edge of the Lomond diapir and encountered a 42ft hydrocarbon accumulation. Toad North is 1km up-dip of the Toad discovery well and has a significantly decreased Vp/Vs and increased hydrocarbon attribute response. Reservoir parameters are considered to be very similar to those encountered in the Toad discovery well. The connection between the discovery well 23/21-5 and the Toad North anomaly is unclear, however, seismic attribute analysis suggests a separation between the anomaly identified in this study and the well. The possibility that the Toad North anomaly is the gas cap to the oil leg encountered in 23/21-5 also cannot be discounted. Toad and Toad North have a similar trapping geometry to that of the Columbus discovery with a combination trap that relies on dip closure except along the NE edge of the prospect.

Furasta is a gas discovery that is sourced by underlying Carboniferous coals. The reservoir interval is the Bunter Sandstone unit capped by the overlying Leine halite member. The trapping geometry for this reservoir is a four-way dip closure formed during the halokinesis of the underlying Zechstein salt and related deformation of the overlying strata. The analogue for this field is the Agincourt gas field due to its nearby locality and similarity in reservoir intervals.

trap_type_comment: Salt Diapir - inner side seal against Zechstein evaporites and top seal by Tertiary mudstones
summary_comment: A low risk, diapir flank trap sealed against Zechstein salt and prospective at Cretaceous/Danian chalk and Palaeocene sandstone levels. Closest analogues are Machar, South Pierce and Mungo fields. Diapir flanks are challenging to image seismically, with common seismic processing/interpretation pitfalls, and the Isolde trap is not imaged on most 3D data. Analogue calibration data coupled with an up-to-date structural model have been used to generate a top Palaeocene depth map with c. 1500m of relief. The map has been structurally validated and is supported by partial imaging on dual azimuth 3D, thereby reducing trap risk. 23/26-17, some 900m down-dip, found oil shows in Palaeocene sandstones and by analogy with similar fields is interpreted to lie a short distance below the OWC. Leakage of gas and oil is proven by shallow well 30/1-7 and since leakage is ubiquitous over analogous fields, is not a significant risk. All 13 of the analogous CNS diapirs hold hydrocarbons in flank traps.

The targeted structure sits to the east and in the hanging wall of the F1 fault system. This fault system demarcates two broad pressure cells with Pre-Cretaceous reservoir being normally pressured west of the fault and over pressured to the east. The Assynt J40 prospect targets Callovian age (J40 sequence) sands. These turbidite sands were deposited as a result of region wide erosion of the emergent East Shetland Platform and through local footwall degradation of the major Beryl Field rotated fault blocks. The prospect is up-dip from the 9/14-15a wet well drilled in 2014 by MPX testing a larger Upper Jurassic concept, although this well did not drill deep enough to test the J40 sequence.  The Assynt J40 prospect can likely be stacked with the Assynt J60 and Ard prospects.

summary_comment: Ferrobustamite is a large, very uncertain 3-way dip closed structure against the major Rona Ridge bounding fault. It sits in a large basement embayment which is likely to have been a favourable position for sediment deposition. Seals are likely to have formed within the Early Cretaceous and Jurassic, creating potential for three separate columns defined at K60, K40 and Top Jurassic. Volcanic sills, significant burial depths and a gap in the 3D seismic in the middle of the lead mean that the lead is poorly imaged and largely model driven. Gas is assumed to be the most likely phase, in which case the traps are thought to be limited by column height, and much smaller in area. Key risk is Reservoir Deliverability or quality.

Key risk is charge access.

The Bonneville reservoir comprises Tay and Cromarty sandstone members of good quality; porosities greater than 30% and core air permeabilities in the region of 6-8 Darcies. The reservoir is made up of remobilised injectite sandstones.   Trapping is stratigraphic.  The nearby Catcher Area fields and Laverda Discovery are all considered excellent analogues.  Only the Tay reservoir has been evaluated to date.  Cromarty volumes are considered too small to be worth detailed investigation.
Evaluation work to date has concluded that the optimal development of Bonneville will be a single well drilled into Bonneville East from the Burgman Field Drilling Template 2, c. 3.5km to the North.  Production would be commingled with the Burgman fluids, and transported to the Catcher FPSO for processing.  With current plans for development drilling at Burgman, all the required facilities to drill and control a development well at Bonneville exist.'

The K2 prospect is a Forties Member prospect, adjacent to but structurally separated from the Everest Field.  K2 is a four-way, dip closed structure with general structural conformance of hydrocarbon attributes.
K2 has a strong Class 2 reflectivity response, indicating high-GOR fluids.  The anomalously low Vp/Vs ratio and associated hydrocarbon attributes broadly conform to the prospect?s 4-way closure. Using the distribution of hydrocarbon attributes, two separate compartments have been identified within the mapped closure of K2. In this application the two accumulations are termed K2-North and K2-South. Structural mapping and the hydrocarbon attributes lateral distribution indicates the K2 OWC is at 8650 ft TVDss. 
Pressure depletion from Everest production represents the main risk to K2. Additional risk comes from the possibility that the hydrocarbon signal could be produced by uneconomic, low-saturation gas.

The trap for the Asiago lead is a stratigraphic pinch-out of the Lower Cretaceous sandstones on the western flank of a NW-SE trending, fault-bounded depocentre (Figure 6-26 and Figure 6-27). The stratigraphic pinch-out edge is defined by isochore contours, with the 21/14b-3 well providing an updip well control point where the Lower Cretaceous sands are present, conceptually thinning away from the depocentre, as seen in the analogous Brodgar basin to the north. The eastern limit of the lead is constrained structurally by the juxtaposition against the Jurassic South Bennachie prospect and has therefore been mapped as a 3-way stratigraphic closure towards the west. It should be noted that the prospects crosses the license block boundary.

summary_comment: The prospective reservoir at Bacchus South is the Jurassic Fulmar sandstone. The Bacchus South structure is a hanging wall fault block juxtaposed against interpreted Rattray volcanic footwalls to the south and west. Faults and a basin low trending NW-SE separate the Bacchus South determined area from the producing main Bacchus blocks. The structure of the Bacchus South block is shown in Figure 6-4 and the area consists of a number of fault blocks. The crest of the structure is estimated at -3583m TVDss.

The Fulmar is interpreted to truncate against Rattray volcanic highs to the North and West, analogous to the main Bacchus field. It is constrained further to the Northwest by the 21/10-7 well which did not encounter any Fulmar sand, Figure 6-16. The area has an average mapped thickness of 30m (Figure 6-3), near the tuning thickness of 26-34m. The interpretation of the Fulmar suggests that there is structural continuity of the main Bacchus field to Bansko. A structural low (Figure 6-2) indicates a potential spill point disconnecting the two areas, though this is dependent on depth conversion and OWC used.

summary_comment:
'The Bennachie structure is a 3-way dip closure against a fault at the BCU. The prospect relies on Upper Jurassic Fulmar reservoir sandstone being trapped on the Forties-Montrose High (Figure 6-20). 
The 21/15a-2 well was the initial discovery on Bennachie. Subsequently a number of follow-on wells failed to find sand or hydrocarbons (21/15a-3) in an up-dip location to the initial 21/15a-2 well (21/15a-7 & 21/15a-8). Apache have re-interpreted the Bennachie area, and propose that a potential down-dip extension of the Bennachie discovery is located in an area of mappable Fulmar reservoir. Such an extension to Bennachie relies on fault sealing to the NW to isolate any accumulation from the 21/15a-5 dry hole. 
Formation pressure evaluation shown in Figure 4-14 clearly demonstrates the ability of faults to act as pressure barriers as there are significant variations in the formation overpressure between the wells in the Bennachie area. It is the combination of the thickening of the mapped Fulmar Formation reservoir interval towards the West Central Graben and the observed pressure isolation that makes Bennachie an exciting opportunity.

The Forties sandstone reservoir is a Palaeocene turbidite channel complex fed from thick Palaeocene deltaic deposits in the Buchan and Witch Ground Grabens. The top seal is provided by pelagic shale of the Sele Formation, which was deposited in anoxic bottom-water conditions. Good reservoir quality has been proven with an average porosity of 26%, permeability of 500 mD and a 75% net to gross typically encountered throughout the Forties field.

With migration from the South Viking Graben unlikely the Dora prospect relies on a fill-spill migration pathway from Agnes. The risks are increased relative to Agnes to reflect the downfaulted nature of the trap, increase migration distance from the Wytch Ground Graben and increased risk to reservoir higher on the platform.

summary_comment: The Michael prospect is a combined structural-stratigraphic trap that relies on up dip pinch-out on to a Devonian high in order to seal towards the south. At the time of application the downdip extent of the prospect was highly dependent upon the AVO attribute. The prospect outline has been revised following the Pip well, resulting in a much-reduced prospect outline. Reservoir is not considered a significant risk to the Michael prospect, but migration is, due to the long distance from the SVG and a lack of shows in the Jurassic and older stratigraphy in wells situated to the east of the prospect.

The Peggotty prospect (Appendix A) is a 3-way dip-closure situated on a downfaulted terrace in the southwestern part of the P2365 licence. The key risk to the prospect is trap seal due to cross-cutting faults that could act as leakage points. The prospect outline has been slightly modified based on the new reprocessed seismic data with the eastern dip closure being pushed slightly further east, but the prospect has not changed significantly since access. The Upper Jurassic Piper Fm is still considered to be present in the Peggotty prospect, however, this does carry a considerable risk. The prospect is believed to be charged from the KCF in the Wytch Ground Graben.

The Fulmar is interpreted as being deposited in an interpod formed on the northern at the head of the West Central Graben basin along the margin of the Orkney High. Arolla consists of a combination 2-way dip and pinch-out to the NW and the NE on a Triassic pod. The mapping of the trap is constrained by 21/14b-2 to the South of Arolla which penetrated the Permian Zechstein after drilling a relatively thin Kimmeridge Clay interval. Despite the relatively poor seismic character over Arolla, it is clear that there is a potential Upper Jurassic interval which pinches out to the north-west.

trap_type_comment: pair of east-west half-grabens located on the southern margin of the Forties high
summary_comment: La Plagne consists of pair of east-west half-grabens located on the southern margin of the Forties high (Figure 6-16). Well 21/10-9 discovered an oil accumulation in the southernmost half graben and was subsequently followed up by a dry hole with the 21/15a-5 appraisal well. The 21/10-9 and 21/15a-5 wells limited the size of any accumulation in the southern half-graben; however, an opportunity still remains in the northern half-graben. The prospect consists of Jurassic Fulmar equivalent sands which may pinch-out before the northern bounding fault.

The Lecht prospect sits on a structural nose to the west of the Forties field and is separated by a saddle. The prospect is supported by an amplitude response which requires further technical investigation. The trap is a combination structural stratigraphic trap with dip closure to the south, east and north; whilst in arc oriented north-west to south-west the trap is interpreted to be stratigraphic. The structure continues to rise towards the stratigraphic pinch-out. Seismic evidence indicates that a channel and lobe complex terminates the Lecht channel in this up-dip direction.

The trapping mechanism in the South Bennachie prospect is a fault-bounded structural anticlinal trap, shown in Figure 6-22. Two wells have been drilled nearby, 21/15a-1 and 21/15a-6, both of which encountered Fulmar Sandstones oil shows. Well 21/15a-6 is located within the structural closure and any potential hydrocarbon accumulations will be updip of this well in a shallow 4-way dip closure.

South Glencoe is a combination stratigraphic and structural trap, located along strike from West Glencoe in a small half graben. It consists of the Fulmar Sandstones onlapping to the west and east onto the Pentland or Rattray below. A half-graben-bounding fault system delineates the prospect to the south, whereas to the north the prospect is limited by the pinch-out geometry of the Fulmar on to the rotated footwall of the northern half-graben fault.

The Mertz lead is a structurally enhanced stratigraphic pinch-out trap within the Lower Cretaceous Britannia Sandstone. The southern margin pinches out onto the pre-Cretaceous Rattray High whilst the north and eastern limits rely on dip closure. There is a slight element of fault seal to the north-western region although it is possible that this is not required depending on column height. The down-dip 15/29b-4z and recent 15/29c-16 wells both have a large section of Britannia Sandstone and contain shows.

The Perez prospect is a downthrown fault bounded closure updip of the 21/2-10 which was water-wet in the Sgiath reservoir. It underlies the Volgian Erebus prospect. The northern margin is the basin-edge fault south of the Rochelle Field. The eastern edge is formed by a southeast-northwest trending fault down-throwing to the west. The western edge is formed by a north-south trending fault also down-throwing to the west.

The Rennick prospect is a fault enhanced stratigraphic trap. The western margin is defined by stratigraphic pinch-out of the Lower Cretaceous Britannia Sandstones onto the pre-Cretaceous Rattray High. The northern limit utilises a proven fault seal which separates the Leverett accumulation from the Brodgar Field.

Scaramanga is an Upper Jurassic Fulmar interpod, analogous to the Howe and Bardolino discoveries. It is currently mapped as being an isolated interpod, bound on all four sides by Triassic pod material (akin to the Bacchus field). Charge is challenged by overlying immature Kimmeridge Clay, and would require a thin connection to the interpod network to the north-east. Fulmar reservoir is sourced locally from exposed Skagerrak highs. Top seal and side seal are provided by the Kimmeridge Clay and Triassic pod material respectively.

Trevelyan is an Upper Jurassic Fulmar interpod, analogous to the Howe and Bardolino discoveries. The prospect contains a four-way dip closure in its centre, and has three potential leak points to the north-west, north-east and south. Charge requires migration through the interpod network from the mature Kimmeridge source area to the south-east. Fulmar reservoir sands are predicted to fill the interpod, with top seal provided by the overlying Kimmeridge Clay.

summary_comment:
Crawley is a stratigraphic/structural trap on the northern margin of the Westray Ridge. It is a T34 basin floor fan complex prograding from the Westray Ridge, with proven reservoir in surrounding wells (e.g 204/18-1). 
Charge migration is provided through small scale faulting and sills emplaced in the lower Palecocene (T10-20) but may be challenged due to thick Paleocene shales and a lack of migration
focus. Lateral and top seal is provided by upper T34 shales. 
Crawley is characterised by a bright far stack amplitude anomaly.

Morgan is a remapped closure at T36 level and is located above the Westray Ridge basement high. 
The structure is a combinatation of 4-way dip connected to 3-way dip against a sill in the south-west. 
The basement high provides a favourable migration focal point for hydrocarbons to overlying stratigraphy, enhanced by the proximity of the sill adjacent to Morgan. 
Whilst the sill can act as a lateral seal and pathway for mirgating hydrocarbons, it also presents an element of seal risk and reservoir degradation risk by guiding hot fluids to reservoir levels. 
T36 shales are a well-known regional seal and provide top and lateral seals for the overall closure.

The Tonale prospect, shown in Figure 6-12, is a Tertiary prospect with far stack amplitude support. The prospect has a similar seismic response to offset accumulations within the Supra-Charlie (at Forties field), and at the Scolty, Crathes and Torphins discoveries. The trap is a 3-way dip closure with stratigraphic closure along a channel edge forming the southern margin of the prospect. The prospect is bound on its northern and southern margins by faults associated with compaction of overlying units around the Cromarty channel system.

The seismic pick is well defined on the modern, high quality Rona Ridge (RR13) 3D survey, and also the AMR and NSR 2D seismic datasets.

At the time of application, Well 205/15-1 (Craster Prospect) was being drilled approximately 5 km to the north-west of Well 206/11-1 to possibly explore for a deeper contact reliant on a stratigraphic trap against the Rona Ridge to the south-east. Should this well prove to be successful, the structure could form part of a far larger accumulation within a stratigraphic trap against the Rona Ridge.

The Buzz Prospect has been defined by mapping the top of the basement across the Rona Ridge. The seismic pick is well defined on the modern, high quality Rona Ridge (RR13) 3D survey, and also the AMR and NSR 2D seismic datasets. Well 205/20-1 provides a robust seismic-to-well tie for the basement reflector.

The Buzz Prospect is a Lewisian basement reservoir in a structural upthrown horst block. The fractured Lewisian Basement reservoir is well established on the Rona Ridge and has produced at economically viable production rates over short periods of time at the nearby Lancaster discovery.

The spill point of the structure is mapped to be towards the south-west towards Well 205/20-1. The structural crest is located in the centre of the prospect at 2,300 mTVDss and the closure potentially extends over an area of 5.2 km2 (P10 case).

Skua was developed by Shell as part of the Heron cluster which is a subsea tie-back to the ETAP platform. There are two exploration / appraisal wells (22/24b-7 and  9) and one development well, S01s1.  Skua was on production from 2001 to 2006.  The licence was relinquished by Shell in 2016, but the subsea infrastructure remains in Shell ownership.  The development well has integrity issues and will need to be abandoned by Shell

BPs overall objective in securing the sub-area of 22/24f covering the Skua field is to reach an FDP or drop decision for a Skua redevelopment within 4 years of being awarded the licence. This will encompass the facilities upgrades required and potential two-well redevelopment comprising a central Skua attic producer in the same fault block as the original Shell S01s1 well, and a southern producer in the Upper Skagerrak in the same fault block as well 22/24b-9.

Brightening of reflector strength at Top Ormkirk can be observed on the seismic section and in amplitude maps.

The structure represents a separate culmination of the Rona Ridge to the Johnnie Prospect and lies directly beneath the Lower Cretaceous Victory gas discovery. It has a very similar setting to Lancaster-Halifax discovery to the south where a shallower gas discovery in Lower Cretaceous sandstones was also made (Well 205/23-2, Bombardier gas discovery), before the potential of the basement was recognised.

The Paddy Prospect has been defined by mapping the top of the Devonian-Carboniferous Clair Group within the West Shetland Basin, and towards the south-western flank of the Rona Ridge. The seismic pick is reasonably defined on the modern, high quality Rona Ridge (RR13) 3D survey, and also the AMR and NSR 2D seismic datasets. 
The crest of the trap is at 2,800 mTVDss. The spill point of the structure is mapped to be towards the north-east towards the analogue Clair Field.

The reservoir is a continental Devonian / Carboniferous clastic reservoir as found in Clair.

The prospect has been defined by mapping the top of the Commodore Sandstones tied to Well 206/11-1. The seismic pick is well defined on the modern, high quality Rona Ridge (RR13) 3D survey, and also the AMR and NSR 2D seismic datasets.

In Well 206/11-1, over 400 m of sandstones were penetrated from 3,500m TVDss, with a DST flowing 1.65 MMSCFD gas from the upper section (3,522 to 3,531 mTVDss). Oil and gas was also observed seeping from fractures in the core taken, and gas shows were noted continuing down to 3,880 mTVDss. At the time of application, Well 205/15-1 (Craster Prospect) was being drilled approximately 5 km to the north-west of Well 206/11-1 to possibly explore for a deeper contact reliant on a stratigraphic trap against the Rona Ridge to the south-east. Should this well prove to be successful, the Screwball Prospect could be demonstrated to form part of a large stratigraphic trap.

Carver is an Upper Jurassic Fulmar interpod, analogous to the Howe and Bardolino discoveries. It is currently mapped as being an isolated interpod, bound on all four sides by Triassic pod material (akin to the Bacchus field), but may have a thin connection to the interpod network to the south. Charge is provided by downward migration from the overlying mature Kimmeridge Clay, which also acts as the top seal. Fulmar reservoir is ubiquitous in surrounding well penetrations (22/7-1, 22/7-2RE and 22/8a-4), and modelled to be sourced from local Skagerrak highs. Top seal and side seal are provided by the Kimmeridge Clay and Triassic pod material respectively.

summary_comment: The Wherry NE lead is based on RMS amplitude extractions and detailed seismic extraction. Trapping mechanisms involve a rotated normally faulted block with a dip closure to the SE, a 3D dataset for the North of block 48/24a will have to be acquired to accurately define the trapping geometry. De Keyser lineaments compartmentalise the Wherry field into West and South, this lineament can be traced through the NE-SW fabric, so it is highly probable that potential leads are limited within that rotated block. With the reservoir compartmentalised, the lead can be sub-divided into Wherry NE and Wherry East.

The Roda Prospect is located in the North of block 208/11. This feature is interpreted as a deep-marine mass transport turbidite system deposited in the T20s accommodation space created by post rift subsidence. It is surrounded volcanics and stands out as a fairly transparent distinct unit overlaid by strong reflectivity packages associated to the T30 and T20 stratigraphic sequences (Fig.1.39). Uncertainty on the age of the Roda sandstones is de-risked by the well 208/11-1 (Fig.1.38). It may belong to the Lower Vaila interval T20 sequence.
The amplitude of the top reservoir reflection is lower than the amplitude commonly observed for intrusions (Fig.1.40). This extends over 100km2 and could potentially host a very thick sand body as observed in well 2018/11-1. There is no evidence of trap breach across the top seal and Roda is within the low risk top seal zone presence. Roda brightens on the Far offset and fluid cube confirms gas.

Reservoir T30 sandstones

Seal Overlying Vaila Shales
Source Kimmeridge Clay Fm
Most likely hydrocarbon phase Gas
Charge/Migration 'Storage Tank Concept'

summary_comment:
The Medina prospect sits to the east of Amethyst just before a salt wall and is undrilled. 
GWCs have been set deep at 2700 m TVDss to separate the two prospects in the case that the discontinuous faults separating the two blocks are not sealing.
Proximity to the edge of the diapir distorts seismic reflectors at Leman level and structural uncertainty is high. Medina sits in a square shaped block of c. 9.5 km2 bound by a major fault trending NNW-SSE to the east and two E-W Dekeyser faults to the north and south. The separation from the main field is defined by a string of small NNW-SSE faults which show little to no throw on reflection data.

13/23-1 was drilled on a four-way dip closed feature, the well encountered good quality oil in a series of thin stacked sands equivalent to the Upper Ettrick sequences. 
Average log porosity of 13.3% was discouraging as was the high water saturation recorded (45%). 
A 30ft interval flowed at very low rates (266 bbo/d)

Well 43/13b-4, Pegasus East discovery well, was drilled by Lasmo in 1991 in a fault bounded anticlinal structure. 
It lies primarily in the licence P1727 but extends into licences P1724 and P2457 and is located about 11km east of the 43/13b-7 well. The well encountered gas-bearing sandstones of Namurian A and B age (Chokerian and Kinderscoutian) with gas shows within poor reservoir quality sandstones. Three unsuccessful DSTs were attempted across the Namurian B (Kinderscoutian) and the well was plugged and abandoned. 
Pegasus East is a structural closure with faults bounding the Eastern and Northern extents. At the location of the 43/13b-4 well, the Westphalian has been fully truncated however there is potential for Westphalian gas downdip, which has been evaluated as the Pegasus East Flank prospect. As the 43/13b-4 well was drilled in a downdip position on the Pegasus East structure, it is possible that the Alportian is gas bearing updip and prospective volumes have been computed for this interval.

The Pegasus Northeast Flank Prospect is a Carboniferous Stratigraphic Trap to the east of the Pegasus North Discovery. The Reservoir is predicted to be Late Namurian and Early Westphalian A aged shoreface.

The pre-award prospectivity for the Avalon Channel prospect was based on a reflectivity anomaly that correlated with a channel system up-dip of the Avalon discovery.
Studies indicated that the Avalon Channel was likely to contain gas within a small 4-way dip closed structure within its westerly up-dip extent. Unfortunately, the down-dip oil leg of the prospect was found to consist of a predominantly water wet response with only sporadic indications of hydrocarbons possibly indicative of a hydrocarbon migration pathway, residual saturations or possibly gas in a low-quality reservoir.
The Phase A work programme proved effective in evaluating the Avalon Channel prospect and provided a clear result that indicated a significant decrease in likely in-place volumes.

Freya and Fulla both are situated on the Rona Ridge 20km to the north-east of the giant Clair Field.
The main reservoir units for Freya are the Clair Group Carboniferous/Devonian sands. These sit atop the basement Rona Ridge. The trap mechanism for Freya is a three-way dip closure, with the west bound by the main Freya fault. Cretaceous shales form the seal both above and at the fault.
Hydrocarbons are sourced from Jurassic Kimmeridge clays from the Foula sub-basin to the west.
The giant Clair field to the South-east, of which Freya could be considered an extension, is the best 
analogue field.

summary_comment:
Faraday is a gas condensate accumulation in the Jurassic Heather turbidites; it was discovered in 2011 with the drilling of the 30/1a-11 well. The discovery well encountered 90ft of hydrocarbon bearing sandstone with good reservoir properties; however, due to wellbore complications neither fluid samples nor pressure data for the accumulation could be collected. Extrapolation of pressure from the underlying Fulmar sandstone suggests the accumulation to be HPHT with estimated temperature of 375°F and formation pressure of 15,750psi. 
Faraday is a tilted fault block system. Faraday is a combination sub-unconformity trap and fault bound trap at Heather Formation level. The overall structure dips to the south-west with up-dip truncation by the Base Cretaceous Unconformity (BCU) to the north-east. The north-eastern limit of the Heather reservoir is constrained by the 30/1f?8 well, which penetrated thin, ratty, Heather sands. To the east, the discovery is separated from the Oakwood discovery by north-east to south-west trending faults.

A series of north-east to south-west trending faults bisect the structure and were active in the late Jurassic, with some inverted during the Lower Cretaceous. The main control on the spill point is the western fault separating Oakwood from the Faraday discovery.

The Aumerle amplitude anomaly lies along the same northwest-southeast trending turbidite fairway as the Banks discovery, and its similar characteristics and magnitude suggests a similar good-quality reservoir with a condensate and/or gas fill. This prospect is defined within the Zechstein Z2 hauptdolomit as a large structural 4-way dip closure with upside stratigraphic potential. The majority of the prospect (ca. 80%) is located within block 38/21 with the remaining portion within block 38/22. The hauptdolomit reservoir is well developed in the area and overlies sulfate platforms that can relatively easily be mapped out on seismic data. The hauptdolomit has good inter- and intragranular porosity and fair permeability with additional fracture permeability. Effective side and top seal is provided by anhydrite. Gas (and possibly minor condensate or oil) is provided by Lower and Upper Carboniferous coal-bearing strata mature for gas generation south of the prospect. Analogue fields have been found in the UK Central Graben (e.g. Auk and Argyll), as well as in the Netherlands and Poland.

Gas (and possibly minor condensate or oil) is provided by Lower and Upper Carboniferous coal-bearing strata mature for gas generation south of the prospect.

This prospect is defined at the base of the Zechstein evaporite interval as a medium sized but low relief structural 4-way dip closure. The reservoir consists most likely of the Lower Carboniferous Cementstone which has fair porosity but low permeability, with potential for additional fracture permeability. Effective top seal is provided by the overlying anhydrite and salt of the Zechstein Group. Gas (and possibly minor condensate or oil) is provided by Lower and Upper Carboniferous coal-bearing strata mature for gas generation south of the prospect. Analogue fields are the Breagh and Crosgan discoveries in the Southern Gas Basin.

summary_comment: Quoys Prospect is a relatively low risk appraisal opportunity on Block 3/18, up-dip of the 3/19b-2 Nansen sandstone oil discovery. The prospect is defined as a Lower Jurassic shoreface sandstone package confined to the west by a basement block. To the north of this block a north south fault is mapped with the prospect downthrown against Triassic claystones as seen at nearby 3/17-1 and 3/12b-3. Oil down to is defined as 3840m TVDSS from DST #2 in 3/19b-2 and 3999m TVDSS from logs in the 3/18c-1 appraisal well. Block 3/12b contains the Unst prospect. This is an Eocene Frigg feeder channel recognised on 3D seismic, exhibiting a strong amplitude anomaly at the proposed top Frigg sandstone reflector. The anomaly appears to conform to depth structure suggesting that it is representative of a fluid filled closure. The proposed fluid type is gas based on the down-dip occurrence of gas at the Nuggets fields in Block 3/19. An oil leg is also considered possible, but the magnitude of the 'soft' seismic anomaly is suggestive of a compressible fluid and most likely gas. The prospect appears to be structurally controlled with spill likely to the north and north west related to the amount of counter regional dip created by the differential compaction of the sands. The lateral controls appear to be sand limit either as channel or over-bank with surrounding facies mud dominated. To the south the sands are likely to continue basin-ward towards the Tryfan minor gas discovery made by Apache in 3/17-2.

Colter East is a rotated fault block containing Sherwood Sandstone reservoir sealed by Mercia Mudstone, charged from Liassic oil-prone source rocks in the Wessex-Channel Basin to the south of the prospect. Late Jurassic to Cretaceous rifting formed tilted fault block traps and buried the source rocks to maturity. Migration occurred by face-loading of mature Liassic with Triassic Sherwood sandstone in footwalls. Effective Mercia Mudstone caprock preserved trapped oil through a period of inversion and tilting during the mid-Tertiary.

The Colter well (98/11a-6) was drilled as a vertical well with the Ensco-72 jack-up rig and reached a Total Depth of 1870m MD in the Sherwood. The well remained on the southern side of the Colter bounding fault but encountered oil and gas shows over a 9.4m interval at the top of the Sherwood Sandstone reservoir (net pay of 3m). Similar indications of oil and gas were encountered in the 98/11-1 well, within the Colter South fault terrace.

The Mane prospect is a Palaeocene target in the Heimdal formation, targeting deep marine sandstones similar to the Chimera prospect in the neighbouring licence, P2312. 
The results of the 3/17a-3 well targeting Chimera (Sept-Oct 2019) were directly applicable to informing the Heimdal play in P2466.
Following evaluation of the datasets available and integration of the results of the Chimera 3/17a-3 exploration well in the neighbouring block, the P2466 licence area was deemed too high risk and not commercially viable to justify moving to the next phase of the licence.

This prospect is defined within the Zechstein Z2 hauptdolomit in P2331 as a large structural 4-way dip closure with upside stratigraphic potential. The majority of the prospect (ca. 80%) is located within licence P2331 with the remaining portion within blocks 38/22 and 38/23. The hauptdolomit reservoir is well developed in the area and overlies sulfate platforms that can relatively easily be mapped out on seismic data. The hauptdolomit has good inter- and intragranular porosity and fair permeability with additional fracture permeability. Effective side and top seal is provided by anhydrite. Gas (and possibly minor condensate or oil) is provided by Lower and Upper Carboniferous coal-bearing strata mature for gas generation south of the prospect. Analogue fields have been found in the UK Central Graben (e.g. Auk and Argyll), as well as in the Netherlands and Poland.

Titan is an oil prospect defined on seismic as a Four-dip closure in the Fladen Ground Spur consisting of Devonian aged Buchan reservoir, proven throughout the area, and sourced by Upper Jurassic aged Kimmeridge Clay Formation, proven in the South Viking Graben. Oil production from the same reservoir has occurred at the Buchan Field in the Moray Firth and Argyll Field in the Southern Central Graben.

The Surprise Punt structure is also relatively low relief (Figure 8), with a fault defining the northern edge of the smaller structure tested by the 13/21b-7 well (referred to as the ‘core area accumulation’, OWC -5,513ft TVDSS). On average, the final reservoir surfaces interpreted on the 2019 WG PSDM data are deeper across all reservoir closures when compared to interpretations made on the previous seismic data (WG Inner Moray Firth Merge 2012 – Q13 Phase II).

The Dunbeath prospect is wholly located in Block 11/23. The prospect is a simple downthrown trap against the Helmsdale fault. Maximum relief mapped is approximately 600m. The lateral cross fault seal is against Devonian ORS, with top seal provided by Uppat and Heather mudstones. 
Anticipated reservoir quality is fair to good, given the shallow depth of the anticipated Beatrice section, and hydrocarbon charge is expected to be via the adjacent Beatrice sub-basin. However, the chance of success is now considered to be very low, with the failure at Wick potentially confirming the inability of the Helmsdale fault to act as a cross fault seal against the Devonian ORS.

Bottlenose is a four-way dip closed prospect. The reservoir section is anticipated to be within the Lista Formation (Balmoral Sandstone?), however, the exact age and stratigraphic horizon is poorly defined. The dip closure is robust at Top Lista level and the structure has around 300 feet of relief; it is underlain by a grounded Triassic pod. The nearest offset well (28/4b-1A) is around 2.5 km east; this well very limited sandstone development at the target horizon. However, a seismic package that is not present within the well is present at Bottlenose, and wells to the NE contain sandstones within the Lista Formation and underlying Maureen Formation.

Prospective area to immediately to the north of the Elke Main Discovery. Updip pinch-out to the west, with lateral pinch-out to the north.

Sinclair prospect is a robust horst aligned West to East.  its Early Jurassic reservoirs are of fine grained alluvial flood plain sands (N:G 40%) that young upwards into Middle Jurassic barrier bar sands (N:G 75%).
Effective Top and lateral seals are provided by thick overlain Oxfordian shales and mudstones. 
The Beatrice oil field was charged from the same Caithness Basin.  The Sinclair prospect was more deeply buried so the acknowledged early Jurassic and possibly Devonian source rocks will have also attained maturity in proximity to Sinclair.
Seismic to Well correlations from Beatrice and closer well control indicate the comparative similarity of Sinclair's hydrocarbon potential.

Narwhal was discovered by well 28/2-1, which was drilled by Arco in 1993. The well encountered heavy oil in the Eocene Tay sandstone and a good sample of 13º-14° API oil was recovered, the viscosity recorded in the Narwhal well was in excess of 2,000 cP.

It is updip of Elke Main Discovery, the latter of which has an updip stratigraphic component of trapping.  It is likely that Elke Updip West is in communication with Elke Main, and the effective stratigraphic pinch-out is the updip margin of Elke Updip West. Between Elke Main and Elke Updip West, it is likely that there is a sub-seismic communication.
 
Elke Updip West is isolated from the updip Narwhal Discovery.  The Narwhal sands have been age dated to be slightly older than the Elke Main sands, and given the separate Narwhal and Elke Main OWCs and the seismic mapping, the separation between to two trapping systems is placed between Narwhal and Elke Updip West.

Mesozoic flower structure creating Jurassic and Triassic sequence repetition underlying the Wick prospect in blocks 11/24b and 11/25b on Wick Detachment. Wick structure results from late Jurassic and early Cretaceous compression, enhanced by Alpine inversion and shearing. Stacked low angle thrust sheets, repeating Jurassic and Triassic section. Fracturing may extend into the Devonian creating conduits for oil migration from Devonian source and fracture storage capacity.
For estimating of potential fracture and storage volumes in the Wick and Alpha  inversion features, the Lancaster Field West of Shetland provides a useful analogue. Well 205/21a-7 flowed at 10,930 bopd using an ESP with all the flow coming from the large fractures at the top of the basement. Porosity range for the main fracture zones is 2/5/8 percent with average fracture zone porosity 4.8 percent.  Net to gross for the fractures is 100 percent and water saturation is very low with oil saturation of 90 to 98 percent

name_others: REL02155 Alpha Fracture REL02155 Alpha Fracture
summary_comment:
The structure is created by a mapped left-stepping jog on the right-handed shear system which cross-links Helmsdale and Great Glen Faults. The side-step is some 4 km wide. This step is a compressional structure comprising a zone with at least 4 main reverse faults, all dipping to southwest and all northeast-vergent, operating to drive the brown-shaded sub-thrusting block obliquely under the hanging wall. Associated with these is a fold which is Alpha Prospect, indicated by the dotted green contours. Alpha is expressed only in the sub-thrust footwall.
In the monocline hanging-wall the shears created a small dome which was tested by 11/24a-2 (Knockinnon), it traps a minor oil pool in Callovian, the well terminated in a described repeated section in mid Jurassic sediments. In the footwall, however, a large compressional fold is mapped with 75 msecs dip and fault closure down to 1725 msecs, covering around 5.5 square km.

Dunrobin forms part of the Central Ridge structural high. The high is a focus for migration out of the Beatrice / Great Glen sub-basin. Effective charge and trapping is indicated by the presence of a DHI at the crest of the structure. Reservoir is present and charged in a separate structure downdip, where well 12/27-1 tested gas from an oil-stained Beatrice sandstone. High quality sandstone of the Dunrobin Bay Group is also present in 12/27-1. Reservoir can be mapped with confidence from 12/27-1 to Dunrobin on high quality 3D seismic. With shallow depth of burial reservoir quality in offset wells is high, with average core porosity >22% and permeability of hundreds of mD.  Effective top seal is expected to be provided by Heather Formation which is in shale facies in nearby wells. Seal in the hanging wall of the structure is against both Kimmeridge Clay and Lower Cretaceous Valhall Formations.  Both formations are expected to be argillaceous in the area surrounding the Dunrobin Prospect

The Ashes Lead is the potential attic volume in the fault block tested by 13/22b-19 updip of the well. This is a very narrow, elongate fault block structure to the west of the -19 well. Potentially the Early Volgian Phoenix Reservoir Unit could be hydrocarbon bearing at this location. The overall feature is very similar to the Phoenix discovery to the northeast, being the next fault terrace to the south. 
Hydrocarbon charging is considered to be low risk, as the fault block would be able to access the same hydrocarbon kitchen that sources Phoenix itself. All of the properties of the reservoir and fluids are expected to be similar to those in the Phoenix accumulation, or even slightly improved, as this culmination is at a depth of 10,500 ftTVDSS, about 1,000ft shallower than the Phoenix discovery.

The Raiden lead is a shallow 3-way dip, fault bounded BPU/Devonian closure that is covered by 3-4 2D lines from the PP162DGOGA survey. The BPU gradually deepens in all directions and is significantly down-thrown to the South by a large East-West trending fault which juxtaposes the Devonian reservoir onto upper Cretaceous Chalk. The Devonian lies on a seismically opaque basement with little reflectivity. Raiden has a clear migration pathway from the East Orkney Devonian kitchen to the Northeast. In addition, there are bright amplitudes less than 10km from the crest of the structure that may indicate the presence of hydrocarbons.

The Sonya Bade lead is within blocks 13/10 and 14/8, 8km directly to the East of the Raiden lead and lies on the same Caithness structural trend. This is a prominent horst block that dips to the east and west and is defined by large throw faults to the North and South which juxtapose the Devonian reservoir against Palaeocene shales. Furthermore, the lead is most likely internally faulted by smaller normal faults. 
However, only one available seismic line directly crosses this lead therefore the exact nature and extent of the closure to the East and West is uncertain. Similarly to the Raiden lead, this structure is very shallow and the Palaeocene top seal has been incised by a large glacial canyon.

The Kano lead has been interpreted as a comfortable 3-way dip closure within the Devonian footwall of the main Eastern basin bounding fault of the EOB. The TWT closure is entirely within block 14/1 and is covered by three OGA lines. The Northwest-Southeast trending fault that defines the lead juxtaposes Devonian reservoir against Palaeocene shales and Cretaceous chalk. The Kano lead is reliant on a vertical charge route from the West as it is situated directly above the Devonian EOB source kitchen.'

name_others: REL02151 Camster REL00812 Camster REL00813 Camster South
summary_comment:
The Camster prospect is located in Block 11/24c immediately east and downthrown against the Knockinnon discovery. 
The prospect is a simple downthrown trap against the Great Glen fault at Upper Jurassic Volgian level. Maximum relief mapped is approximately 600m. The lateral cross fault seal is against Devonian ORS, with top seal provided by Uppat and Heather mudstones.
Anticipated reservoir quality is very good for the Volgian, given surrounding intersections and the proximity of the Forse Channel Fan system indicating significant coarse clastic input into the basin at Volgian times related to shedding of sediment from the Helmsdale fault. 
The deeper Beatrice target reservoir quality is anticipated to be fair to poor, given the depth of the anticipated Beatrice section. 
Hydrocarbon charge is expected to be via the adjacent Beatrice sub-basin.
Given the failure at Wick, the lateral cross fault seal anticipated at Camster against the ORS appears to be compromised. As a result, the chance of success has been significantly downgraded.

name_others: cp11_25_1 REL02148 Whaligoe REL02148 Whaligoe REL01601 Whaligoe
summary_comment:
The Whaligoe prospect is located in Blocks 11/24b, 11/24c and 11/25b immediately east and downthrown against Wick prospect. 
The prospect is a simple downthrown trap against the Great Glen fault at Upper Jurassic Volgian level north and along strike from the Camster prospect.
Maximum relief mapped is approximately 860m. The lateral cross fault seal is against Devonian ORS, with top seal provided by Uppat and Heather mudstones. Anticipated reservoir quality is very good for the Volgian, given surrounding intersections. The deeper Beatrice target reservoir quality is anticipated to be fair to poor, given the depth of the anticipated Beatrice section. Hydrocarbon charge is expected to be via the adjacent Beatrice sub-basin. The Whaligoe Beatrice prospect has a similar structural style to the overlying Volgian prospect. Similar to Camster above, given the failure at Wick, the lateral cross fault seal anticipated at Whaligoe against the ORS appears to be compromised. As a result, the chance of success has been significantly downgraded.

Recovery efficiency is considerably lower in the Surprise and Nutmeg Coracle reservoirs, 6% and 10% respectively in the MC depletion model, driven by the combination of a relatively thin oil column and an unfavourable transmissibility ratio between the heavy, viscous, and biodegraded oil and the reservoir permeability.

The Frigg Field is Eocene aged, Frigg Formation consists of unconsolidated sandstone, layers of shale and calcareous strings. The reservoir has excellent production properties with a porosity of about 30%, a permeability of 1 to 5 D and an initial water saturation of 8% - 30%. The Frigg sand has multi-Darcy permeability and the gas will redistribute according to gravity relatively fast.

Upper Jurassic gas condensate accumulation known as Phoenix that was discovered and tested by UK well 13/22b-4 in 1990. Phoenix is an east-west elongate trap formed by three-way dip closure to north and bounded to south by an east-west trending down-to-the-south dipping fault. The reservoir is of Early Volgian age and lies within one of the main Hot Shale source intervals within the Kimmeridge Clay Formation.
Phoenix Deep Lead comprises a potential accumulation at Permian level within the same tilted fault block as the Phoenix Jurassic discovery, in Permian Sand reservoir up-dip of the 13/22b-4 well.
It is a typical Cenozoic prospect, we consider it is likely there is a significant stratigraphic component.
The area around 110/9a-2 needs mapping with the best available (2D) seismic data and an appraisal well drilled to assess deliverability and size of the accumulation.

name_others: cp11_24_23 cp11_24_19 cp11_24_5 REL02146 Wick REL01600 Braemore
summary_comment:
The Wick exploration well targeted a P50 prospective recoverable resource of 17 million barrels of oil equivalent, (mmboe) with an upside (P10) possible outcome of 58 mmboe recoverable. 
The technical chance of success predrill was estimated 36% probability of encountering moveable oil.
The key risk was considered to be containment of hydrocarbons, as the prospect is an Alpine related compressional fault trap requiring downthrown fault sealing against Devonian meta sediments for an upside outcome. Seismic reprocessing had been recently undertaken to improve imaging, and this resulted in recognition of an independent upthrown core to the trap, further improving the chance of success. However, the lack of hydrocarbons in the well proved that the cross-fault sealing lithologies that had been anticipated predrill, did not seal in the up-dip location of the trap. This outcome combined with the noticeably sandy section encountered in the regional sealing Uppat mudstone section has had a negative impact on much of the prospectivity for the licence.

name_others: cp11_24_3 cp11_24_20 cp11_24_15 Lead A REL02150 Latheron REL00817 Latheron
summary_comment:
The Latheron prospect is mapped as an upthrown tilted fault block on the Sutherland Terrace located in Block 11/24c. The target reservoir is Beatrice A and B. The prospect is mapped on the original Reach 3D dataset, and data quality are good, with the resulting time and depth maps covering the prospect of high confidence. Anticipated reservoir quality is moderate to good, given the conflicting results at nearby discoveries Knockinnon and Lybster. Hydrocarbon charge is anticipated to be from the Beatrice sub-basin located immediately to the east of the Sutherland Terrace. 
Charge is considered low to moderate risk given that wells drilled to date on the terrace have both intersected hydrocarbon bearing intervals. Top seal is Uppat / Heather Formation mudstone and cross fault seal was previously considered low risk with the Beatrice in the footwall juxtaposed against the Uppat mudstones / Heather Formation. 
The Wick well result has increased this cross-fault risk with the Uppat being sandier than expected and the overlying Kimmeridge section being sand prone.

name_others: cp11_24_24 cp11_24_21 J3  REL02147 Knockinnon REL00816 Knockinnon
summary_comment:
The Knockinnon discovery made by wells 11/24b-2 and 2Z is a Beatrice aged oil discovery of moderate to poor reservoir quality. Hydrocarbons were discovered by the Talisman operated well and side-track with the two well intersections having markedly different Beatrice A and B sands.
Both, however, were unusually tight given the shallow depth of the reservoir and it is likely that the structure has been inverted considerably during Alpine compression. Porosities of maximum 12% are measured on cores and logs and associated permeabilities are low. Testing was inconclusive, as were reservoir pressure measurements, with RFT points not appearing to establish a hydrocarbon gradient. Updated mapping suggests that the accumulation may not be fault dependent as previously
thought, with fault independent closure potentially providing the trapping mechanism for the hydrocarbons encountered in the wells. As a result, the low case (P90) outcome is considered more likely and is too small to consider further appraisal.

The Forse Channel prospect is located on the northern edge of the Forse Channel depositional system mapped in Block 11/24c and 11/25b. The prospect is a fault bounded channel on the western side of the Great Glen fault at Upper Jurassic Volgian level immediately north of the Knockinnon discovery. 
The prospect is recognised within the Volgian Forse Channel fan system as a result of the very high amplitudes observed at the Volgian sandstone level. Whilst only covering a small area (0.5 sq km), it was thought that the prospect could contain a commercial volume of oil and gas as a result of the significant mapped column associated with the amplitude anomaly and predicted thickness of Volgian sandstone.
Marram is a proven gas field at shallow depth with a high proportion (40% approximately) of inert gasses.

The Hard Times K1 West prospect is located in the north of the application acreage as a westerly extension of the Hard Times K1 Main prospect, located in blocks 12/15 and 13/11. The prospect is defined by a Lower Cretaceous Coracle / Punt Mbr. sandstone reservoir in a 2-way structural trap. The prospect is down-faulted against the NE-SW trending boundary fault of the Wick Sub-Basin, a NW-SE trending conjugate fault splay acting as a barrier to towards the Hard Times K1 Main Prospect, and dip-closed to the SW and SE.  The prospect is poorly defined on sparse 2D seismic data, and the data quality of the legacy data sets is challenging for detailed stratigraphic and structural interpretation. Well 13/11- 1 constrains the mapping and reservoir presence is regarded as low risk. The isochore of the lowermost Cretaceous illustrates the depositional thick in which the prospect sits, south of the Wick Fault. Trap seal is regarded as the critical risk element for the prospect.

name_others: cp15_11_8 cp15_11_20 cp14_15_34 REL02015 Penny West Mey REL00820 Hudson
summary_comment: The Hudson Prospect is a 4-way dip-closed trap mapped on 3D seismic. The trap is formed by draping over a Mesozoic structural high, enhanced by differential compaction of reservoir sands and contemporaneous mudstone, which provides seal. The closure exists in time and depth. The crest is at approx. 1300m TVDSS. The reservoir is high-quality sandstone of the Palaeocene Balmoral Sandstone Member. Seal is provided by overlying Lista Formation muds. Analogue fields include MacCulloch and Dumbarton. Analogue discoveries include the nearby Rowallan, Yeoman and Crown discoveries.

The Bering Prospect is a 4-way dip-closed trap mapped on 3D seismic. The trap is formed by draping over a Mesozoic structural high, enhanced by differential compaction of reservoir sands and contemporaneous mudstone, which provides seal. The closure exists in time and depth. The crest is at approx. 1289m TVDSS. The reservoir is high-quality sandstone of the Palaeocene Balmoral Sandstone Member. Seal is provided by overlying Lista Formation muds. 
Analogue fields include MacCulloch and Dumbarton. Analogue discoveries include the nearby Rowallan, Yeoman and Crown discoveries.

The Sissy Jupe prospect concept is a combined stratigraphic - structural trap, involving  termination of an upper Jurassic isopach thick on to the southern flank of the Wick sub-basin defined north of the Smith Bank High.  A J60's reservoir interval is proposed, with the top, lateral and base seal by claystones of the Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation (KCF).  Source intervals are organic rich claystones of the KCF and Heather Fm.s are, but an additional contribution from a deeper Mid Devonian source may have occurred.

This Liu Kang lead is a 3-way dip closure. The structural crest is within block 14/1 but part of the structure extends into the neighbouring 7/26 block to the North which is not part of this application. The Lui Kang lead is situated to the North of the Kano lead and although Liu Kang is smaller, utilises the same petroleum system and lies on the same structural trend as the Kano lead. These leads may even be connected to form one larger structure, however, due to the sparse 2D grid this remains uncertain.'

The Kitana lead straddles blocks 6/28 and 6/29 on the Northern edge of the East Orkney Basin. It has been defined as a Devonian 3-way dip hanging wall closure against the Northern EOB basin bounding fault. The extent of the closure to the Northwest remains uncertain due to the seismic data density. The Zechstein provides the top seal within the hangingwall, whereas the (Dalradian) basement acts as footwall side seal. The lead requires short range migration from the Devonian source kitchen to the East.

The Goro lead is situated on the down-thrown hangingwall of the same basin bounding fault that defines the Kano lead in block 14/1. The BPU and older reflectors dip upwards and steepen with proximity to this fault which forms a small closure within the basin. The lead is directly above the Devonian kitchen and like the Kitana lead is sealed by the Zechstein and juxtaposed against (Dalradian?) basement'

Within the East Orkney Basin, there is a Northwest-Southeast trending mound-like feature within the Devonian section that is easily mappable on several OGA 2D lines. This feature has no structural closure but thins to the East and West within the basin. The mound itself may contain reservoir that stratigraphically pinches out either side, however, the application area is out with the Devonian kyle limestone reef trend identified on the Mid North Sea High (MNSH). Alternatively, if the Zechstein is deeper as suggested by Richardson et al, 2005, the mound could be salt with pinch outs on the salt flank trapping hydrocarbons from the basin. Stratigraphic pinch out plays may exist within blocks 13/3 and 13/4 as seismic packages can be seen to thin to the West as the basin shallows. trap_type_comment:
The Joanne segment of the Isabella prospect is a fault bounded stratigraphic (truncation) salt flank trap on the northern limb of the Jane Salt Diapir (Figure 1, 2). Top seal is provided by Upper Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous shales unconformably overlying the Top Triassic; base seal is the Julius Mudstone mb of the Skagerrak Fm. The Jane Salt Diapir plus the main bounding fault to the J Ridge act as lateral seals. The Upper Jurassic Heather and Kimmeridge Clay fms also constitute the source rock that is proven present and mature in the Harrier Graben. The Joanne sst is truncated by the Mid Cimmerian Unconformity along a ENE trending line north of the Jane Salt Diapir, and is absent to the south of the diaper. Consequently, the underlying Julius mdst and Judy sst members have a shallower crest than the Joanne sst up against the diaper, and the Judy spill point is controlled by the saddle between the Jane Salt Diapir and the J Ridge. Seismic data and data from the analogue Triassic fields on the J Ridge suggest that the Julius mdst is a more than 70m thick competent shale unit that provides an effective Joanne base seal. Thus most of the Triassic analogue fields nearby have separate Joanne and Judy columns. Main risk for the Joanne main objective is considered to be lateral seal towards the J Ridge.
As the Judy sandstone mb is believed to carry a very high risk it is only considered as upside potential. Main risk is on migration as migration would rely on indirect charge from Joanne via fault juxtaposition from a limited number of faults west of the main prospect area. Further, because of the relative shallow position of the Judy crest and the steep limbs up against the salt a material Judy HC accumulation carries a high top seal risk (pressure analysis indicate relative high risk of blown trap). The Judy Segment is a 4-way dip closure against the Jane Salt Diapir limited by structural spill to the J Ridge. Top seal is the Julius Mudstone and base seal is the Triassic Smith Bank Fm. The Jane Salt Diapir acts as lateral seal.

summary_comment: Kessog South (Jurassic) is situated at the SW end an elongate NW-SE orientated tilted fault block with a total area of approximately 30km2. Erosion of the Pentland Formation at the crest forms a stratigraphic trapping mechanism, with three-way dip closure likely downflank. The structure is complex due to the effects of salt-mobilization and late Jurassic rifting.  Kessog (Jurassic) was discovered by 30/01c-4, drilled by BP in 1986, and tested at 4418bopd / 8.8mmscf/d. Subsequent appraisal wells tested hydrocarbons across the majority of the reservoir section. The Pentland Formation is subdivided into three members which record evolution of the depositional system from lacustrine delta and sheetflood environments towards incised-valley fill deposits, crevasse splays and coal horizons. There are no other examples in the CNS of fields producing from the Pentland Formation as the primary reservoir, only Franklin as a secondary reservoir.

summary_comment: Jolene is a late Jurassic (Oxfordian, J52) Franklin Sandstone Member discovery made in well 30/01c-9 by Total in 2007. A distal lower shoreface expression of the Franklin Sandstone was encountered and cored at this well location. The Franklin Sandstone is absent in the other appraisal wells in the underlying Kessog disovery, but regional mapping suggests the possible development of a shoreface system fringing the J-Block structure to the south. The trap is closed to the north by erosion of the late Jurassic section, and to the west and south by dip or stratigraphic pinch out. To the east, faulting may control the extent of the accumulation. The extent of the accumulation is ~15km2, with a potential column height of ~1000ft. The Franklin Sandstone consists of a thin basal turbidite channel fill overlain by shoreface deposits.

summary_comment: The Holder prospect is a seismic amplitude anomaly sitting within the Tor/Hod Formation of the Cretaceous chalk. The chalk is known to be a commercially viable reservoir at the nearby Stella & Kyle fields and is currently under development at Harrier. The prospect has been intersected by 29/10-2, in which gas peaks of 6% and 15% were observed at 9750 and 9790 ft respectively. Correlation with offset wells places the shows in the uppermost section of the Hod Formation, at a significant kick in the sonic log. The interval was tested, and following acidization of the reservoir, flowed 140 bbls of oil to the surface.

Tufnel is a Tertiary reservoir prospect above the Marr discovery. It is within the anticlinal closure and comprises Eocene aged reservoir sands and silts of the Lower Stronsay Group (likely Tay formation equivalent). It exhibits a strong seismic amplitude response which could be indicative of hydrocarbon presence, and offset wells indicate good quality, 30% porosity have been encountered at this stratigraphic level.

summary_comment: Fripp Lead is an HP/HT gas condensate lead within the Fulmar Formation positioned at the core of the anticlinal structure within the application area. The reservoir has already been drilled by 29/10-2 well, which encountered 670 ft of water bearing Upper Jurassic shore-face sandstones. Potential exists for a three-way faulted accumulation at the crest of the tilted fault block in an up-dip location from the 29/10-2 well

The Strummer Lead is an HP/HT gas condensate opportunity within the Skagerrak Formation positioned at the core of the anticlinal structure within the application area. Well 29/10-2 encountered a 150 ft section of water bearing Triassic sediments, although it is ambiguous from the well data whether the Triassic sediments were part of the Skagerrak Formation or the poorer quality Smith Bank Formation. Nevertheless, the seismic character of the interval is more akin to a Skagerrak interval. Potential exists for a three-way faulted accumulation at the crest of the tilted fault block

summary_comment: The Shinoi prospect was identified initially by its obvious diapiric structure close to numerous relevant analogues. The diapir sits within the Tay and Forties sand fairway, with the stratigraphy on the north to north-eastern side of the diapir estimated to be the thickest and best quality for both Forties and Tay reservoir intervals.  Reservoir seal is believed to be provided by the salt core of the diapir in combination with Sele shales, Balder tuff and Eocene aged Horda shales. While the Maureen may provide a lateral seal to the chalk in some locations, it is likely that the interbedded sands would create a connected hydrocarbon column with the Forties.

summary_comment:
Ben Lawers is a T31 structural-stratigraphic prospect situated within the prolific deepwater Paleocene reservoir province at the SW corner of the Foinaven sub-basin. 
It is a multi (6) - segment prospect, with a mature description consisting of low impedance deep-water channel segments, which are within a greater channel complex, adjacent to BP's SW Foinaven (204/23-2) T31 discovery (drilled in 2008). These segments are located across the BP 100% P2293 Licence and extend into the open block 204/23c application area. 
The prospect is mapped on good quality 3D seismic data (2016 Westray survey). 
The key risk is the presence and sealing capacity of an up-dip lateral seal.

opportunity_comment: Developing a means to improve the producibility of the fluid from the Piper is a focus for the whole of the Bowmore area.
summary_comment: Bowmore is an elongate fault and dip-closed gas-condensate discovery mapped at Base Cretaceous level with a crest at approximately 13,800ftTVDSS, bounded to the N by a fault and to the S and SW by dip-closure. Bowmore is proven by the 15/24a-4 and 15/24a-9 wells. An easterly thinning of the Upper Jurassic across the structure results in pinch-out of Upper Jurassic Claymore and Galley turbidite sandstones onto the underlying tilted fault block, overlying deeper shoreface Piper Sandstone. Wireline log analysis confirmed all three sandstones as hydrocarbon-bearing.  Logs indicated that the Piper Sandstone was hydrocarbon-bearing down to 14,520ftTVDSS in the 15/24a-4 well, proving the extent of the discovery at this level. However, on DST the Piper did not flow, confirming low permeability, poor-quality reservoir. Mean recoverable reserves for the Piper Sandstone are calculated at 19mmbbls condensate and 67.2bcf gas.

opportunity_comment: Exploration target east of Bowmore discovery
summary_comment: Bowmore East is an undrilled elongate WNW-ESE trending fault terrace located immediately E of the Bowmore Discovery. As per Bowmore, the structure is fault closed to the N and dip closed to the S. The Upper Jurassic Galley Sandstone reservoir is interpreted to pinch out onto the structure, the crest of which lies at a depth of approximately 13,200ftTVDSS. The prospect is considered moderate in risk on account of proven effective reservoir and hydrocarbon charge in the nearby 15/24a-4 and 15/24a-9 wells. For volumetric calculations, a hydrocarbon-water contact at 14,342ftTVDSS has been extrapolated from that seen in the Galley Sandstone in 15/24b-9. The key risk is trap definition. Seismic data imaging is poor, and it is unclear as to where cross-cutting NW-SE faults may be present to separate the structure from the Bowmore Discovery, and to close the structure to the E. Mean recoverable reserves for the Galley Sandstone are calculated at 9.0mmbbls condensate and 47.6bcf gas.

summary_comment: The Prospero Lead is a four-way, low-relief dip-closed structural trap at Top Forties Sandstone. It has been penetrated by two wells, 23/27-2 and 27/27-1. Log analyses and RFT data indicate that hydrocarbons are present in both wells above a free-water level at 10161ftTVDSS. The Cummings Lead is a Lower Cretaceous sandstone stratigraphic target, located in on the north-west margin of the West Central Graben and Western Platform high.  
It is defined by strong RMS amplitudes and pinchouts onto structural highs in the West, North and South.  
It is separated in the east from the Smith Lead by a salt wall structural high.  Reservoir presence as the Lower Cretaceous thins up onto the Western Platform high is the key risk for this lead.  
The Cummings lead has a crest at 2,650 mSS and it has a P50 resource of 38.7 mmbbls.

The Smith Lead is a Lower Cretaceous sandstone stratigraphic target, located in a depositional low within the NW area of the West Central Graben and central in the AOI.  It is defined by strong RMS amplitudes and structural high pinchout edges to the west, and in highside cases the north and south.  Salt diapir highs also exist within the lead where no reservoir has been deposited.  On the SW pinchout margin, petrophysics on 21/19-1A shows a thin Lower Cretaceous Sand with interpreted hydrocarbon pay. The crest of the lead is 3,150 mSS and it has a P50 resource of 91.1 mmbbls.  At present two possible P90 closures exist, both 20 km2, one in the NW and other in the SW.  A P5 structural closure is interpreted at ~3,800 mSS which is approximately 215 km2.

The Lyon Lead is a Lower Cretaceous sandstone stratigraphic target, located to the east of the structural highs of the Jurassic Mallard and Gadwall oil fields.  It is defined by strong RMS amplitudes, with pinchout edges to the west, south and east which is controlled by salt tectonic structural highs.  Immediately to the north, 21/15a-6 and 21/15a-1 both intersected thin Lower Cretaceous sandstones with hydrocarbon pay which thin onto a separate structure.  Reservoir presence within the structural lows is the key risk for this lead.  The Lyon Lead has a crest at 4,000 mSS which potentially increases the chance of a reservoir sands being in the HPHT range.  Lyon has a P50 resource of 44 mmbbls.

The Agar Lead has Fulmar or Puffin Sandstone stratigraphic targets in the Upper Jurassic and is located in an isolated graben, ponded by surrounding salt upwelling and onlapping onto older, either Middle Jurassic or Triassic claystones. Mapping the lead was on moderate quality 3D seismic data and interpretation is fair. Crest of the target is ~3,500  mSS and it has a P50 resource of 57 mmbbls. The critical risk of the Lead is reservoir presence and effectiveness.  There is adjacent well control to support the lead, with good reservoir intersected in 21/13a-5 located ~5 km to the west and 21/13b-2 1 km to the south, where the reservoir was absent, demonstrating the sealing and trapping potential of the surrounding highs.

The Bancroft Lead is a Fulmar Sandstone stratigraphic target in the Upper Jurassic, located adjacent to the Kittiwake Oil Field. The trap is sealed up-dip, to the south by the onlapping Fulmar sands onto older Middle Jurassic and/or Triassic claystones. Side seal for the lead are the younger claystone filled channels incisions, possibly of Volgian age.  The events can be mapped seismically and are interpreted to intersect vertically through the reservoir interval and create the potential for lateral seals to the north and south of the Lead. The crest of the target is ~3,500 mSS and the P50 resource is 20 mmbbls.  A number of wells intersect the reservoir adjacent to the lead with numerous oil discoveries. Reservoir presence, effectiveness and charge are considered low risk.  The critical risk is the trap and specifically the presence of a lateral seal that are sufficient to hold a commercially viable quantity of hydrocarbons.

The Stoinis Lead is a Fulmar Sandstone stratigraphic target in the Upper Jurassic, located within the north western corner of the play fairway. The trap is a pinchout of the Upper Jurassic sands onto older, either Middle Jurassic or Triassic claystones. Mapping the lead was on moderate quality 3D seismic data and interpretation is fair. Crest of the target is 3,020 mSS and the P50 resource is 19 mmbbls. The critical risk of the play is trap definition with an effective base seal.  Nearby well control includes the 21/13a-5 well drilled ~3 km to the east which intersected good quality Upper Jurassic Fulmar sands as well as underlying Triassic sand reservoir. Although the well was dry, it was drilled on the edge of a structure leaving >100 m of up-dip potential (the Turner Prospect, see below, being up-dip of this well) making it difficult to assess the impact on charge migration risk to the Stoinis Lead.

The Turner Prospect is the up-dip potential of the Fulmar Sandstone previously drilled by the 21/13a-5 well. It is a 4-way dip closure above a salt diapir and the 21/13a-5 well has demonstrated the presence of a reservoir/seal pair. Although the well was water-wet it was drilled on the very flank of the structure and could have either drilled just off structure or drilled down-dip of the pay zone. All other wells drilled on structure within the AOI and targeting the same play level have intersected hydrocarbons so this well is an anomaly.  Mapping the lead was on moderate quality 3D seismic data and interpretation is fair. The crest of the target is ~3,000 mSS, which is >100m up-dip from the well intersection and the P50 resource is 14 mmbbls. The critical risk of the prospect is presence of a commercially viable accumulation of hydrocarbons.

Morgan W is a four-way closure located approximately 10km west of the Morgan oil discovery. It is proposed that this may be a similar structure to that of the Morgan oil discovery and may be a tie-back opportunity, should oil be discovered. Deterministic prospective resource (recoverable) volumes for Morgan West sit at 1.9 mmbbls.

opportunity_comment: The opportunity is to evaluate and mature the Zechstein potential play sweet spot as identified by our extensive regional Zechstein Play Based Evaluation (PBE) over Quads 35 to 44. This work was initiated early 2019, incorporating various legacy studies by Shell, former BG Group and others. The PBE work is continuing at the time of submission of the licence request. The 2D seismic currently available to Shell over the requested blocks is sparse and of variable quality.  As a result of this, the current Technical Evaluation is largely based on play concepts resulting from the latest PBE context and specific seismic observations. Although notional volume potential and risk profiles are presented, maturation of individual lead/prospect has not taken place at this stage and forms part of our Phase A work program.
hc_case_comment: Our drilled hole analysis and our 3D basin models suggest gas to be the only hydrocarbon phase. Although on the fringes of the Zechstein basin oil generation and preservation cannot be excluded, the chances for finding an oil accumulation in the license area are - at present - considered very low (Ref. section 4.1.3 Appendix B).
summary_comment:
The primary level of prospectivity is the Z3 Plattendolomite interval, tested in the analogue Endeavour undeveloped field (discovery well 41/25a-1) and with reported gas shows in several offset wells. 
The Z2 Hauptdolomite carbonate interval, analogue to the Crosgan discovery, the Pensacola prospect and fields onshore UK, the Netherlands, Germany and Poland, and Early Carboniferous sandstones are secondary objectives. 
The Plattendolomite reservoir objectives are locally thickened shelf/slope carbonates in structural traps, sealed by either salt-facies and/or diagenetic-control. Traps have been formed or enhanced by late stage compression during the Alpine orogeny and presumably resulted in significant secondary fracturing of the dolomitic carbonates. Charge is anticipated from the Carboniferous (Westphalian/Scremerston) via faults or fractures across the Werra Anhydrite, laterally from the east onto the shelf, or alternatively via Cenozoic dykes.

summary_comment: The Upper Jurassic Elcho Prospect is a combination structural/stratigraphic trap within the Peterhead Graben. The target Ettrick Sandstone Member reservoir is interpreted to have been deposited as a northwest-southeast trending turbidite channel. The reservoir package is defined on 3D seismic data by mapping the gross J72-J66 package (Top J72 to Top J64 reflectors) and cut-offs applied to the resulting isopach to define the pinch-out of the Ettrick Sandstone Member reservoir to the southwest, northwest and northeast. The prospect is dip-closed to the southeast. The P90-P10 GRVs are defined by the mapped isopach thickness clipped to 160m (i.e. no reservoir at thickness less than 160m) applying OWCs at -2,550 and -2,710 mtvdss respectively.
