summary_comment: The Konta Lead forms a discrete untested package of Buzzard age reservoir stratigraphically trapped in a trough along the crest of the ridge bounding the southern edge of the Ettrick Sub-Basin. The gross reservoir package is entirely defined on 3D seismic data where the J64 soft reflector marks the top of the gross Buzzard reservoir package and the J56 Heather forms the base. The overall gross Buzzard package thins to the southeast onto the crest of a trough penetrated by the 20/8-1 well where the legacy biostratigraphy report confirms that the J64-J56 package is entirely absent. The gross Buzzard package is interpreted to transition into a condensed section up-dip of Konta towards the southwest and the lead is dip-closed on its eastern edge at -2769m TVDss into the Ettrick Sub-Basin.

summary_comment: The Crawford Oil Field was primarily developed from the Jurassic strata. In 2007, the appraisal well of the 9/28a-18 well confirmed the extension of the Triassic to the North which was oil bearing. The main wells are 9/28-2, 9/28a-13, 9/28a-16 and 9/28a-18. These wells all intersect oil bearing Triassic strata. The new well confirms that the Triassic was overlooked and holds significant potential for future development. summary_comment: Gilderoy Lead is an elongate W-E trending four-way structural closure at Top Forties level. The extent of Gilderoy (white dashed polygon on map) is a representation of the seismic amplitude expression on the full-stack data  Gilderoy shows unusual amplitudes on the full-stack data updip & principally west of well 15/28a-5 (thin hydrocarbon pay zone at top of Forties Sand interval). opportunity_comment: 4-way dip closed structure with three stacked prospects: Bell Rock (Clair Grp.), Podlie Craig (Kimmeridge Fm. Rona Mbr.), Lamb Rock (Lower Cretaceous, Cromer Knoll Grp.).
summary_comment: Bell Rock is a 15 km2 4-way dip closed structure in the crest a gently rotated horst block of the easterly splay of the Corona Ridge situated mostly in block 213/26a. Teh reservoir is prognosed Clair Grp., likely similar to that at 213/27-1z, 213/27-2 and 213/23-1, which are the known occurrences of Clair Grp. nearby. The reservoir sediments are likely to be interbedded claystone and sandstone deposited in a terrestrial setting and are likely to be red beds. Reservoir quality is expected to be fair, with NTG from 0.03 to 0.91, and porosity from 6% to 16% expected. Topseal is likely to be the overlying Kimmeridge Fm., comprising a basal Rona Mbr., and the Kimmeridge Clay above. Reservoir is the critical risk.

opportunity_comment: 4-way dip closed structure with three stacked prospects: Bell Rock (Clair Grp.), Podlie Craig (Kimmeridge Fm. Rona Mbr.), Lamb Rock (Lower Cretaceous, Cromer Knoll Grp.).
summary_comment: Podlie Craig Prospect is a 30.4 km2 4-way dip closed structure at the crest of a horst block with a gentle tilt to the west. The prospect is located in the westerly splay of the Corona Ridge mostly in block 213/26a. The reservoir is predicted to be the Rona Mbr., of the Kimmeridge Fm., which can be tied on the existing 3D seismic to well 213/27-1Z (Lochnagar), where the Kimmeridge Fm., was 155 m thick and the Rona Mbr. was 149 m thick (gross). At Lochnagar there was 8.6 m of net pay in the Rona Mbr. (27?API oil), which was significantly underfilled, probably due to a breached seal resulting from Paleogene uplift. The Rona Mbr., displays a very poor correlation of porosity with depth (R2=0.2) regionally, which is due to the variable facies exerting control. The source rock is the Kimmeridge Fm. claystone, which is directly overlying the prognosed reservoir and is in the oil window presently.

opportunity_comment: 4-way dip closed structure with three stacked prospects: Bell Rock (Clair Grp.), Podlie Craig (Kimmeridge Fm. Rona Mbr.), Lamb Rock (Lower Cretaceous, Cromer Knoll Grp.).
summary_comment: Lamb Rock Prospect is a 4-way dip closed structure at the crest of a gently tilted to the west horst block, which is part of the westerly splay of the Corona Ridge. The prospect represents a new play in the area, as the stratigraphy has not been drilled nearby. The reservoir is proposed to be early syn-rift deposits of the Lower Cretaceous Cromer Knoll Grp., which we do not subdivide into the recognised formations at this stage,although we recognise that the Lamb Rock location is distal from the sediment input (in the east), so the more marine Commodore Fm. is more likely. The Cromer Knoll Grp., shows a weak correlation between porosity and depth (R2=0.5). At depth, the marine sediments can preserve remarkably high porosity (e.g. Edradour) approaching the theoretical maximum. . Seal is likely to be the overlying Upper Cretaceous post-rift claystones. The underlying Kimmeridge Fm. is presently in the oil window.

summary_comment: Prospect 205_P-A was mapped on PGS Megasurvey Plus and part of ST12003, the prospect is defined by Horizon N, which is Colsay 1 Unit, where it is drilled by wells.  The extent of Horizon N is limited to the west, where the reflection picked terminates shortly into the Faroes Islands acreage, which represents the depositional limit, providing stratigraphic trapping potential. The prospect is defined by a 4-way dip closure of 16.3 km2, which may be related to inversion of the underlying Corona Basin against the Corona Ridge (e.g. Podlie Craig). The reservoir is hypothesised to be Colsay 1 Unit, which can be tied on the existing seismic to 205/01-1 (Rosebank)  and 204/05b-2 (Blackrock) which both discovered oil in the unit (Figure 27-30). Colsay 1 Unit is a fluvial to estuarine sandstone deposited in a fairway running approximately SW to NE (see Appendix 9.5) and the NTG is influenced by proximity to this fairway. Seal is claystones and volcaniclastic sediments.

At Rosebank, Horizon L represents the Colsay 3 Unit reservoir sandstone, but at Blackrock a disconformity surface at the top of the RLV is represented; both instances show oil at this level. We consider the 204/05b-2 well to have drilled the Colsay 3 Unit prospect (Redrock) up-dip of the pinchout of Colsay 3 unit and that and Prospect_205-P-B is on the fairway. The reservoir is proposed to be the Colsay 3 Unit similar to Rosebank, a fluvial-estuarine sandstone with good reservoir properties. Evidence from Rosebank suggests that if present porosity should be excellent. The seal is proposed to be similar to Rosebank, with Colsay Mbr., claystone and volcaniclastic sediments providing topseal. The source is the Kimmeridge Fm. claystone.

summary_comment: Bowmore Terrace is an undrilled NW-SE trending downthrown fault terrace located immediately N of the Bowmore Discovery northerly bounding fault. opportunity_comment: Part of a sequence of stacked Upper Jurassic reservoirs. Claymore Sst. holds significant part of the resource base.
summary_comment: Bowmore is an elongate fault and dip-closed gas-condensate discovery mapped at Base Cretaceous level with a crest at approximately 13,800ftTVDSS, bounded to the N by a fault and to the S and SW by dip-closure. Bowmore is proven by the 15/24a-4 and 15/24a-9 wells. An easterly thinning of the Upper Jurassic across the structure results in pinch-out of Upper Jurassic Claymore and Galley turbidite sandstones onto the underlying tilted fault block, thereby providing a combination stratigraphic-structural trap, overlying deeper shoreface Piper Sandstone. Wireline log analysis confirmed all three sandstones as hydrocarbon-bearing.  Core from 15/24a-4 indicated modest but effective Claymore Sandstone quality. This was confirmed by a DST which flowed 3024bbls condensate per day. A hydrocarbon down-to (HDT) at 14,602ftTVDSS was observed in 15/24b-9. Mean recoverable reserves for the Claymore Sandstone are calculated at 19mmbbls condensate and 67bcf gas.

opportunity_comment: Exploration target east of Bowmore discovery
summary_comment: Bowmore East is an undrilled elongate WNW-ESE trending fault terrace located immediately E of the Bowmore Discovery. As per Bowmore, the structure is fault closed to the N and dip closed to the S. The Upper Jurassic Piper Sandstone reservoir is interpreted across the structure, the crest of which lies at a depth of approximately 13,200ftTVDSS. For volumetric calculations, a base-case hydrocarbon-water contact at 14,520ftTVDSS has been extrapolated from the hydrocarbon down-to observed in the Piper Sandstone Galley Sandstone in 15/24b-4. However, the failure of the DST to flow means that this prospect has high reservoir quality risk. There is additional risk on trap definition. Seismic data imaging is poor, and it is unclear as to where additional cross-cutting NW-SE faults may be present to separate the structure from the Bowmore Discovery, and to close the structure to the E. Mean recoverable reserves for the Piper Sandstone are calculated at 35.3mmbbls condensate and 125bcf gas.

summary_comment: The Dapperling Lead is an elongate low-relief, three-way dip-closed footwall structure on the southern margin of a W-E trending fault, mapped at Upper Jurassic Top Piper Sandstone level. The structure was penetrated by the 15/24a-7 well which encountered the reservoir at just below mapped closure.  The well encountered a 75ft gross interval of clean quartzose sands with a blocky log character at 13,687ftDDBRT, overlain by 120ft of poorer quality silty sand with cleaning upward log character, suggestive of a stacked shoreface system. Fluorescence was observed throughout, and log analysis suggests that these sands are hydrocarbon bearing. However, on account of burial diagenesis, reservoir quality is poor, with average core porosity of 9% and average permeability 0.1mD. Dapperling is estimated to contain 3.5mmbo mean recoverable reserves. The key risk is reservoir effectiveness.

opportunity_comment: Small lead updip from oil shows in poor Piper Sst. needs improved reservoir quality and thickness.
summary_comment: The Charmer Lead is an elongate fault and dip-closed structure mapped at Upper Jurassic Top Piper Sandstone level. It is located on the same W-E trending fault and ridge lineament that forms the northern margin of the Bowmore structure and is also controlled by a NW-SE cross-cutting fault which downthrows the Piper interval to the east. The structure was penetrated by the 15/25a-4 well, which encountered the reservoir within the mapped structural closure at 12,738ftDDBRT. The well encountered a 47ft gross Piper Sandstone interval, and wireline log analysis suggest that a bona-fide oil column was present. However, only one good RFT point was obtained indicating that the reservoir is of low permeability. This was confirmed by core analysis which indicates average porosity of just 10% and average permeability of around 1mD. Charmer is estimated to contain 4.2mmbo mean recoverable reserves. The key risk is reservoir effectiveness.

summary_comment:
The Amanita Lead is an elongate, triangular-shaped lead mapped at Base Cretaceous level, with a depth to crest of around 12,600ftTVDSS and about 300ft of vertical relief. The trap is set up by an intersecting W-E and NW-SE fault pair, and is dip-closed to the S and SW. The structure was penetrated down-flank to the S by the 15/23a-11 well which encountered thick Upper Jurassic Galley Sandstone reservoir at 13,242ftDDBRT. These sandstones can be clearly seen sub-cropping the Base Cretaceous Unconformity. The sandstones exhibited good oil shows and appear to be oil-bearing on wireline logs. They were tested, flowing 880bwpd with 5% water cut, suggesting a transition zone with potentially-significant remaining up-dip reserves. Amanita is estimated to contain 8.2mmbo mean recoverable reserves. 
Key risk is reservoir presence up-dip where the reservoir pinches out.

The Draco Lead is an entirely stratigraphic trap mapped within a thickened Lower Cretaceous section in a sub-basin to the north of the Bowmore Discovery high. The lead is defined by a high amplitude event on 3D seismic and is postulated to contain deep marine turbidite sandstones of Aptian age, equivalent to the reservoir in the Britannia Field. The anomaly, which is indicative of lithological variation as opposed to fluid fill, has not been penetrated by any wells to date. However, none of the wells on the application blocks have encountered evidence of sand at this level. The Draco lead covers a large area, with mean recoverable reserves of 14.7mmbls condensate 147bcf gas. However, the lead is high risk, particularly in terms of reservoir presence and charge (migration).

The Earthstar Lead is a combination stratigraphic and dip trap mapped within a thickened Lower Cretaceous section in the sub-basin that exists between the Bowmore Discovery and Alder Field highs. The lead is defined by a high amplitude event on 3D seismic and is postulated to contain deep marine turbidite sandstones of Aptian age, equivalent to the reservoir in the Britannia Field. The anomaly, which is indicative of lithological variation as opposed to fluid fill, pinches out stratigraphically to the north, and extends southwards into a thickened area below an arbitrary contact mapped at 13,900ftTVDSS. The Earthstar lead is large, with mean recoverable reserves of 20.7mmbls condensate 207bcf gas. Up-dip and to the north of the pinch-out, the 15/23d-13 well encountered Aptian sand stringers which could indicate thicker sands present down-dip within the lead, but conversely increases the risk on lateral seal.

summary_comment: The Harry Prospect lies within a Palaeocene Forties turbidite channel sandstone that is on the same trend as the Ptarmigan Discovery to the SE and the Galley Field to the NW, where excellent quality reservoir sandstones were encountered. The Harry trap is formed by a combination of compactional drape to the NW & SE, minor fault closure to the NE & SW, and possible stratigraphic trapping against mudstone filled channels and mudstone-dominated over-bank deposits. A potential flat spot at 1920mS TWT could indicate a fluid contact. Well 15/23b-10 constrains the SW extent of the prospect. Drilled just off the channel axis, it encountered oil shows in the Forties Sandstone within overbank channel sandstones and siltstones at a depth of 6,450ftDDBRT.  The Harry Prospect is estimated to contain mean recoverable reserves of 25.4mmbo and 26.3bcf gas. Overall risk is low, with the biggest risk being reservoir presence within the whole of the mapped closure.

The Hedwig Lead is a small but well defined Palaeocene four-way dip-closure mapped at Top Forties Sandstone level located immediately SE and downdip of the Harry Prospect. Like Harry, it lies within the same Ptarmigan Discovery to Galley Field channelized turbidite sandstone fairway. It is fault bounded to the south and dip closed in other directions, and similarly exhibits a potential flat spot possibly indicative of a fluid contact. Depth to crest is around 6200ftTVDSS. The Hedwig Lead is small, with mean recoverable reserves of 4.9mmbo. Overall risk is low, with the biggest risk being reservoir presence within the whole of the mapped closure.

The Percy Lead is a small but well defined Palaeocene four-way dip closure mapped at Top Forties Sandstone level to the ESE of the Harry Prospect and Hedwig Lead. It is a mounded trap formed by compactional drape and has a small time and depth closure and a depth to crest of around 6450ftTVDSS. The Percy Lead is small, with mean recoverable reserves of 6mmbo. Overall risk is low, with the biggest risk being reservoir presence within the whole of the mapped closure.

The Gingertail lead is an Eocene combination structural and stratigraphic trap mapped at Grid Sandstone level. It comprises a potential stacked channel sandstone complex, identified on 3D seismic data as a sinuous high-amplitude anomaly. Up-dip to the NW, the trap requires a fault offsetting the potential reservoir interval against sealing mudstones. The lead stratigraphically pinches out in other directions. Evidence for the potential of the Gingertail Lead is seen in a number of nearby wells that contained thin but high porosity oil-bearing Eocene sandstones, most of which were drilled outside the mapped high amplitudes. Mean recoverable reserves for the Gingertail Lead are 126mmbo and 16bcf gas. However, the lead carries multiple risks including presence of reservoir sandstones within the seismic amplitude anomaly, in combination with fault seal to the NW without which an up-dip stratigraphic pinch-out is required.

opportunity_comment: An Emerald sandstone oil discovery drilled by Amoco in 1974.
summary_comment: The Oulton 3/11-1/1ST discovery well intersected a 114 ft Emerald sandstone section which flowed 41? API oil on test. 3D seismic interpretation of the area reveals a well-defined dip and fault closed up-thrown block comprising three main fault compartments. The Oulton Discovery is sourced from the Kimmeridge Formation to the east of the block in deeper, more generative hydrocarbon kitchens. Hydrocarbon migration from the east is considered to have travelled primarily through Jurassic stratigraphy. The Emerald Sandstone regionally is observed as a laterally extensive marine transgressive sheet sand that is generally well sorted, fine to medium grained quartz with feldspar and minor heavy minerals. The Emerald Sandstone intersected by the 3/11-1/1ST Oulton discovery well exhibits poorer quality reservoir than seen at Cheviot with an average porosity of 15.5%. Thick Heather and Kimmeridge Clay form the top seal.

opportunity_comment: A structural / stratigraphic trap at Emerald Sandstone level up-dip of a structural saddle that connects the prospect with the 3/11-1 oil discovery (Oulton)
summary_comment:
The Oulton West prospect is located on a fault terrace between the down dip 3/11-1/1ST Oulton discovery, and the Cheviot Field to the north. A potential stratigraphic component exists to the north-west within a NW-SE trending orientation. 3D seismic mapping defines a thinning of the Jurassic interval onto a palaeo-high to the north and north-west. A pinch-out of the Emerald Sandstone is supported by the 3/11-4/4z well, which intersects the Heather Formation siltstones directly overlying what is likely basement, suggesting an absence of the Emerald Sandstone. 
The structure to the south- west is closed by a large throw fault which is likely sealed laterally by Heather and Kimmeridge Formations, and to the north-east, closure is provided through north-east tilting. Depth mapping suggests the Top Emerald structure between Oulton Discovery and Oulton West Prospect could be connected.

opportunity_comment: A small low risk Frigg sandstone gas opportunity with a DHI which overlies the Oulton West Jurassic sandstone structural / stratigraphic prospect up-dip of the Oulton discovery.
hc_case_comment: Up-dip of Tryfan discovery and Nuggets Field
summary_comment:
The Oulton West Frigg gas target is related to the Eocene age sandstone formation that is intersected by well 3/11b-4 at 2940-3020 ft measured depth. This sand is thought to be part of the early Eocene age Frigg formation that is occurring at the basal part of the Hordaland group.  The seismic morphology and 3/11b-4 well data confirm sands, with geometry suggesting a channel complex. These channels are thought to be terminated in the high-quality reservoir sandstone distal turbidite lobes of the Nuggets field. Based on analogues from the Nuggets field and the Frigg field, and based on the well data from the 3/11b-4 well, the reservoir is anticipated to be of excellent quality. Seal can be provided by Horda Formation mudstones. 
A small structural closure was identified within the channel complex from the seismic interpretation. A larger up-dip stratigraphic or structural trap might also be possible, but the up-dip section extends off the edge of the seismic data coverage toward the NW.

The reservoir is developed within a low net/gross system and consists of sandy lobe or channel deposits in a submarine fan setting (interpreted from logs). New Corallian regional mapping of the Vaila Formation supports the depositional environment at Laxford being a system of deep-water channels, with fan lobes recognised down dip to the north and to the west at the Scourie prospect. The discovery well intersected a reservoir gross thickness of 36m, with a net to gross of approximately 40%, average porosity 19% and high calculated water saturations of average 51%.  Updip of the discovery a series of channel forms have been mapped on the available 3D seismic data.

Block 214/29b contains the Scourie prospect, a Palaeocene Vaila Sandstone target exhibiting a seismic amplitude anomaly similar to that seen at the Glenlivet gas field located directly south of opportunity. 
The Scourie prospect contains an estimated Pmean prospective recoverable resource of 107 bcf and 1 million barrels of condensate. 
The prospect is mapped as an amplitude anomaly observed west of Laxford. The anomaly is thought to represent a deep-water fan lobe outboard of the Glenlivet system. A recognised feeder channel appears to cut into the Glenlivet reservoir, and the resulting clay plugged scour appears to be non-reservoir bearing, compartmentalizing the Glenlivet field. This provides evidence of up-dip sealing for the channel and the Scourie prospect.

Seismically, the thickening apparent in the Auk Deep build-up does not appear to be repeated in the Chiron structure although the seismic quality in this location is not good. Although no detailed volumetric analysis has been undertaken, analogue data suggests that a lead the size of Chiron might be expected to contain around 100mmbbl STOIIP with 20mmbbl recoverable resources. summary_comment: Earn is a dip and fault closed structure at Rotliegend Leman Sandstone level and is composed of a number of tilted fault blocks. Fault juxtaposition mapping suggests that there is potential for fault compartmentalisation at Earn, therefore the prospect has been separated into four segments, North, Central, South and West. GRVs for each segment have been calculated stochastically. Each segment has been assigned its own GWC range and built using area vs. depth pairs (top and thickness method), a thickness range, and then rolled-up. The prognosed reservoir thickness distribution has been guided by offset analogue fields and wells, such as Cleeton, Tolmount, Mongour and the 42/27a-3 well.  The same reservoir distribution has been applied to each segment. The minimum, maximum and mode of the distributions of reservoir properties (NTG, porosity and gas saturation) are controlled by and reality checked against offset field and discovery values.

summary_comment: The Aspen Prospect comprises a large Upper Jurassic stratigraphic trap formed by a basin-floor fan deposited into the Cladhan sub-basin. The reservoir is interpreted to be J62 (Ptarmigan) age. This is age-equivalent to oil-producing sandstones in the nearby Cladhan Field. These sands are interpreted to represent the more distal basin-floor fan equivalent of the channel sands which form the cladhan Field reservoirs.

summary_comment: The Pine Prospect is an oil-prone stratigraphic trap also located in the Cladhan sub-basin and sits stratigraphically above the Aspen Prospect, although it is geographically partially offset to the south. The gross reservoir interval is defined on 3D seismic data by mapping the J66 and J62 flooding surfaces which define the top and base of the reservoir-bearing interval. An isopach of this interval shows a thickening away from the shale-prone 210/30-1 well. The reservoir for the Pine Prospect is mapped to sit within the J64 (Magnus) interval and similar to Aspen is age-equivalent to oil-producing sandstones in the adjacent Cladhan Field. It is believed that the Pine Prospect reservoir sands were deposited as a basin-floor fan, likely sourced from a slope channel system to the west that can be imaged on seismic amplitude data and has been penetrated by the 210/29c-5 well. The Pine prospect thickening sits to the south of the Aspen prospect, likely due to lateral stacking.

summary_comment: The Ash Prospect is mapped to be a Late Volgian  Early Ryazanian age basin-floor fan sandstone in the northern part of the Cladhan sub-basin, adjacent to the bounding fault. The trap is stratigraphic and believed to be oil-prone. The gross reservoir package is defined on 3D seismic data by mapping the Base Cretaceous Unconformity and the J72 flooding surface which form the top and base of the gross reservoir-bearing interval. The Ash Prospect trap is defined as a stratigraphic pinch-out to the south and east with the north and western edge of the trap being defined by a basin-bounding fault. It is not clear at this point if the sands rely on cross-fault seal, or if they pinch-out prior to reaching the bounding fault.

summary_comment: The Ash South Prospect is mapped in the age equivalent gross package as Ash, but the two prospects are seperated by an intervening are of thinning which may define two seperate basin-floor fan systems. Similar to Ash the prospect is a stratigraphic trap sealed by encasing Kimmerdige Clay shales. Channel like geometries in thickness & amplitude maps and thin sands in the 21/29c-5 well indicates a similar depositional model to Ash where sands are being transported from the Pobie platform across the Cladhan terrace and down into the Cladhan sub basin. The gross reservoir package can be tied to the 210/30-1 well, which encountered traces of well cemented, fine-grained sandstone with oil shows at the equivalent stratigraphic level.

summary_comment:
The Willow prospect is located in the Heather sub-basin and forms the oldest of three potentially stacked Upper Jurassic sandstone prospects. The gross reservoir package for the prospect is defined on 3D seismic data by mapping the J66 and J62 flooding surfaces which form the top and base of the reservoir interval. The reservoir is interpreted to have been deposited as a series of massflow sandstones sourced by erosion of the East Shetland Platform to the west and deposited as a series of deep-water channel sandstones and/or basin slope fans. 
The Willow Prospect trap relies on pinch-out of the reservoir sands to the northwest and southeast, dip closure to the northeast and fault seal against impermeable basement rocks to the southwest where they are downthrown against the East Shetland Platform. The top and base seal are provided by the Kimmeridge Clay formation deep marine shales.

summary_comment:
The Hemlock Prospect forms the third and youngest of the three stacked Upper Jurassic prospects in the Heather sub-basin. The gross reservoir package is defined on 3D seismic data by mapping the Base Cretaceous Unconformity and the top J72 sequence which form the top and base of the reservoir interval respectively. The reservoir is interpreted to have been deposited as a series of massflow sandstones sourced by erosion of the East Shetland Platform to the west and deposited as a series of deep-water channel sandstones and/or basin slope fans. Similar to Willow and Spruce, the deposition of these sands is thought to have been guided by NE-SW trending fault system to the north, which separates the Heather sub-basin from the Cladhan sub-basin to the north.

summary_comment:
The Yew Prospect is located in the Broom sub-basin and comprises an Upper Jurassic down thrown structural trap. The gross reservoir package is defined on 3D seismic data by mapping the J62 flooding surface and top Heather Formation, which form the top and base of the reservoir interval. The package is mapped as thinning to the east onto the downthrown north  south trending antithetic fault. The J62 (Ptarmigan sandstone) reservoir is interpreted to have been deposited as a series of basin-floor fan sandstones, likely sourced from the platform area to the west. 
The Yew Prospect trap is defined by a down thrown northern and western fault that is juxtaposed against tight metamorphic basement. The seismic package thins to the east until it meets the north  south trending antithetic fault. This antithetic fault creates a local graben between it and the main fault to the west allowing the eroded sands to collect into a possibly high net to gross package.

summary_comment: The Barracuda Prospect comprises an Upper Jurassic oil-prone combination stratigraphic/fault-bound trap within the main depositional basin of the South Viking Graben. The prospect has been mapped primarily on 3D MegaSurvey seismic data, with the wider prospect area mapped on 2013 3D Broadband seismic data and reprocessed legacy 3D data (MegaSurvey Plus). Definition of the gross reservoir package has been achieved through mapping the top Brae Formation (J60) reservoir and underlying top Heather Formation. The Barracuda Prospect reservoir is interpreted to be J66 (Brae Formation) age. This is age-equivalent to the adjacent oil producing sandstones in the nearby the Thelma Field. The Barracuda Prospect is sealed to the southeast by the lateral pinch-out of basin-floor sandstones proven by well 16/23-5 where a thin condensed age-equivalent shale prone interval has been penetrated. The prospect is fault bound to the northeast and dip closed to the northwest.

summary_comment: The Amberjack Prospect is Middle Jurassic gas condensate faulted 4-way dip closure sealed by overlying Heather Fm shales and located on the western edge of the Sleipner Terrace and adjacent to the South Viking Graben. The prospect has been mapped on 3D MegaSurvey seismic data where a top Middle Jurassic coal marker can be mapped as a proxy to the top Hugin Formation reservoir. The Hugin Formation reservoir is characterised by massive sandstones, coaly sandstones and heterolithics that have been deposited in coastal plain, tidal channel bar, tidal flat, mouth bar, shore face and shallow offshore depositional environments. Charge to the Amberjack Prospect is sourced from gas condensate prone Sleipner Formation and gas prone deep Kimmeridge Clay Formation within the South Viking Graben basin to the northwest. Anticipated reservoir fluids are gas condensate of around 44-47?API having a GOR in the range of 3,800-5,100 scf/bbl based on offset fields (Utgard and Sleipner Fields).

summary_comment: Bennet East is a Carboniferous prospect straddling Blocks 43/15 & 43/20. It is a 3-way closure with fault seal to the south, truncated by the BPU and overlain by the Silverpit Fm. Reservoir is anticipated in several stratigraphic levels, from Langsettian (Westphalian A) to Alportian. The Westphalian interval is heavily eroded in this area and BPU is a relatively flat structure forming the top of the effective reservoir unit. The shallowest defined structural closure in Bennet East is at Yeadonian level.  The Westphalian in this area is interpreted to sub-crop the BPU at an Intra-Langsettian level. The sands were deposited in a low relief, fluvial fan system as channel sandstones, tidally re-worked sands & infilled incised-valley deposits.  These are producing reservoirs in the nearby Cavendish and Trent Fields & the Pegasus, Kepler, Copernicus and Browney discoveries.  The anticipate hydrocarbon type is dry gas, with Westphalian coals being the most likely source rocks.

Reservoir is anticipated in several stratigraphic levels, from Langsettian (Westphalian A) to Alportian. The Westphalian interval is heavily eroded in this area and BPU is a relatively flat structure forming the top of the effective reservoir unit. The shallowest defined structural closure in Bennet East is at Yeadonian level.  The Westphalian in this area is interpreted to sub-crop the BPU at an Intra-Langsettian level. The sands were deposited in a low relief, fluvial fan system as channel sandstones, tidally re-worked sands & infilled incised-valley deposits.  These are producing reservoirs in the nearby Cavendish and Trent Fields & the Pegasus, Kepler, Copernicus and Browney discoveries.  The anticipate hydrocarbon type is dry gas, with Westphalian coals being the most likely source rocks.

summary_comment: Somerville is a Carboniferous prospect located immediately to the east of Cavendish Field.  It is a Westphalian opportunity with prospectivity within Westphalian B (Duckmantian), which is a potential new play in this area.  The structure comprises an infill of Westphalian B deposits sub-cropping the BPU with lateral inter-carboniferous seal against a 4-way dip closure of slightly older Westphalian A age deposits, forming the Somerville East prospect.  Proven reservoir rocks occur within Westphalian A and Namurian in this part of the basin. These sands were deposited in a fluvial fan system that covered most of the area, as channel sandstones, tidally re-worked sands & infilled incised-valley deposits.  The younger Westphalian B interval is preserved in pockets in this area but is a producing interval in Q44 in the Cygnus Field.  The anticipate hydrocarbon type is dry gas with Westphalian coals & shales being the most likely source rock.

Somerville East is a Carboniferous prospect located immediately to the east of Somerville and Cavendish North and south of Bennet East prospects.  It is a Westphalian opportunity with prospectivity within Westphalian A (Langsettian). The Westphalian B interval is eroded at the crest of this structure.  The prospect comprises a 4-way dip closure at effective top Langsettian surface. No other closures can be observed within the deeper intervals. Reservoir sands were deposited in a fluvial fan system that covered most of the area, as channel sandstones, tidally re-worked sands & infilled incised-valley deposits.  Top seal for the Somerville East prospect is the Silverpit Fm.  Intra-Carboniferous lateral and base seals are provided by Subcrenatum (base) and Listeri marine bands within the Langsettian.  The anticipated hydrocarbon type is dry gas with Westphalian coals & shales being the most likely source rock.

opportunity_comment: The opportunity is to evaluate and mature the Zechstein potential play sweet spot as identified by our extensive regional Zechstein Play Based Evaluation (PBE) over Quads 35 to 44. This work was initiated early 2019, incorporating various legacy studies by Shell, former BG Group and others. The PBE work is continuing at the time of submission of the licence request. Moreover, available 2D seismic for investigation over parts of the requested blocks is sparse and of variable quality. As a result of this, the current Technical Evaluation is largely based on play concepts resulting from the latest PBE context and specific seismic observations. Although notional volume potential and risk profiles are presented, maturation of individual lead/prospect has not taken place at this stage and forms part of our Phase A work program.
hc_case_comment: Our drilled hole analysis and our 3D basin models suggest gas to be the only hydrocarbon phase. Although on the fringes of the Zechstein basin oil generation and preservation cannot be excluded, the chances for finding an oil accumulation in the license area are - at present - considered very low (Ref. section 4.1.3 Appendix B).
summary_comment: The primary level of prospectivity is the Z2 Hauptdolomite carbonate interval, analogue to the Crosgan and Resolution discoveries, Pensacola prospect and fields onshore UK, the Netherlands, Germany and Poland. The Z3 Plattendolomite carbonates and Early Carboniferous sandstones are secondary objectives. The Zechstein dolomite reservoir objectives are locally thickened shelf/slope carbonates in combined structural-stratigraphic traps, sealed by either salt-facies and/or diagenetic-control. Lower Bunter could act as the ultimate top seal. Traps have been formed or enhanced by late stage compression during the Alpine orogeny and presumably resulted in significant secondary fracturing of the dolomitic carbonates. Charge is anticipated from the Carboniferous (Westphalian/Scremerston) via faults or fractures across the Werra Anhydrite, laterally from the east onto the shelf, or alternatively via Cenozoic dykes.

opportunity_comment: The Cluin prospect is well imaged by 1980-90's vintage seismic. The prospect was thoroughly evaluated as part of Licence P2105 which Premier Oil operated, Cluin was the main lead not hidden under the salt, but volumetrics proved to be non-commercial as a tie-back to Tolmount.  The new 2019 seismic is not expected to make any difference to the interpretation of Cluin.  The existing interpretation of Cluin will be checked in the new seismic data, but the work program  focus will be on hidden sub-salt opportunities.
summary_comment: The Cluin prospect is a fault controlled closure bounded by faults on 3 sides.  The main fault boundary is NW-SE trending fault dipping towards the West. Two perpendicular WSW-ENE trending faults limit the North end and South end of the prospects.  These two faults both dip toward the SSE.  Cluin is a low relief structure, and as such, the configuration and position of the closure is sensitive to different depth conversion models which in turn dictates the degree of fault superposition and the fault seal risk.  The Cluin prospect reservoir consists of a Permian Rotliegends Lower Leman Sandstone Formation. The seal is the overlying Lower Permian Silverpit Shale Formation, with the ultimate seal provided by the Zechstein evaporites.

opportunity_comment: Lower to Middle Triassic Teist and Lomvi formations sandstone reservoir
summary_comment: The Nemo II prospect is a poorly defined downfaulted trap located in the Outer Unst Basin, below the Middle Jurassic Snagsby prospect. The Intra-Triassic unconformity, defining the top of the prospect, is clearly seen on 2D data of high quality, and this has been used to define the prospect. The critical trap towards south, separating the Unst Basin and the East Shetland Platform, is considered robust as 210/29a-3 is proving crystalline basement in the footwall of the fault. Due to lack of seismic data it is unclear if there is a spill-point towards west, and at what depth this spill-point might be located at. Nemo II is located in close to the Upper Jurassic Cladhan discovery in the East Shetland Basin, and may receive hydrocarbons from there.

summary_comment: Audrey NW is a structural high, in the northwestern part of the original Audrey Field, previously drilled by the 48/15a-1 well and with some modest production from the 48/15a-B3 well (26 Bcf).  The structure lies beneath the flanks of the Audrey Salt Wall.  On the time processed data, available on the NDR, this structure is difficult to map, however a high clearly exists at the location and the results of the two wells demonstrates the existence of a valid structure.  The structure appears compartmentalised, with two, or possibly more, structural compartments.  However, currently available seismic data is not sufficient to map these accurately.  Current mapping has the main structure bisected by a NNW-SSE fault. The fault and dip closed structure is mapped at top Rotliegendes horizon. Target reservoir is the Leman Sandstone. The Leman sandstone is comprised of aeolian, fluvial and lake margin facies.

summary_comment: The Charlie downthrown structure represents inverted normal fault associated with Alpine inversion. Fault propagation folds provide a small closure that is unlikely to provide commercial volumes. The positive inversion of the Charlie fault was not sufficient enough to thrust the hangingwall passed the null point and therefore relies on fault juxtaposition or other mechanisms for fault seal. This would require the Silverpit mudstones on the hangingwall to be juxtaposed against the Leman Sst on the footwall and the Leman Sst on the hangingwall to be juxtaposed against the Westphalian Coal Measure shales. Alternative measures of fault seal are feasible, clay smear from the Silverpit mudstones and/or fault catacalasis from fault reactivation from the Alpine orogeny.

summary_comment:
Mimas, prior to being decommissioned, has produced 36bcf over eleven years. Mimas production discontinued due to the LOGGS pipeline and Theddlethorpe terminal undergoing decommissioning in 2018. 
Mimas was produced using one well, limiting its drainage radius, suggesting it has remaining potential within that produced compartment. Volumetric analysis by Tangram suggests that the horizontal 48/09-N1 well targeted a single compartment of the structure which is compartmentalised by a De-Keyser lineament; suggesting an additional compartment has not been produced. The 48/09-N1 well DST proved a sustained production at commercial flow rates of 43 mmscf/d without intervention. 
The volumetric analysis and production data suggests that Mimas met its P87 reserve case and the remaining potential of the produced compartment is ~30Bcf to meet the P50 reserve case. Below illustrates the probabilistic determination of recoverable volumes.

summary_comment: Mimas resembles a complex response to major reactivation during Alpine dextral transpression. As previously mentioned by Ligtenberg (2008), the structural evolution of pop ups within the Southern North Sea route back to a deep seated NW-SE fabric. Mima has an oblique slip component and may be labelled positive flower structures where the fault plane becomes near vertical. The structures have been thrusted ~200m beyond the null point providing robust closures which is sealed by the overlying draped Zechstein shales and evaporites.

This would require the Silverpit mudstones on the hangingwall to be juxtaposed against the Leman Sst on the footwall and the Leman Sst on the hangingwall to be juxtaposed against the Westphalian Coal Measure shales. Alternative measures of fault seal are feasible, clay smear from the Silverpit mudstones and/or fault catacalasis from fault reactivation from the Alpine orogeny.

summary_comment: Roseisle is a prominent Lower Cretaceous four-way dip target, characterised by bright soft seismic amplitudes. The prospect lies 30km north-east of the North Uist (213/25c-1v) gas-condensate discovery. The estimated mean recoverable resource for Roseisle is 340 mmboe, with gas the expected phase. The reservoir is interpreted to be shallow marine clastics. As this interval is entirely uncalibrated on the Corona Ridge, reservoir is considered to be the main risk to the prospect, both presence and quality. Time equivalent shallow marine facies are known from the West Shetland Basin, but are not at a comparable burial or structural setting to provide the best analogue. Seal is provided by a thick interval of Upper Cretaceous shales, with charge from the Kimmeridge Clay. Roseisle directly overlies the Galloway Jurassic prospect.

Below the tested J62 interval in the 21/20b-4Y well on the same anticlinal structure, a secondary hydrocarbon discovery was encountered in the Late Oxfordian  early Kimmeridgian (J56), Fulmar mbr. A 140ft sequence was logged, an interval limited by a fish which was lost in hole. Net to gross was calculated at 50% and average porosity for the interval was 16%. Hydrocarbon saturation is calculated at 50% though it likely that it is impacted by the poor-quality density log affected by the washed out hole and the resistivity that is likely invaded by overbalanced water based mud by the time the hole was logged. This interval was again drilled with WBM and at 1500psi over balance in order to try and mitigate against the sloughing and swelling shales. Pressures were taken and the interval was cored and logged, initial indications showed low saturation, so no further tests were carried out by Shell, who in hindsight had not appreciated the impact on hole conditions in evaluating the well.

The Christian J54 prospect is located on a Jurassic anticline approximately 4km from north to south and 2.5km from east to west situated on the western margin of the Western Central Graben. The Top Pentland horizon (which defines the Puffin Sand reservoir) was not penetrated by the 21/20b-4Y well but is a relatively strong seismic event that is tied to the nearby 21/20d-8 and 21/20a-5 wells. The structure is very similar to the overlying Fulmar Sand, but instead of spilling to the west the 4-way closure spills to the east and in doing so can join the Bligh structure. In drilling the section in 21/20b-4Y below the Fulmar in attempting to drill to underlying Puffin Sand the well experienced a twist off of the drill pipe which left a fish in the hole. The section where the Puffin should have been encountered was not logged and drill cuttings were dominated by barite, added to the mud to maintain weight. Gas shows remained high throughout despite the well still losing mud.

trap_type_comment: 4-way dip closure above a salt-cored anticline
summary_comment: As no defined hydrocarbon water contact has been found in the Puffin mbr, there is the potential that the whole of the Greater Bligh structure (Christian and Bligh) could be hydrocarbon bearing at the Puffin interval proving a significant in place resource. Volumetrics have therefore been calculated for the Greater Bligh structure which includes the previously mentioned Christian J54 prospect and Bligh discovery. Recovery factors have been adjusted to reflect the poor reservoir quality at depth.

The Bellinii lead is an identified untested closure at BCU. The nearest well control is 21/20a-1 drilled by Amoco in 1979. This well encountered over 1300ft of Kimmeridge and Heather section before finding a high-quality section of Puffin equivalent sandstone albeit water wet. These were directly on top of the Pentland formation like that seen over Christian and Bligh. There is also the potential for the J56 aged Fulmar albeit high risk due to lack of presence in the nearby well. The current understanding of the distribution of the Christian turbidites concludes that they are not likely to be prospective at the Bellini structure.

Bucephalus is a Carboniferous prospect on the western edge of Block 43/11. 
The structure is a 3-way closure, which has been truncated by the BPU & overlain by the Silverpit Fm. Closure is anticipated in the Westphalian A; all deeper sub-stages sub-crop BPU to the west of 43/11 & are not in closure here. 
The primary focus and prospect definition is based on the presence of a Langsettian (Westphalian A) interval comprising of sands deposited in a fluvial system.  Proven reservoir rocks occur within Westphalian and Namurian in this part of the basin. These sands were deposited in a low relief, fluvial fan system that covered most of the area, as channel sandstones, tidally re-worked sands & infilled incised-valley deposits.  These are producing reservoirs in the nearby Cavendish and Trent Fields & the Pegasus North & West, Kepler, Copernicus and Browney discoveries.  
The anticipate hydrocarbon type is dry gas, with Westphalian coals & Namurian shales being the most likely source rocks.

summary_comment:
Losgann is a follow-up target within the ‘Gamma area’ to be drilled following the drilling of the Gamma 1 and Gamma 2 prospects, the results of which will determine the final planned well path for Losgann. 
Losgann will be side tracked from the Gamma 1 horizontal sidetrack to the northeast where an approximate 2.6 km long horizontal section will test the prospect. Losgann targets  Tertiary sand injectites in the inner dyke area and brecciated zone of the Gamma Injectite structure. The Gamma inner dyke and brecciated zone was previously penetrated by 5 wells with varying amounts of oil and gas pay. Well data available to Apache for 9/19-16 and 24/9-3 and 24/9-4 shows the expected facies are thin dykes, sills and breccia. Recent wells drilled by AkerBP in the same area (Froskelar) have encountered similar facies. Losgann has been mapped on far stack seismic.
Reservoir quality is expected to be excellent (32% porosity, multi-darcy sands) based on offset well data.
The main risk at Losgann is lateral seal and the prospect has a Pg of 90% 
The main uncertainties are the Recovery Factors and NTG encountered along the well.

summary_comment:
These two exploration prospects were identified to the south of the Skye and Block 6 discoveries. They are formed from two adjacent fault blocks with stratigraphic closures to the north and east (due to erosion of the Tarbert) and dip closure against contacts determined from structural closure and offset wells. 
Reservoir is interpreted to be Tarbert as in the Skye prospect with additional potential in the Ness interval as in Block 6.
Charge is interpreted to be updip from the basinal area to the west. Reservoir thickness estimates and petrophysical parameters from the offset wells in the discoveries to the north have been used to estimate volumetrics of 26.3 MMbbls in Skylark A and 29.3 MMbbls in Skylark B.

Three leads have been identified in the P101 relinquishment area. These are Benbow West, Central and South. Reservoirs are considered to be Triassic Skagerrak sands
trapped within a complex system of faults around the Lomond salt dome. 
The most likely source rock is considered to be Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay in the syn-rift sequence deeper in the graben to the west. 
Migration occurs via carrier beds through a series of toppled Triassic fault blocks. This is the charge model for the sub-economic Lacewing Triassic discovery to the south.

The Camilla lead is a small, Lower Cretaceous level fault-dip trap on the downthrown side of the main Smith Bank Fault, possibly with a small amount of fault-independent closure. 
It is poorly defined on seismic and geological reviews suggest very low GRVs may be encountered in the Lower Cretaceous interval across the lead. 
Volumes have not calculated due to its size and poor definition.

The Jenna prospect is a fault controlled rollover anticline targeting possible attic volume in Upper Jurassic Burns Sandstone on the structure on which 12/23-3a was drilled. 
The eastern part of the closure is bounded by a fault to the north; the western part by faults to the south and west (Smith Bank Fault). 
Fault leakage is a critical risk since bounding faults reach the surface.

The Kate prospect targets Lower Cretaceous sandstones in a small fault-controlled rollover anticline bounded to the north by the Smith Bank Fault. Top seal at KCF level is unlikely to be present due to a predominance of sand close to the downthrown side of the Smith Bank Fault, so a shallower seal is required. Charge and migration is a critical risk since there are no shows in the Lower Cretaceous in nearby wells. Fault leakage is also a critical risk since the Smith Bank Fault reaches the surface.

The Vanna lead targets Lower Cretaceous or Upper Jurassic sandstones in a fault controlled rollover anticline. Fault seal is a critical risk since all faults reach the surface, as is the top seal risk shared with the Kate Lead due to the abundance of sands in the Lower Cretaceous.

North Burrigill is interpreted in the 3D as a three-way dip closure that partially rolls into a NW bounding fault.
It is very shallow (0.25 sec) and there is no brightening in the seismic. Closure against the fault is only partial, and the fault at the northern edge of the prospect appears to propagate to the surface, indicating breach of the structure. Due to this high level of structural risk, Equipoise Solutions Ltd did not quantify the volumetric potential of the North Burrigill lead.

The Polo Lead comprises a linear area of subtle mounding and chaotic character on seismic data within the Sola Formation interval. 
This could suggest the presence of a Britannia Sandstone channel of Aptian-Albian age. However, there is no support for a sand filled channel, either from amplitude studies or from differential compaction in the overburden. 
The nearest well 14/15a-4 did not contain any sand at this level. 
The trapping mechanism is entirely stratigraphic, and the lead is considered to be very high risk.

The 9/13-3a discovery well (drilled 1973) tested the four way dip closure, encountering a 40’ net pay section in the Frigg formation sands, down dip of the structural crest. The deepest closing contour and estimated OWC was used at -4150’ TVDss for volumetric calculation. 
One DST was run but it failed to produce oil to surface. One quart of heavy tar like oil, estimated at 10o API, was recovered from below the packer in the DST tail pipe. 
AVO assessment shows significant non-conformance to structure, implying either a complex stratigraphic trapping mechanism or a complex velocity field warping the structure in TWT. This adds considerable uncertainty to the static volume.
The mean reserve estimate of 1 Mmboe is deemed sub-economic.

Within the 43/22b block, the Carna structure is cut by a northwest-southeast fault towards its eastern end resulting in a separate structure referred to as the Carna Extension.

The prospectivity in the Forth Approaches Basin is believed to be in the sub-salt Carboniferous package. 
One large prospect, Skywalker, is identified in the hanging wall to the main basin bounding fault. Mature Carboniferous coals source the Visean reservoir with intraformational clays and muds providing a local seal beneath the more spatially extensive salt.

The Vernon Lead is stratigraphic trap within the Lower Cretaceous located between wells 20/10-1 and 3 as shown on the BCU TWT map. A seismic amplitude anomaly within the Lower Cretaceous had been identified within the Lower Cretaceous section which lies up-dip from the well 20/10-1 in which thin sandstone stringers were developed at the same stratigraphic level. 
The observed increase in amplitude could represent better development of these sands.

Around the 42/14b-2 well the Zechstein Lead (named Lead Z) is identified by an increase in the isopach between the Top Z2 Hauptdolomit and the Base Zechstein. 
This Lead forms an oblate shape in area, is thicker in the centre and thins towards the edges. 
The 42/14-2 well lies within this mapped Lead and has gas shows in the Zechstein Z2 Hauptdolomit.

The Camster prospect is located in Block 11/24c immediately east and downthrown against the Knockinnon discovery. 
The prospect is a simple downthrown trap against the Great Glen fault at Upper Jurassic Volgian level. Maximum relief mapped is approximately 600m. The lateral cross fault seal is against Devonian ORS, with top seal provided by Uppat and Heather mudstones.
Anticipated reservoir quality is very good for the Volgian, given surrounding intersections and the proximity of the Forse Channel Fan system indicating significant coarse clastic input into the basin at Volgian times related to shedding of sediment from the Helmsdale fault. 
The deeper Beatrice target reservoir quality is anticipated to be fair to poor, given the depth of the anticipated Beatrice section. 
Hydrocarbon charge is expected to be via the adjacent Beatrice sub-basin.
Given the failure at Wick, the lateral cross fault seal anticipated at Camster against the ORS appears to be compromised. As a result, the chance of success has been significantly downgraded.

The Whaligoe prospect is located in Blocks 11/24b, 11/24c and 11/25b immediately east and downthrown against Wick prospect. 
The prospect is a simple downthrown trap against the Great Glen fault at Upper Jurassic Volgian level north and along strike from the Camster prospect.
Maximum relief mapped is approximately 860m. The lateral cross fault seal is against Devonian ORS, with top seal provided by Uppat and Heather mudstones. Anticipated reservoir quality is very good for the Volgian, given surrounding intersections. The deeper Beatrice target reservoir quality is anticipated to be fair to poor, given the depth of the anticipated Beatrice section. Hydrocarbon charge is expected to be via the adjacent Beatrice sub-basin. The Whaligoe Beatrice prospect has a similar structural style to the overlying Volgian prospect. Similar to Camster above, given the failure at Wick, the lateral cross fault seal anticipated at Whaligoe against the ORS appears to be compromised. As a result, the chance of success has been significantly downgraded.

Falcon is a Palaeocene Vaila intra T35 lead situated to the north of and down-dip from Foinaven. 
Like many Palaeocene traps it is a complex combination trap, in this case requiring fault seal to the south and stratigraphic seal to the east. 
To the north, fault seal (with possible sand on sand juxtaposition) is also required to separate Falcon from the downthrown Falcon North Lead.
To the north, fault seal (with possible sand on sand juxtaposition) is also required to separate Falcon from the downthrown Falcon North Lead.

The Horsham prospect is a nebulous 4 way dip closed structure at Top Rotliegendes sands recognised in well 49/30a-5. 
The structure is covered by the Western Geco Q49/53 survey and Shell propriety Sean survey. 
Local well penetrations confirm the presence of thick excellent reservoir quality sands in the Rotliegendes with 17-23% porosity and high net sand content. 
The Zechstein carbonates and Bunter shales provide and excellent top seal.

The Reedham prospect is a 4 way dip closed structure tied into the Spilsby sands recognised in well 49/30a-5. 
The structure is covered by a Western Geco survey which shows an early Cretaceous depocentre extending westwards from the well onto the Reedham Prospect. 
The depocentre has been inverted during Tertiary inversion. The Spilsby sands pinch-out to the west and this pinch-out provides further stratigraphic closure on the prospect. 
Early Cretaceous claystones provide a topseal.
Oberon West lies northwest of Oberon and similarly comprises Upper Jurassic Piper sands within a faulted trap.
Lead E is a 3-way dip and fault closed structure at BPU level.

summary_comment:
The Culzean N/NW prospect consists of two stacked prospective reservoir intervals. 
The deeper of the two prospective intervals is the regionally extensive Pentland Formation (mid Callovian-mid Oxfordian in the Culzean area) coastal plain which underlies an Upper Jurassic interval with potential for shoreface and deepwater sand reservoir development. 
The trap for both intervals is a 2-way fault, 1 way stratigraphic pinch out, which in part relies on a salt ridge to the west, and dip closure to the east. The Pentland trap is more extensive than the Upper Jurassic trap. The Pentland interval relies on a base seal of the Triassic Jonathan mudstone interval, a proven pressure seal at the Culzean discovery. 
The base seal for the Upper Jurassic would be intra Heather Formation shales. The top seal for both segments is a combination of intra Heather Formation shales and the Cromer Knoll Group marls. 
The charge route into the prospect is from the Lomond deep to the east where the Kimmeridge, Heather and Pentland Formations are all mature.

The improved seismic over the Banquo/211/8a-2 discovery has provided a much clearer understanding of the structure. 
The north-south crestal fault (Banquo Horst Fault) is clearly seen bending to the south-east forming a ramp feature separating Banquo (211/8a-2) from Helena. The re-interpretation also shows that two compartments are formed by the Banquo Horst Fault on the crest of the horst.

The prospect is isolated in a graben between two West - East aligned faults one to the north and one to the south providing good lateral seals against thick shales seen in the 204/14-2 well.

The Whale and Dolphin Leads are structural closures that rely on a combination of fault-sealing and down-dip closure. 
The reservoir target for both prospects is Upper Jurassic, shoreface sandstones of the Sgiath Mbr.

The Griffon West Prospect is a Lower Cretaceous stratigraphic trap. 
The reservoir is postulated to be the Punt Member sandstone.
The development of an adequate reservoir facies within the Punt Member is considered to be high risk; the adjacent 19/04-2 well has no sandstone developed within the Lower Cretaceous and uppermost Jurassic stratigraphy. Charge to the structure is also high risk for the Griffon West Prospect due to the western Grampian Arch having a tortuous migration pathway from the mature parts of the Moray Firth basin. The absence of shows in the nearby wells support the hypothesis that this area has not been charged.

4-way and 3-way dip closures in the area are characterized by their low-relief nature, commonly spilling in strike direction (NW-SE). 3-way dip closures are bounded by NW-SE trending faults. 
These faults have an offset in the Lower-Zechstein, Rotliegendes and Carboniferous strata, but cannot be seen to extend into Upper-Zechstein halite and Triassic strata above.

This is a weak lead that centres around an apparent Maureen fan that appears to onlap onto the Base Tertiary. 
It is defined on legacy 2D seismic data. The prospective area lies south of the Scylla fairway in the southern part of block 8/5. As shown in Figure 20, the downlap is well defined on a
strike section. However on a dip section, a northerly pinchout is difficult to determine, mainly due to sparse coverage of lower quality 2D seismic. 
No volumes have been calculated. The lead is poorly defined and lacks a well-defined updip stratigraphic trap, additionally a lateral seal in the Mesozoic is also required as the lead lies unconformably on the Base Tertiary.

Lower Macduff is the second Upper Jurassic prospect defined in the Kimmeridge Fm. 
This play is characterized by the Miller-type sandy turbiditic deposits as seen in the downdip well 9/4A-2a well (oil shows). 
Lower Macduff is defined as the strati-structural trap at top J62; it is a 3-way closure against basement or fault escarpment with a spill point to the north at 4750m TVDSS. 
The two wells, 9/4a-2A and 9/5a-4 penetrated alternate sand-shale sequence and thin sand stringers in Kimmeridgian respectively. 
Considering the lack of seismic support for sands presence, the reservoir presence on Lower Macduff is the key risk. 
Lateral Seal is a relatively high risk as all along the trap structure, the juxtaposition of the J62 sands varies from place to place.
Untested four-way dip closure in the Maureen sands to the north of the 9/12-3 well.

Luna is a strati-structural trap at Upper Jurassic Volgian level.
The trap is defined by the up-dip stratigraphic pinch-out to the West-SW. The prospect is located to the Southwest of the producing Franklin field and Northern down dip of the Puffin discovery. 
The trap geometry is well defined by seismic mapping of top and base of the slumped geo-body. 
The extent of pinch-out of the Upper Jurassic Volgian gravity flows deposit is identified as a major uncertainty on the Luna prospect

At the time of application the Blodwyn lead was poorly defined on legacy 2D data, where structural closures were identified at BCU and Palaeozoic levels. 
With the new 3D seismic this lead matured into a prospect with stacked reservoirs in the Jurassic and Permian similar to the Wyvern concept. 
Both reservoir intervals have clearly defined structural closures, with the Jurassic also exhibiting stratigraphic trapping potential

Theo is an Upper Jurassic Fulmar lead that would target a stratigraphic trap on the Western flank of the Komodo high. 
On the new 3D seismic the pinchout/truncation of the Upper Jurassic package can be clearly mapped, but this does not derisk the presence of reservoir within the structure. Notable changes in seismic character occur towards the crest of Theo, but it has not been possible to attribute this to the presence of hydrocarbons. 
The disruption/brightening seen above the crest could be indicative of a gas chimney, but this would suggest that there is a seal/containment failure, which remains as the key risk for Theo.

Gaian West, Gecko and Icefyre identified during the interpretation of the new 3D data and are small structural traps targeting Fulmar sandstones. 
These structures have all benefited from the petroleum systems modelling that suggests they have received charge. 
Although these prospects/leads are lower risk, they are small shallow structures and any accumulation would be sub-economic.

Soup and Elliott were both defined as complex structural/stratigraphic traps in the Upper Jurassic, with Fulmar sandstones being the prognosed targets. 
These structures are now thought to be stratigraphic traps, but are high risk due to the difficulty in mapping the reservoir units and demonstrating a viable migration pathway.

Piers, Icefyre, Gila and Gecko were all identified during the interpretation of the new 3D seismic and are all structural traps at Top Palaeozoic level with primary reservoir being Permian Rotliegendes sandstones. All four leads appear to be robust structural closures, even Piers which extends south and west beyond the licence area and is therefore not fully covered by the 3D dataset. 
Icefyre and Gecko are favourably placed to receive charge and are below similar Jurassic structures, but even with the benefit of this their volumes remain sub-economic.
Demonstrating migration into Gila and Piers is possible via Dulcy, but again, any accumulation is likely to be subeconomic.

Lee was defined as a structural closure at Top Palaeozoic level with the primary reservoir being Permian Rotliegendes sandstones. 
The original structure was partially defined on 3D data, and this remains the case as the southern part of the lead extends beyond the licence area and is not covered by 3D. 
Given the low relief of the Lee structure, lack of 3D coverage and that it extends beyond the licence area, Lee was not recognised as a viable lead and no further evaluation has been conducted.

Monitor was identified during the interpretation of the new 3D data and is a structural trap in a downthrown fault terrace on the eastern side of the Komodo high. 
Primary target would be Upper Jurassic Fulmar sandstones.
The key risk in Monitor would be containment as reservoir would be juxtaposed against Palaeozoic sediments in the Komodo high, but the lead is also challenged as any accumulation would likely be sub-economic.

The original interpretation of Wyvern had reservoirs in the Upper Jurassic Fulmar sands, Zechstein carbonates and Rotliegendes sands. The prospect comprised two segments, an upthrown three-way fault dependent trap in the north (segment 1) and a downthrown faulted structure in the south (segment 2).
It was always recognised that there was considerable containment risk on the downthrown segment 2, and following re-interpretation on the reprocessed TOMO ML seismic, it was considered that segment 2 was no longer viable due to lack of fault seal. This re-evaluation was also applied to the southern bounding fault of segment 1, which was judged as unlikely to seal below the juxtaposition of the downthrown Jurassic/Zechstein against upthrown Permian reservoirs.
Conwy NW is a fault bounded structural prospect at both Upper Jurassic and Triassic levels located to the north of the Deep Banff gas and condensate discovery.
A small dip closed Ekofisk Chalk prospect was identified in the north of the license above a salt high, but recoverable resources are small.

Cretaceous - Numerous Lower Cretaceous leads over P.2101 were defined by the western most stratigraphic pinch out of the Punt age-equivalent sandstones. 
The up-dip offset well, 19/08-1 contains Punt age-equivalent sandstones that are interpreted to be shoreface sandstones that have been reworked by wave action. 
The key horizons used in these Lower Cretaceous lead evaluations are the BCU and the Top Valhall Marl. The Top Valhall Marl has been identified in the 19/10-1 from a synthetic well tie and was mapped across the P.2101 licence area where it represents an approximate Punt-equivalent age reflector. A thickness map between the Top Valhall Marl and the BCU shows the main westerly pinch-out can be separated into a number of scalloped shaped features, as shown in Fig. 5.7. 
The event at the BCU appears highly erosive in this area and is followed by sediment infill. However, down-dip offset well data does not indicate that Punt age equivalent sandstones are present and as a result has placed a high risk on reservoir presence.

FLETT FORMATION LEADS - The Cumberland are defined at T40 seismically, partially on 3D data but the critical up-dip fault closure is not fully covered by fully migrated 3D. The seismic pick used is the Top T40, which corresponds to the top of the Colsay Mbr., lava sequence, within which is siliciclastic sandstone in 164/25-1z
and 164/25-2. The tie to these wells is on good quality RR14 2D data and is robust.
No direct mapping of the reservoir interval is possible. Siliciclastic sandstone is present down-dip in 164/28-1A in the same seismic interval. Top and base seal is interbedded volcaniclastic claystone and is considered robust. The fault seal is juxtaposition of the Colsay Mbr., sequence and the sealing fault up-dip which is a significant risk, although
sealing faults in such sequences are proven (see Walker et al., 2013). The trap is formed by normal faulting in the Eocene, for which the downthrown block to the west is the Cumberland leads. Tilting from the Eocene to present formed the dip component, which dips westwards. 
Both leads are substantially the same, separated by a ~E-W trending normal fault. Migration is prognosed to be from the NERB to the west, where oil shows were encountered in 164/28-1A. 
There is no mapped stratigraphical or structural break between 164/28-1A and the leads.

A number of large undrilled leads have been mapped within the Carboniferous. 
These are four-way dip closed (and potentially stacked) structures, partially sub-cropping the Base Permian Unconformity (BPU), with Yoredale and Scremerston Formation reservoirs (analogue to the Breagh field). 
Top seal is a combination of BPU and Carboniferous intra-formational seal (analogue to the Pegasus field).

summary_comment:
The well 205/10-2B has found a 4m oil bearing sand just above the Base Tertiary. 
The sand is described as a fine grained sandstone, silty and partially calcareous cementation. The sample fluid is a light oil: 46 API, GOR 77m3/m3 according to available PVT Study. 
The oil accumulation penetrated by 205/10-2B well is considered to be limited. 
Although there is a regionally mapped, small 4 way dip closure around the well a review suggests that the discovery is a small, stratigraphically limited, ponded “pocket” of sand on a paleo-slope evidenced by the fact that the four nearby wells (205/10-1, 3,4 & 5) did not encounter sand. A preliminary evaluation of this oil sand indicates resources in the range of 1 to 5 MMboe.

Sleadale is a Royal Sovereign strati-structural trap defined by a 4 way component around its crest (at 5850m TVDSS) and a 3 way component combined with the pinch of the Royal Sovereign on the Flett ridge. 
Spill is at 6230m to the SE towards Craster structure.

The Gasta 4-way structure was subject to detailed mapping and fault picking. The structure comprises a NE-SW trending anticline cross cut by a dominant WNW-ESE to NW-SE fault trend dividing the structure into two tilted fault blocks referred to as North Gasta and South Gasta.

The Te-3 lead was identified as a NW-SE trending channel feature in Balmoral Sandstone Unit. Spectral decomposition as well as differential compaction evidently show the extent of the sand channel. 
Well 20/05b- 12 was drilled downdip of the lead to the east and encountered sandstone, however with no shows at this interval. Given this interval is sand-rich in this area, a significant risk of lateral seal failure is considered.

The Bruson prospect is located immediately to the east of Hannay field (ceased production) and to the south of Finlay discovery (well 15/26b- 9) which encountered oil in the Upper Jurassic, Sgiath Formation (J52) Sandstone Member. The top of reservoir sandstone is seismically mappable as an amplitude anomaly just above the Pentland Formation coal, analogous to the J2 (well 20/05a- 10Y) and Finlay oil discoveries.

The Ju-1 lead was identified on an amplitude anomaly observed in Upper Jurassic interval, where it is stratigraphically trapped. 
Well 20/05b- 3 was drilled within 1km to the south of the lead and encountered no sandstone in Upper Jurassic interval. Therefore, reservoir presence is perceived a key risk for this lead.

The Ju-2 lead is defined in Upper Jurassic Burns Sandstone Member with a stratigraphic trap. 
The Ju-3 lead is located to the north of lead Ju-1 and ca 2 Km north of well 21/05b- 3. Similar to Ju-1, reservoir presence is considered a key risk for this lead given well 20/05b- 3 encountered no sandstone (apart from minor stringers) in the Upper Jurassic interval and meanwhile, the lead location does not present sufficient accommodation space for sediments as observed on the Upper Jurassic thickness map.

The back-basin lead was originally defined in Upper Jurassic, Burns Sandstone Member, with a three-way dip closure trapped against a north easterly fault close to 20/05b- 3. 
The new PGS 3D seismic data reveals a different fault structures than that originally mapped on the CGG 3D seismic data. On the new mapping, JOG did not interpret a three-way dip closure and therefore, the validity of a trapping mechanism is questionable

The Doughnut lead was originally defined in Upper Jurassic Piper Formation Sandstone forming a ring shape around a mini basin, where it is stratigraphically trapped with a pinch out. In the original imaging, a fault separates the sandstone from that observed in well 20/05b- 12, however in the revised imaging using the PGS seismic, there is no evidence to separate well 20/05b- 12 from the lead area, and since this well is water bearing at Piper Sandstone level, it is perceived hydrocarbon charge represents a significant risk.

The prospect 44/19-3 Upside lies north of the 44/19-3 Discovery separated by an E-W fault. 
The reservoir consists of the Upper Ketch sandstones only. The FWL 3651m is taken equal to the 44/19-3 Discovery. There is a reservoir effectiveness risk for the Upper Ketch.

The NW North Valiant exploration lead is a low relief, undeveloped fault block to the northwest of the PD segment and southeast of the Frigate structure, and hence 
outside the P.033 licence but within the North Valiant Field area in P.008. It is separated from the North Valiant Field and the Frigate structure by two NNE-SSW trending De Keyser fault lineaments labelled DKN and DKS.

The SP07/02 well was drilled in 1991 to develop the SP Southeast segment. The well was drilled close to a De Keyser fault, and the near-well region may have suffered 
enhanced diagenesis. 
The well was completed in the poor-quality Zone A and Zone B sandstones. Zone C is below the GWC in SP Southeast.

Victor North East is a small, tilted fault block which is entirely below the Victor Field gas water contact and has an estimated P50 gas-in-place of 53 Bscf unrisked. 
Key risks are fault seal and the possibility of depletion through the aquifer. 
In the low case, the structure could be wet with no gas in place.

Glengorm Deep is evaluated as a 2-segment, 4-way faulted anticline, with predicted reservoirs in the Upper Triassic Skagerrak Group sands (Judy Fm.). 
The source rocks are anticipated to be organic shales and coals of the Mid Jurassic Pentland Fm.  
It is also possible that there is secondary charge from the Upper Jurassic Heather Fm. 
The shale-dominated lower Pentland Fm forms the main top seal to the prospect anticline.

trap_type_comment:
Plunging Horst structure with Jonathan Mudstone, in addition to the overlying Jurassic sequence, acting as a southerly side-seal in the sand-on shale fault juxtaposition. 
Top seal is controlled by overlying Jonathan Mudstone, which is proven to be robust as acting top seal in Jade Central Horst.
hc_case_comment: Jade Central Horst gas condensate / volatile oil analogue
summary_comment: Large untested plunging horst, similar to the Western Central Horst Jade field. Targeting the Joanne reservoir, which is producing from the Jade field. Expected fluids are gas condensate, with a compositional gradient controlled by column height. The Jade Field HDT established by 30/2c-J12z is below a structural saddle which connects the prospect to the Jade Central Horst, however seismically interpreted faulting in the saddle and reservoir quality at depth leave charge into the structure a risk along with seal and retention.

The Hidden Rose lead is a low relief BPU closure located to the very southern extent of the P2126 licence. 
The crest of the lead is within in the Breagh licence. The reservoir is anticipated to be Middle Limestone below the BPU.

The Aurora West lead is a fault compartmentalised feature, which is difficult to close at the BPU level. 
The Fell Sandstone target is reliant on unlikely fault-seal to the north, where the Fell Sandstone is juxtaposed against the Fell Sandstone.

The Aurora South prospect is a hanging-wall fault block to the south of the Aurora East horst. The trap requires fault seal to the North against the SCF and is 3-way dip closed to the South, East and West. 
The main reservoir is the Yoredale Fm. which has a top seal partly against the BPU (Zechstein Group) and partly against Upper Carboniferous shales.

The Bonnie Brae prospect is an off-platform, isolated sulphate mound with a Hauptdolomit carbonate buildup draped on top. The Hauptdolomit has been mapped as a 4-way dip closure, sealed by the overlying Zechstein evaporites. 
It is estimated that the prospect has received charge from the underlying Carboniferous Scremerston Fm. and potentially a minor charge contribution from an intra-Zechstein source 
rock. The key risk associated with the Bonnie Brae prospect is reservoir effectiveness.
