Both the Alpha and Alpha East prospects are injectite wing features within the Eocene Frigg formation host shale.
Both wings straddle the 9/9f and 9/14d block boundary. These injectite prospects appear disconnected on lithology inversion datasets although a small possibility remains that these units connect to one another via sub-seismic sands. 
Both prospects are near to the 9/9d-17 exploration well, drilled in 1997, which found wet Balder sands and did not encounter sand in the Frigg injectite target interval.

The Plantain South prospect is an Upper Frigg geobody that shows similar seismic characteristics to the Agar discovery. 
The Upper Frigg geobody is located updip of the Agar OWC and also requires a stratigraphic trap. There are also some Lower Frigg geobodies identified. These are considered higher risk because there is potential for connection to water wet sands updip.

Kinlochaline: A fault bounded structural closure in between the Janus and Gylen prospects. 
The closure exists at the Fulmar and Pentland levels as well. 
Kinlochaline is interpreted to be compartmentalised with internal faults.

Structure X is a smaller ‘sibling’ structure of Callanish and shares the same reservoir and seal characteristics. It is bounded by two normal faults. Structure X sits at a water depth of ~1250m with the crest of the structure at 4430mSS. The structure spills into North-Uist at 5390mSS. The ultimate top seal is a thick section of Cretaceous shales (up to 1800m thickness). The reservoir is considered HP/HT. 
Structure X is located between Callanish and North Uist on the ‘fill-to spill’ migration pathway and so if Callanish was fully charged, hydrocarbons would spill into Structure X. The two structures are fully dependent in terms of risk and volume uncertainty.

The Westphalian subcrops the BPU in a north-easterly thinning wedge. Sediments in the subcrop are considered to be Westphalian A in age. The nearest wells show moderate to poor reservoir quality in thinly interbedded sands, shales and coals. The Westphalian A is very thick but NTG is less than 50% and sand connectivity is likely to be mostly poor. 
A small structural closure exists, at the BPU; the potential for larger closures is limited by continued spill of structure to the NW. Seal potential at the BPU is linked to reservoir development in the Leman sand.

Blue Sky IV is an oil and gas lead, comprised of Sele Sandstone Formation turbidite slope canyon sands in a stratigraphic trap. 
It is seen as a seismic anomaly to the west of Blue Sky III that is separated by a structural spill point and low amplitude zone. 
The extent of the reservoir is interpreted to be defined by seismic amplitudes and inversion lithology prediction. It is possible that the bright far-angle PSTM seismic amplitudes may define the hydrocarbon extent

The Browney North prospect is mapped as a small, faulted four way dip closure to the NW of the Browney discovery. 
The top structure ( Figure 5 2) is mapped as the top of the gas bearing sand in well 43/18-1.  
The top seal is assumed to be within the Langsettian shales above the reservoir.

hc_case_comment: High confidence in oil in the success case
summary_comment: The Fleetwing structure was interpreted to be the most promising prospect given its proximity to the mature source rocks in the West Central Graben, and comprised a four-way with an additional column upside potential provided by a small fault on its southwest side. Fault seal analysis was performed on the fault, which suggested a 30% chance of sealing; however, the fault is small- tipping out to beyond the limits of seismic resolution within a short distance from the maximum throw and showed a complex interaction with other faults and salt withdrawal-based structuration, so it was unclear how much weight could be placed on this upside.

summary_comment: The Hawkstone structure was entirely a stratigraphic trap, relying on lateral/top seal along the south side of the Greeves Container.

Another infill opportunity is seen in a block east of Amethyst East and west of Medina. 
The block is triangular in shape with strong fault definition on the northern and southern sides but discontinuous fault closure on the east side adjacent to the Medina block. The exploration well 47/15- 2 sits in this block and proves gas at Leman level. A GDT of 2670 m TVDss was used in the P90 case. Should the faults separating this block from Medina not be sealing and a GWC of 2703 m TVDss be used, the East and Medina prospects are joined.

Asland North Deep is a prospect identified in the Pre-Triassic interval, located in the northern part of Block 110/9a. The reservoir is identified as Permian fluvio-aeolian sandstones of the Collyhurst Sandstone, sealed by the Cumbrian Coast Group and sourced by the same Carboniferous shales as the Triassic reservoirs in the area. The structure has been constrained with 3D seismic data and reservoir and seal quality estimation is based on regional studies of the Collyhurst and nearby wells as control points.
Asland North Deep is a small three-way closure on a southern, downthrown terrace of the Deemster Platform, partly within Block 110/9a. It is sealed to the east against the East Deemster Fault. Depending upon the sealing potential of the South Deemster Fault and the depth of the hydrocarbon contact there is a possibility Asland North Deep is in communication with the Kappa-Asland Permian Lead to the south.

A steep to vertical Chalk raft may be present on the northeast flank of the salt diapir.
The raft would need to lie between the 22/27a-3 and -3Z wells and a structural restoration study in 2004 concluded that this was an unlikely scenario, and that the structure of the Chalk on the NE side of the diapir is not a raft but is the steep limb of a fold generated by salt movement.

summary_comment:
Gair well 9/18-43 found Beryl formation at higher pressure than the Garten Filed. An oil water contact was identified at -12,706 ft tvdss, nearly 1000 shallower than the 9/18-41Z ODT (-13,650 ft tvdss). The fault between Garten and Gair is clearly sealing. In 9/18-43Z the Beryl was wet and no successful formation pressures were obtained.
The shallower contact in Gair is explained as a result of partial seal failure along the western bounding fault to Garten and Gair across which the Garten and Gair reservoirs are juxtaposed against the Triassic of the Beryl Field horst block. These result only impact the Gair area prospectivity.
Insufficient hydrocarbon found at Gair for completion. Shallow contacts at Gair indicate it must be separated from Garten by a sealing fault.

The presence of a valid trap at Ada West is unlikely, with the apparent structure being produced as a result of imaging artefacts below the E-W trending salt wall.
Recoverable volumes from an Ada West well could be very low, based on regional analogues.
Review of the development concepts and facilities required makes Ada West unattractive.

This lead is a small but robust 4-way closure on top of the L Jurassic Statfjord Group. 
The main reservoir objectives are Statfjord Group continental clastics and the underlying continental Triassic. 
An adjacent well, 211/2-1, was drilled below the prognosed spill point, but had very low gross sand intervals, which were tight, fine-grained and not massive. 
The calculated volumes are probably too optimistic section with respect to the sand quality, so quality of reservoir is clearly a very high risk. 
The middle Jurassic and Lower Cretaceous shales will be a good regional top-seal, and charge will have a significant risk as the structure may be in a migration shadow, situated as it is behind a spur of the Albert Tryggvason structure.

The apex of the closure is 3802mMSL with a mapped spill point of 3959m, giving a column height of 154m. 
The total area is 7.2km2  and the resulting in-place volumes are significantly larger than the 'A' lead. 
There is again a large uncertainty on reservoir parameters and the same inputs were used as in Lead 'A'.

Seismic mapping on the TGS data revealed the presence of a closure at the Upper Jurassic level, termed the ‘Boatswain’ prospect. The 13/21a-1A well (1990 West Wick exploration well and a dry hole at Jurassic level) is the closest offset well to Boatswain (~100 m from the crest) and plays a critical role in understanding the prospect’s risk profile. Seismic interpretation, factoring in well positional and depth uncertainty, suggests that the -1A well drilled the hanging wall side of the Jurassic fault block (potentially a slumped crestal block), and therefore did not test the Boatswain Upper Jurassic closure. All other wells on the block reached TD in the Lower Cretaceous interval.
Boatswain is mapped as a 2-way structural trap bounded by two faults (Figure 7), located within a recognised Oxfordian shallow-marine fairway which trends East – West along the western extent of the Halibut Horst. The reservoir likely consists of fluvio-deltaic sands of the Oxfordian-age Ross Sandstone Member (a proven reservoir in the greater Captain area), with charge occurring from the Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation.

After receiving the reprocessed 2D data, clinoforming geometries within closures of up to 100 ms were identified. They are the Anne Bonny Prospect  with follow up leads Black Beard and Calico Jack.

The Southern Fault Block does not have a well within it to prove, or otherwise, whether the contact is the same, but the appearance of the fault on seismic is suggests that this block is also a non-communicating compartment. Depending on where within the block a well was to be placed, there is potential it could be drilled from the platform but the volumes are marginal (27 Bcf), especially considering the poor historical production of the field likely due to the poor reservoir conditions.

This opportunity is only a lead at this stage and would require a lot of further work before it could be progressed. It is a low relief area to the south of the main structure. The low relief means that structural uncertainty is crucial - a surface 20 m deeper reduces the Gas in Place from 44 Bcf to an uneconomic 13 Bcf. The lead is outside the drilling window of the Galahad Platform so would need to be a sub-sea development. Considering the reservoir conditions, the well would need to be stimulated which is cost prohibitive in a sub-sea development.

The Dordogne prospect is an extension of Bordeaux to the west. It appears to be separated from Bordeaux by the 14/18-4 well but could share the same oil-water contact. The crest of the stratigraphic trap is at about 8350 and has over 700 ft of relief from the water-up-to in 14/18-4. An exploration well is required to prove up this area and hence the focus was on Bordeaux.

Bader North is a smaller separate basement depth structural closure, mapped to the north-east of the structure drilled by Well 205/23-3A (Halifax). 
Given the disappointing results of the recent Hurricane Energy activity along the Rona Ridge, this opportunities is considered to be a high risk prospect.

• Lead G is a 3-way dip closed structure, fully covered by 3D seismic data, and is mapped as a Scremerston prospect. It is, however, difficult to characterise / interpret as it coincides with a poorly resolved structure in the foot-wall, beneath the salt high and collapse zone. 
• By analogy with other structures against the EW fault believe it is likely to be a small 3-way dip closed structure
• The well 44/8-1z is difficult to tie as it penetrates a fault section at this level. It had some gas shows

The structuration of the Orchid discovery is caused by a similar catastrophic slumping of platformal units into the basin as the Centurion complex and thus stands to reason that there is also deeper potential in the Jurassic. However, the seismic facies across Orchid Deep is highly transparent and lacking any notable internal reflections, which tends to be characteristic of the Smith Bank Formation shales, suggesting reservoir presence is a considerable risk. 
Furthermore, well 28/5a-4 on the platform is located just up-dip from where the sediments making up the Orchid deep structure would have initially been deposited, also failed to encounter any reservoir prone intervals, thus increasing the reservoir risk than based on seismic alone.

The Challenger structure was a small 4-way that becomes potentially a faulted 3-way depending on interpretation (it may just be folded due to the salt withdrawal). Given the contours of the Fulmar map, it was difficult to consider a stratigraphic upside without it leaking up-dip to Silverstone structure.

Silverstone is a small 4-way with potential stratigraphic upside beyond the drawn polygon against the western edge of the Greeves container. If Smith Bank Formation was 
present around it, providing adequate seal, it would fill eastwards towards Challenger, potentially containing relatively large volumes.

Similar to the Pegasus West discovery, the Pegasus North flank prospect relies on a combination BPU and intra-carboniferous seal trap. It corresponds to the remanent section of Westphalian A-Upper most Namurian age sediments left following BPU erosion on the flank of the Pegasus North discovery.

Well 43/13b-7, drilled by Centrica in 2014, is the second well drilled by the Joint Venture in the GPA and penetrated a gas charged lower Westphalian A to Namurian C section and a separate Namurian A accumulation within the Pegasus West segment, see Figure 27 and Figure 28. The shallowest three (Westphalian A - Namurian C) gas bearing sandstones, with moderate to good reservoir quality, were tested individually, yielding a combined flow rate of 92 MMScf/d and an estimated minimum connected volume of approximately 50 Bscf. 
These upper three sandstones lie on the same pressure gradient and share a common free water level. 
The trap for the Pegasus West discovery is a tilted fault block forming a truncated 4-way dip closure with an element of fault seal against the Cavendish-Murdoch fault. The trap requires a combination of BPU and intra-Carboniferous sealing in order to retain the gas column observed in the well.

Similar to the Pegasus West discovery, the Pegasus East flank prospect relies on a combination BPU and intra-Carboniferous seal. It corresponds to the remanent section of Westphalian A and uppermost Namurian age sediments left by the BPU erosion on the flank of the Pegasus East discovery

Additional upside potential exists in the intervals located above and below the Pegasus West discovery:
The well did not penetrate deep enough to test the age-equivalent Westphalian section encountered in the reservoir bearing interval of the 43/13b-7 well, but if the intra-Carboniferous seal lies stratigraphically above the 43/12-1 well sands, they have the potential to be gas-bearing updip and to share the same common contact as the 43/13b-7 well sands.
Gas-bearing sandstones were identified in Alportian age (Secondary Play) sandstones in the 43/13b-7 well.

The Andromeda South Prospect lies within the licence P2128 and is located on the southern side of the CM fault, separated from the Andromeda North discovery by that lineament. 
It is defined as a 3-way dip closure, bound to the North by the CM fault and at least partly traversed by a subsidiary WNW-ESE trending fault that may have the potential to compartmentalise the prospect. Both the primary and secondary play of Andromeda South have been identified as prospective. The main risk element for the primary play opportunity is the CM Fault Zone and whether it provides an effective seal. If the fault is open, such that Andromeda North and South are in communication, no accumulation can exist in the Andromeda South prospect, as the Andromeda North free water level (FWL) lies close to the level of the Andromeda South crest. The secondary play is seen as very high risk due to the lack of gas in the same intervals in the Andromeda North discovery.

summary_comment: Pensacola gas prospect is a Permian Zechstein Hauptdolomite off-platform carbonate build up. The well targets a pronounced top reservoir seismic soft event on its western fringe, assumed to represent platform facies dominated by porous oolitic grainstones. The Hauptdolomite is the only objective level. Key field analogues are the Crosgan gas discovery (block 42/15) and various Hauptdolomite off-platform highs in Germany and Poland. The 2019 Hauptdolomite Ossian oil-gas discovery (well 42/04-1/1Z) is considered partially analogous.

Thunderstorm is a combination trap situated on a terrace area bounded to the north and south by prominent, approximately east-west trending faults. 
Simple dip closure defines the eastern prospect boundary and a shale-out of the target reservoir interval - Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous ‘Scapa-Birch’ turbiditic sandstones - is invoked as the western trap boundary. 
The trap has a crest of 6475 ft TVDSS and closing contour along its eastern margin of 7670 ft TVDSS.
The depth of the closing contour is limited by the 14/29-1 well which encountered water-wet Scapa-Birch sandstones.
